breaths.text: When Erdosain opened the door to the manager’s office, its panes of Japanese glass, he wanted to step back; he understood that he was lost, but it was already too late.

They were waiting for him: the director, a short, thickset man with a boar’s head, grey hair cut “à la Humberto I,” and an implacable gaze filtering through pupils as grey as a fish’s; Gualdi, the accountant, small, thin, honeyed, with scrutinizing eyes; and the sub-manager, son of the boar-headed man, a handsome fellow of thirty with completely white hair, cynical in appearance, a harsh voice and a hard stare like his father’s.

These three figures—the director bent over some ledgers, the sub-manager lounging in an armchair with one leg swinging over the back, and Mr. Gualdi standing respectfully beside the desk—did not return Erdosain’s greeting.
Only the sub-manager bothered to lift his head.
“We have received a complaint that you are a swindler, that you have stolen six hundred pesos from us. ”
“Six hundred and seven centavos,” added Mr. Gualdi as he passed a blotter over the signature the director had just initialled on a sheet.
Then the director, as if making a great effort with his bull’s neck, raised his eyes.

With his fingers hooked between the buttonholes of his waistcoat, he cast a shrewd look at Erdosain through half-closed lids, examining without rancour the emaciated face of the man who stood before him, impassive.
“Why are you so badly dressed?
” he asked.
“I earn nothing as a collector. ”
“And the money you stole from us? ”
“I haven’t stolen anything.
It’s all lies. ”
“Then you are in a position to render accounts? ”
“If you wish, today at noon. ”
The answer saved him for the moment.
The three men consulted one another with their eyes, and at last the sub-manager, shrugging his shoulders, said with his father’s consent:
“No... you have until tomorrow at three.
Bring the ledgers and the receipts...
You may go. ”
The decision surprised him so much that he remained standing there sadly, looking at the three of them.
Yes, at all three.

At Mr. Gualdi, who had so often humiliated him despite being a socialist; at the sub-manager, who had insolently fixed his eyes on his frayed tie; at the director, whose stiff, close-cropped boar’s head turned toward him, filtering a cynical and obscene glance through the grey slit of his half-closed eyelids.
Yet Erdosain did not move from the spot...

He wanted to tell them something, he did not know how, but something that would make them understand the immense misfortune weighing upon his life; and so he remained, standing, sad, with the black cube of the iron safe before his eyes, feeling his back curve more and more as the minutes passed, while he nervously twisted the brim of his black hat and his gaze grew ever more fugitive and sorrowful. Then, abruptly, he asked:
“So I can go? ”
Hand the receipts to Suárez and be here tomorrow at three without fail, with everything. ”
“Yes... everything...
” And turning, he left without saying goodbye.
He walked down Chile Street as far as Paseo Colón.
He felt himself invisibly cornered.
The sun exposed the filthy interiors of the sloping street.
Different thoughts swarmed inside him, so dissimilar that classifying them would have taken him many hours.
Later he remembered that it had not occurred to him even for an instant to wonder who could have denounced him.
He knew he was a thief.
But the category in which he placed himself did not interest him.
Perhaps the word thief was not in keeping with his inner state.

There existed another feeling, and that was the circular silence that had entered like a steel cylinder into the mass of his skull, leaving him deaf to everything that did not relate to his misfortune.

This circle of silence and darkness interrupted the continuity of his ideas, so that Erdosain could not associate, with the downward slope of his reasoning, his home called house with an institution designated by the name of prison.
He thought telegraphically, suppressing prepositions, which is enervating.
He knew dead hours in which he could have committed a crime of any nature without having the slightest notion of his responsibility.
Logically, a judge would not have understood such a phenomenon.
But he was already empty, a husk of a man moved by the automatism of habit.

If he continued working at the Sugar Company it was not to steal more sums of money, but because he awaited an extraordinary event—immensely extraordinary—that would give an unexpected turn to his life and save him from the catastrophe he saw approaching his door.
This atmosphere of dream and unease that made him move through the days like a sleepwalker, Erdosain called “the zone of anguish. ”

Erdosain imagined that this zone existed above the level of cities, two meters in the air, and it appeared to him graphically in the form of those regions of salt flats or deserts that on maps are indicated by ovals of dots, as dense as the roe of a herring.
This zone of anguish was the consequence of men’s suffering.

And like a cloud of poisonous gas it moved heavily from one point to another, penetrating walls and passing through buildings without losing its flat, horizontal shape; a two-dimensional anguish that, by guillotining throats, left in them an aftertaste of sobbing.
Such was the explanation Erdosain gave himself when he felt the first nauseas of sorrow.
“What am I doing with my life?

” he would say to himself then, perhaps wishing to clarify with this question the origins of the anxiety that made him long for an existence in which tomorrow would not be the continuation of today with its measure of time, but something different and always unexpected, as in the developments of American films, where yesterday’s beggar is today the head of a secret society, and the adventurous typist a multimillionaire incognito.

This need for wonders that had no possible satisfactions—since he was a failed inventor and a criminal on the edge of prison—left in his subsequent brooding a furious acidity and teeth sensitive as after chewing lemon.
In these circumstances he would put together absurdities.
He came to imagine that the rich, bored with hearing the complaints of the wretched, had built tremendous cages that teams of horses dragged along.

Executioners chosen for their strength hunted the sad with dog-catching lassos, and a certain scene became visible to him: a tall, disheveled mother ran after the cage from which, between the bars, her one-eyed son called to her, until a “dog-catcher,” tired of hearing her scream, knocked her unconscious with blows to the head from the handle of his lasso.
Once this nightmare had faded, Erdosain would say to himself, horrified at himself:
“But what soul, what soul is this that I have?

” And as his imagination retained the motor impulse the nightmare had given it, he continued: “I must have been born to be a footman, one of those perfumed and vile footmen with whom rich prostitutes have their brassiere hooks fastened while the lover smokes a cigar reclining on the sofa. ”
And again his thoughts would bounce back into a kitchen situated in the basement of a most luxurious mansion.
Around the table moved two maids, besides the chauffeur and an Arab seller of garters and perfumes.
In that circumstance he would wear a black jacket that did not quite cover his backside, and a little white tie.
Suddenly “the master,” a man who was his physical double but who did not shave his mustache and wore glasses, would call him.
He did not know what his employer wanted of him, yet he would never forget the singular look the man gave him as he left the room.

And he would return to the kitchen to talk of filth with the chauffeur who, to the delight of the maids and the silence of the pederastic Arab, told how he had corrupted the daughter of a great lady, a little creature of few years. And he would repeat to himself again:
“Yes, I am a footman.
I have the soul of a true footman,” and he would clench his teeth with satisfaction at insulting and degrading himself in that way before his own eyes.

At other times he saw himself coming out of the bedroom of an old, devout spinster, carrying with unction a heavy chamber pot, but at that moment a priest who was a regular visitor to the house would meet him and, smiling, unruffled, would say to him:
“How are we doing with our religious duties, Ernesto?
” And he, Ernesto, Ambrosio or José, would live a grim life as an obscene and hypocritical servant.
A tremor of madness shook him when he thought of this.
He knew—ah, how well he knew!—that he was gratuitously offending, soiling his soul.
And the terror that a man feels in a nightmare when he falls into an abyss in which he will not die, that terror he suffered while he deliberately went on covering himself with mud.

For at times his urge was toward humiliation, like that of the saints who kissed the sores of the unclean; not out of compassion, but to make themselves more unworthy of God’s pity, who would feel disgusted to see them seeking heaven with proofs so repugnant.
But when those images disappeared from him and only the “desire to know the meaning of life” remained in his consciousness, he would say to himself:
“No, I am not a footman... truly I am not...
” and he would have liked to go and beg his wife to take pity on him, to have mercy on his thoughts that were so horrible and low.
Yet the memory that because of her he had been forced to sacrifice himself so many times filled him with a dull rancor, and in those circumstances he would have liked to kill her.
And he knew very well that one day she would give herself to another, and that was one more added element among the other factors that composed his anguish.

Thus when he first embezzled twenty pesos, he was astonished at the ease with which one could do “that,” perhaps because before stealing he had believed he would have to overcome a series of scruples that in his present conditions of life he could not even know. He would say to himself afterward:
“It’s just a matter of having the will and doing it, nothing more. ”
And “that” made life easier; with “that” he had money that caused him strange sensations because it cost him nothing to earn it.
And what was astonishing to Erdosain was not the theft itself, but that it did not show in his face that he was a thief.
He had been forced to steal because he earned a meager monthly salary.
Eighty, a hundred, a hundred and twenty pesos, for this amount depended on the sums collected, since his pay consisted of a commission on every hundred collected.

Thus there were days when he carried four or five thousand pesos, while he, poorly fed, had to endure the stench of a fake-leather wallet in whose interior happiness lay heaped in the form of banknotes, checks, drafts and bearer orders.
His wife reproached him for the privations she endured every day; he listened in silence to her complaints and later, alone, would say to himself:
“What can I do? ”
When he had the idea, when a tiny idea assured him that he could defraud his employers, he felt the joy of an inventor.
Steal?
Why had it not occurred to him before?

And Erdosain was astonished at his own incapacity, even reproaching himself for lack of initiative, for at that time (three months before the events narrated) he suffered needs of every kind, despite the fact that large sums of money passed through his hands every day.
And what facilitated his fraudulent maneuvers was the lack of administration that existed in the Sugar Company.
There was no doubt that his life was strange, for at times a hasty hope would fling him out into the street.
Then he would catch a bus and get off in Palermo or Belgrano.
He would walk pensively along the silent avenues, telling himself:
–Some maiden will see me, a tall, pale, serious girl who, on a whim, drives her Rolls-Royce.
She will be driving sadly.
Suddenly she looks at me and understands that I will be the one love of her entire life, and that gaze, which was an insult to all the wretched, will rest upon me, her eyes filled with tears.

The daydream unspooled from this foolishness while he slowly slipped along in the shade of the tall façades and the green plane trees, whose shadows broke into triangles on the white mosaic pavements.
–She will be a millionairess, but I will tell her: “Miss, I cannot touch you.
Even if you wanted to give yourself to me, I would not take you.
” She will look at me in surprise; then I will say to her: “And it is all useless, you know?
It is useless, because I am married.
” But she will offer Elsa a fortune so that she will divorce me, and then we will marry, and we will sail away to Brazil on her yacht.

And the simplicity of this dream was enriched by the name Brazil, which, harsh and hot, projected before him a pink-and-white coast cutting with sharp edges and perpendiculars into a tenderly blue sea.
By now the maiden had lost her tragic stiffness and was –beneath the white silk of her simple dress, like that of a schoolgirl– a smiling creature, at once timid and daring. And Erdosain thought:
–We will never have sexual contact.
To make our love more lasting, we will restrain desire, and I will not even kiss her on the mouth, only on the hand.
And he imagined the happiness that would purify his life if such an impossible thing were to happen, but it was easier to stop the earth in its course than to make such an absurdity real.
Then he would tell himself, saddened by a vague courage:
–All right, I will be a pimp. –And suddenly a horror more terrible than all the other horrors would unscrew his conscience.
He had the sensation that every notch in his soul was bleeding as if under the bit of a lathe, and with his understanding paralyzed, dulled by anguish, he would go in mad search of brothels.
Then he knew the terror of the fraud, the luminous terror that is like the explosion of a great sunny day on the convexity of a saltpeter bed.

He let himself be dragged along by the impulses that twist a man who for the first time feels himself at the gates of prison, blind impulses that lead the wretched to stake their lives on a card or on a woman.

Perhaps seeking in the card and in the female a brutal and sad consolation, perhaps seeking in everything that is most vile and sunken a certain certainty of purity that would save him once and for all.
And in the hot hours of the siesta, under the yellow sun, he walked along the mosaic sidewalks still warm in search of the filthiest whorehouses.
He chose preferably those whose entrance halls showed orange peels and trails of ash, and windows covered with red or green baize protected by wire mesh.
He entered with death in his soul.

In the patio, beneath the squared blue sky, there was usually a single bench painted ochre, and onto it he would drop exhausted, enduring the glacial stare of the madam while he waited for the girl to appear, a woman horribly thin or horribly fat.
And the harlot would shout to him from the half-open bedroom door, inside which one could hear the noise of a man getting dressed:
–Shall we go, darling? –and Erdosain would enter the other bedroom, his ears ringing and a swirling mist in his pupils.
Then he would lie down on the bed varnished the color of liver, on top of the blankets soiled by boots that protected the bedspread.

Suddenly he would feel like crying, like asking that horrible dark woman what love was, the angelic love that the celestial choirs sang at the foot of the throne of the living God, but anguish stopped up his larynx while his stomach clenched like a fist with disgust.
And while the prostitute let her restless hand rest on his clothes, Erdosain would say to himself:
–What have I done with my life?

A slanting ray of sun cut across the glass of the fanlight covered with spiderwebs, and the harlot, with her cheek resting on the pillow and one leg thrown over his, slowly moved her hand while he, saddened, said to himself:
–What have I done with my life?

Suddenly remorse would darken his soul; he would remember his wife who, for lack of money, had to wash the clothes herself even though she was ill, and then, sickened by himself, he would leap from the bed, hand the money to the prostitute, and without having used her, flee toward another hell to spend money that did not belong to him, to sink himself deeper into his madness that howled at every hour.
At ten in the morning Erdosain reached the corner of Perú and Avenida de Mayo.
He knew his problem had no other solution but prison, because Barsut would surely not give him the money.
Suddenly he was surprised.
At a table in a café sat the pharmacist Ergueta.
With his hat pulled down to his ears and his thumbs touching over his thick belly, he was nodding off with a sour, bloated expression on his yellow face.
The glassy look in his bulging eyes, his thick hooked nose, the flaccid cheeks and the lower lip almost hanging down gave him the appearance of a cretin.
He had crammed his massive body into a cinnamon-colored suit, and from time to time he would tilt his face and rest his teeth on the ivory handle of his cane.
Because of that listlessness and the low-life expression of his boredom, he looked like a white-slave trafficker.
Unexpectedly his eyes met those of Erdosain, who was walking toward him, and the pharmacist’s face lit up with a childish smile.
He was still smiling when he shook Erdosain’s hand, and Erdosain thought:
“How many women must have loved him for that smile! ”
Involuntarily, Erdosain’s first question was:
“So, did you marry Hipólita? ”
“Yes, but you can’t imagine the row that broke out at home... ”
“What... did they find out she was ‘on the game’? ”
“No... she told them that later.
You know Hipólita worked as a servant before she ‘walked the streets,’ right? ”
“And? ”
“Shortly after we got married, Mom, Hipólita, my little sister and I went to visit a family.
Can you believe the memory those people have?
After ten years they recognized Hipólita as the girl who had been their servant.
Something that has no name!
She and I came back by one road and Mom and Juana by another.
The whole story I had invented to justify my marriage collapsed. ”
“And why did she confess she had been a prostitute? ”
“A moment of rage.
But wasn’t she right?
Hadn’t she reformed?
Didn’t she put up with me, with me, who has given them all gray hairs? ”
“And how are things going for you? ”
“Very well...
The pharmacy brings in seventy pesos a day.
In Pico there’s no one else who knows the Bible the way I do.
I challenged the priest to a debate and he wouldn’t take me up on it. ”
Erdosain suddenly looked at his strange friend with renewed hope. Then he asked:
“Do you still gamble? ”
“Yes, and Jesus, because of my great innocence, has revealed to me the secret of the roulette wheel. ”
“What is it? ”
“You don’t know... the great secret... a law of static synchronism...
I’ve already been to Montevideo twice and won a lot of money, but tonight Hipólita and I are leaving to break the bank. ”
And suddenly he launched into the tangled explanation:
“Look, you bet a hypothetical amount on the first three spins, one on each dozen.
If three different dozens don’t come up, an imbalance is necessarily produced.
You then mark with a dot the dozen that came up.
For the next three spins the dozen you marked will remain the same.
Of course zero doesn’t count and you bet on dozens in series of three spins.

You then increase one unit on the dozen that doesn’t have any cross, you decrease by one, I mean by two units, the dozen that has three crosses, and this single base allows you to deduce the smallest unit from the largest ones and you play the difference on the dozen or dozens that result. ”
Erdosain had not understood.
He held back his desire to laugh as his hope grew, for it was undeniable that Ergueta was mad. So he replied:
“Jesus knows how to reveal those secrets to those whose souls are full of holiness. ”
“And also to idiots,” Ergueta argued, fixing him with a mocking look while winking his left eyelid.
“Since I started dealing with these mysterious things I’ve made blunders as big as houses—for example, marrying that slut... ”
“And are you happy with her? ”
“...believing in the goodness of people, when everyone is only trying to sink you and make you look crazy... ”
Erdosain, impatient, frowned, then said:
“How can you expect them not to think you’re crazy?
According to your own words you were a great sinner.

And suddenly you convert, you marry a prostitute because it’s written in the Bible; you talk to people about the fourth seal and the yellow horse... of course... people have to think you’re crazy because they don’t even know those things exist.
Don’t they think I’m crazy too because I said I was going to open a dog-dyeing shop and metalize shirt cuffs?...
But I don’t think you’re crazy.
No, I don’t.
What you have is an excess of life, of charity and of love for your neighbor.
Now, the idea that Jesus revealed the secret of the roulette wheel to you seems rather absurd... ”
“I won five thousand pesos in the two times... ”
“Let’s say it’s true.
But what saves you isn’t the secret of the roulette wheel, but the fact that you have a beautiful soul.
You’re capable of doing good, of being moved by a man who stands at the gates of prison... ”
“That’s certainly true,” Ergueta interrupted.
“Look, there’s another pharmacist in town who’s an old skinflint.
His son stole five thousand pesos from him... and then came to ask me for advice.
Do you know what I advised him?
To threaten his father with having him put in jail for selling cocaine if he reported him. ”
“You see how I understand you?
You wanted to save the old man’s soul by making the son commit a sin that he would repent of for the rest of his life.
Isn’t that it? ”
“Yes, in the Bible it is written: ‘And the father shall rise against the son and the son against the father’... ”
“You see?
I understand you.
I don’t know what you are destined for...
The destiny of men is always uncertain.
But I believe you have a magnificent path ahead of you.
You know?
A strange path... ”
“I shall be the King of the World.
Do you realize?
I will win as much money as I want at every roulette wheel.
I will go to Palestine, to Jerusalem, and I will rebuild the great Temple of Solomon... ”
“And you will save many good people from anguish.
How many have defrauded their employers out of necessity, stolen money that was entrusted to them.
You know?
Anguish...
A desperate man doesn’t know what he’s doing...
Today he steals one peso, tomorrow five, the day after twenty, and when he notices he owes hundreds of pesos.
And the man thinks.
It’s not much... and suddenly he finds that five hundred, no, six hundred pesos and seven cents have disappeared.
Do you see?
That is the kind of people who must be saved... the desperate, the fraudulent. ”
The pharmacist thought for a moment.
A grave expression dissolved across the surface of his bloated face; then, calmly, he added:
“You’re right... the world is full of bastards, of wretches... but how to remedy it?
That is what worries me.
In what way can the sacred truths be presented again to those people who have no faith?... ”
“But what people need is money... not sacred truths. ”
“No, it’s that this happens because of the forgetting of the Scriptures.
A man who carries the sacred truths within himself does not rob his employer, does not defraud the company he works for, does not put himself in a position to go to jail from one day to the next. ”
Then he scratched his nose thoughtfully and continued:
“Besides, who’s to say it isn’t for the best?
Who is going to make the social revolution if not the swindlers, the wretches, the murderers, the fraudulent, all the scum that suffers down below without any hope?
Or do you think the ink-slingers and the shopkeepers are going to make the revolution? ”
“Agreed, agreed... but while the social revolution is coming, what does that wretch do?
What do I do? ”
And Erdosain, taking Ergueta by the arm, exclaimed:
“Because I am one step away from prison, you know?
I have stolen six hundred pesos and seven cents. ”
The pharmacist slowly winked his left eyelid and then said:
“Don’t worry.
The times of tribulation spoken of in the Scriptures have arrived.
Haven’t I married the Cripple, the Whore?
Hasn’t the son risen against the father and the father against the son?
The revolution is closer than men desire.
Aren’t you the fraudulent one and the wolf that decimates the flock?... ”
“But tell me, can’t you lend me those six hundred pesos? ” The other slowly shook his head:
“I swear I owe them. ”
Suddenly something unexpected happened.
The pharmacist stood up, stretched out his arm and, snapping his fingers, exclaimed in front of the café waiter who was watching the scene in astonishment:
“Get lost, you little bastard, get lost. ”
Erdosain, red with shame, walked away.
When he turned his head at the corner, he saw Ergueta waving his arms and talking to the waiter.
His life was bleeding out.

All his pent-up grief stretched out toward the horizon he glimpsed through the tram cables and trolley wires, and suddenly he had the sensation that he was walking on his own anguish turned into a carpet.
Like horses disemboweled by a bull that become tangled in their own entrails, every step he took left his lungs bloodless.
He breathed slowly and despaired of ever arriving.
Where?
He did not even know.
On Piedras Street he sat down on the threshold of an unoccupied house.
He remained there several minutes, then set off walking rapidly and the sweat ran down his face as on days of excessive heat.
In this way he reached the corner of Cerrito and Lavalle.
Putting a hand in his pocket he found he had a fistful of banknotes and so he entered the Japanese Bar.
Coachmen and pimps sat in circles around the tables.

A Black man in a wing collar and black espadrilles was picking parasites from his armpit, and three Polish pimps, with thick gold rings on their fingers, were talking in their jargon about brothels and procuresses.
In another corner several taxi drivers were playing cards.
The Black man who was delousing himself looked around, as if asking with his eyes that the public ratify his operation, but no one paid him any attention.
Erdosain ordered coffee, rested his forehead on his hand and remained staring at the marble tabletop.
“Where am I going to get the six hundred pesos? ”
Then he thought of Gregorio Barsut, his wife’s cousin.
Ergueta’s attitude no longer concerned him.
Before his eyes materialized the taciturn figure of the other man, of Gregorio Barsut, with his shaved head, his bony bird-of-prey nose, his greenish eyes and pointed ears like a wolf’s.
His presence made Erdosain’s hands tremble and left his mouth dry.
He would ask him for money again that night.
Surely at nine-thirty he would be at his house as usual.
And he saw him again.
Piling up a conversation full of vague pretexts for visiting him, torrents of words that stupefied Erdosain, who, with a parched mouth and trembling hands, did not dare throw him out of his house.
And Gregorio Barsut must have been aware of the repulsion Erdosain felt toward him, because more than once he had said to him:
“It seems my conversation displeases you, doesn’t it?
”—which did not prevent him from coming to his house with tiresome frequency.

Erdosain hastened to deny it and tried, at least in appearance, to interest himself in the other man’s chatter, which went on for hours on end, without rhyme or reason, always spying on the southeast corner of the room.
What was he trying to achieve with that attitude?
Erdosain in turn consoled himself for those unpleasant moments by thinking that the other man lived tormented by envy and by certain atrocious sufferings that had no reason to exist.
One night Gregorio said, in the presence of Erdosain’s wife—who rarely attended those conversations because she stayed in another room and closed the door so as not to hear the voices:
“How remarkable it would be if I went mad and shot the two of you and then killed myself!
” His slanted eyes were fixed on the southeast corner of the room, and he smiled, showing his pointed teeth, as if the words he had just spoken were nothing more than a joke.
But Elsa, looking at him very seriously, said:
“Let that be the last time you speak that way in my house.
If not, you will never set foot here again.
” Gregorio tried to apologize.
But she left and was not seen again all night.
The two men continued talking, the other man paler, his narrow forehead furrowed with tumultuous contractions, at times passing his broad hand over his bronze-colored brush of hair.
Erdosain could not explain the hatred he had conceived for Barsut.
He considered him coarse, yet this was contradicted by certain dreams of Gregorio’s in which there appeared an obscure, strange, delicate nature moved by the most inexplicable feelings.

At other times his apparent or real coarseness became repugnant, and in front of Erdosain, who repressed his indignation by twisting a pale grimace on his lips, Barsut would heap up nameless obscenities, for the sole pleasure of offending the other man’s sensibility.
It was an invisible, hateful duel without any immediate purpose, so irritating that after Barsut left, Erdosain would swear not to receive him the next day.
Yet a few hours before nightfall Erdosain would already be thinking about him.
Many times the other man would arrive and, before sitting down, would begin to speak.
“You know?...
I had a strange dream last night. ”

And with his eyes fixed on the southeast corner of the room, without smiling, with an almost painful expression on his dirty face covered with three days’ beard, Barsut would monologue slowly, recounting the terrors of a twenty-seven-year-old man, the preoccupation that the wink of a one-eyed fish had left in his mind, and relating the one-eyed fish to the prying gaze of an old procuress who wanted him to marry her daughter who practiced spiritualism; from there he would steer the conversation toward such absurdities that suddenly Erdosain, forgetting his rancor, would ask himself whether the other man was not mad.
Elsa, indifferent to everything, sewed in the adjoining room while a profound unease immobilized Erdosain.
He perceived a vibration of impatience, cracking his knuckles, and the effort he made to hide this trembling exhausted him.
If he uttered any word he did so with extraordinary difficulty, as if his lips had been stiffened by a coat of glue.
Resting an elbow on the table and adjusting the knee of his trousers, Barsut would sometimes complain that no one loved him, looking at Erdosain for a long time as he said this.

At other times he would mock his own premonitions and a ghost he claimed to see in a corner of the lavatory in the boarding house where he lived, a ghost that was a gigantic woman with a broom in her hands, thin arms and a harpy’s gaze.
On some occasions he admitted that if he was not ill he would end up becoming so.
Erdosain, pretending to be concerned for his health, would ask him about the symptoms, advising rest and bed, and when he insisted on this, Barsut once replied malevolently:
“Does my presence bother you so much? ”

At other times Barsut would arrive with a sinister cheerfulness, with the joviality of a taciturn drunk who has set fire to a petroleum depot, and sprawling in the dining room, slapping Erdosain on the back with annoying persistence, he would ask:
“How are you?
How’s it going?
How are you? ”

Barsut’s eyes would sparkle, and Erdosain would remain there, sad, shrunken, asking himself what it was that diminished him in the presence of that man, who always sat on the edge of the chair and obstinately spied on the corner of the dining room.
And they avoided looking each other in the eye.
There was between them an undefined, dark situation.
One of those situations that two men who despise each other tolerate for reasons independent of their wills.
Erdosain hated Barsut, but with a gray, treacherous rancor composed of bad dreams and worse possibilities.
And what made this hatred more intense was the lack of motives.
Sometimes he would set himself to weaving images of some atrocious revenge, and with furrowed brow he would arrange disasters.

But the next day, when Barsut rang the doorbell, Erdosain would shudder like an adulteress at the arrival of her husband, and once he even became angry with Elsa because she delayed in opening the door to Barsut, adding by way of comment meant to hide his cowardice before her:
“He’ll think we don’t want to receive him.
In that case it’s better to tell him not to come anymore. ”
There was no concrete motive, and that subterranean rancor spread through him like a cancer.
Erdosain found in every gesture of Barsut reasons to become enraged and wish him atrocious deaths.
And Barsut, as if he sensed the other man’s feelings, seemed to perform on purpose the most repugnant vulgarities.
Thus Erdosain never forgot this incident:
It was one evening when they had gone to drink a vermouth.
With the drink the waiter brought a small plate of potato salad with mustard.
Barsut stabbed a piece of potato with such greed that he overturned the salad onto the marble blackened by the rubbing of hands and cigarette ash.
Erdosain watched him, irritated.
Then Barsut, mocking, picked up the pieces one by one and when he reached the last he wiped up the mustard spilled on the marble with it and carried it to his mouth with an ironic smile.
“You could lick the marble,” observed Erdosain in disgust.
Barsut gave him a strange, almost provocative look.
Then he bent his head and his tongue wiped the marble.
“Are you happy now? ”
Erdosain turned pale.
“Have you gone mad? ”
“What?
Are you going to get worked up? ”
And suddenly Barsut, laughing, amiable, the kind of frenzy that had darkened him all afternoon now dissolved, stood up saying trivialities.
Erdosain never forgot that incident: the bronze-colored shaved head bent over the marble and a tongue stuck to the viscous yellow stone.
And many times he imagined that Barsut remembered him through the days with the hatred one feels toward people to whom one has made too many confidences.
But he could not control himself, because as soon as he reached Erdosain’s house he would pour buckets of misfortunes into the latter’s ears, even though he knew that Erdosain rejoiced in them.

And it was that Remo provoked his confidences, and provoked them with a transitory but spontaneous compassion, so that Barsut felt his rancor toward the other man vanish when the latter advised him seriously.

But his hatred would uncoil furiously when a quick, furtive glance from Erdosain revealed to him that in the latter the pity was vanishing and a malignant pleasure was appearing at the spectacle of his half-ruined life, for although he had enough money to live modestly on an income, he suffered from the terror of going mad as had happened to his father and his brothers.
Suddenly Erdosain lifted his head.

The Black man in the wing collar had finished picking his lice and now the three pimps were dividing up wads of money under the avid gaze of the taxi drivers who, from the other table, looked sidelong with the corner of their eyes.
The Black man looked as if, under the influence of the money, he was about to sneeze, so pitifully did he stare at the pimps.
Erdosain stood up and paid.
Then he went out, saying to himself: “If Gregorio fails me I’ll ask the Astrologer. ”
If someone had told Erdosain that hours later he would plot the murder of Barsut and would witness, almost impassively, the flight of his wife, he would not have believed it.
He wandered all afternoon.
He needed to be alone, to forget human voices and to feel as detached from everything around him as a stranger in a city whose train he had missed at the station.

He walked along the solitary corners of Arenales and Talcahuano, the intersections of Charcas and Rodríguez Peña, the crossings of Montevideo and Avenida Quintana, craving the sight of those streets magnificent in their architecture and forever denied to the wretched.
His feet, on the white pavements, crushed the fallen plane-tree leaves, and he fixed his gaze on the oval windowpanes of the great houses, silvered by the whiteness of the inner curtains.
That was another world inside the filthy city he knew, another world for which his heart now beat with slow, heavy throbs.

He would stop and observe the garages, lustrous as patens, and the green plumes of the cypresses in the gardens, defended by walls crowned with jagged cornices or by thick railings capable of stopping the charge of a lion.
Red gravel snaked between the oval flowerbeds of green.
Some nanny in a grey cap would stroll along the paths.
And he owed six hundred pesos and seven cents!

He stared for a long time at the handrails on the black balconies that flashed with the rounded gleam of gold bars, at the windows painted pearl-grey or milk tinged with a few drops of coffee, at the glass whose thickness must have turned the images of passers-by watery.
The gauze curtains, so light that their names must have been as pretty as the geography of distant countries.
How different love must be in the shade of those tulle veils that dim the light and soften every sound!...
Yet he owed six hundred pesos and seven cents.
And the pharmacist’s voice now repeated in his ears:
“You’re right... the world is full of bastards... of wretches... but how do you fix it?...
How do you present the sacred truths to people who have no faith?... ”
The sorrow, like one of those shrubs whose growth is quickened by electricity, swelled in the depths of his chest and climbed toward his throat.
Standing still, he thought that every grief was an owl leaping from branch to branch of his misfortune.
He owed six hundred pesos and seven cents, and although he tried to forget it by placing his hopes in Barsut or in the Astrologer, his mind kept forking off down a dark street.
Rows of lights seemed to rest on the cornices.
Below, a haze of dust filled the street’s box.
But he was walking toward the land of joy, having forgotten the Limited Azucarer Company.
What had he done with his life?
Was this or was this not the moment to ask himself?
And how could he walk if his body weighed seventy kilos?
Or was he a ghost, a ghost who remembered events on earth?
So many things stirred in his heart!
And what about the other man who had married a prostitute?
And Barsut with his obsession about the one-eyed fish and the spiritist’s firstborn daughter?
And Elsa, who by refusing herself to him had thrown him out onto the street?
Was he mad or not?
He asked himself this because at moments he was surprised by a hope that had risen inside him.
He imagined that from the slatted opening of a blind in one of those palaces a certain “melancholy and taciturn” millionaire was observing him through opera glasses. (He used Erdosain’s exact terms.)

And the curious thing is that whenever he thought the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire” might be watching him, he composed a grief-stricken and meditative expression, and did not look at the maids’ behinds as they passed, pretending to be immobilized by the attention he was paying to some great inner labor.
For he told himself that if the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire” saw him looking at the maids’ behinds, he would conclude that he was not as worried as to deserve his compassion.

So strong was this obsession that afternoon that he suddenly believed a rascal in a waistcoat with red and yellow stripes, who stood at the door of a hotel staring at him brazenly, was the spy of the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire. ”
And the servant would call him.
He would follow.
They would cross a garden bristling with cacti, enter a drawing-room and he would remain alone for a few minutes.
The whole building was in darkness.
A lamp glowed in one corner of the room.
On the piano’s mantelpiece, sheets of music scattered the fragrance of paper always touched by feminine hands.
On the sill of a window draped with violet linens lay the abandoned marble head of a woman.
The cushions of the monk’s chairs were covered in fabrics that looked like cubist paintings, and on the desk stood black-bronze ashtrays and multicolored Punchinellos.
In what circumstance of his life had he been inside that drawing-room that now appeared before his imagination?
He could not remember.

But he saw a great ebony frame whose parallel bevels climbed toward a dazzling white ceiling that poured its plaster light over a seascape: a certain sinister wooden bridge beneath whose cyclopean buttresses seethed a crowd of blurred men stained with reddish shadows, carrying huge bundles in front of a stormy sea of cast iron, blood-red, from which rose at a right angle a stone pier cluttered with forges, rails and winches.
In that room Elsa moved when she was still his fiancée.
Yes, perhaps, but why remember it?
He was the swindler, the man with broken shoes, with a frayed tie, with a suit full of stains, who earned his living in the street while his sick wife washed clothes at home.
He was all that and nothing more.
That was why the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire” had sent for him.

Erdosain, rejoicing in the daydream that was partly made concrete by stretches of time and images reconstructed at the expense of the invisible great gentleman, no longer wanted to linger on his interview with the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire” who offered him money to make his inventions practical; instead, like those readers of detective serials who, impatient to reach the resolution of the intrigue, skip the “dead points” of the novel, Erdosain avoided certain interesting constructions of his imagination and returned to the street, even though he was already in the street.
Then, leaving the corner of Charcas and Talcahuano, or of Arenales and Rodríguez Peña, he would set off walking hurriedly.
And the excesses were displaced by excesses of hope.
He would triumph, yes, he would triumph.

With the money of the “melancholy and taciturn millionaire” he would set up an electrotechnical laboratory, he would devote himself especially to the study of Beta rays, to the wireless transmission of energy, and to electromagnetic waves, and without losing his youth, like the absurd character in an English novel, he would grow old; only his face would grow pale until it acquired the whiteness of marble, and his sparkling pupils, like those of a wizard, would seduce all the maidens on earth.
Evening was falling when he suddenly remembered that the only one who could save him from his horrible situation was the Astrologer.
This thought stirred all his reflections.
Perhaps the other man had money.
He even suspected he might be a Bolshevik delegate sent to spread communist propaganda in the country, since the man had a most singular project for a revolutionary society.
Without hesitating, he hailed a car and told the driver to take him to Constitución station.
There he bought a ticket for Temperley.
The building occupied by the Astrologer stood at the center of a wooded estate.
The house was low and its reddish roofs could be seen from a great distance above the thicket of wild trees.
Through the gaps left by the bulges, amid the genuine swell of grasses and creepers, thick black-bottomed insects buzzed all day long amid the perpetual rain of weeds and stalks.
Not far from the house, the mill wheel turned its three-bladed limp upon a prism of rusted iron, and beyond, above the stable, one could make out the blue and red panes of a screen destroyed by rust.
Behind the mill and the house, beyond the low walls, the bottle-green ridge of a eucalyptus grove darkened the horizon, crowning the sky of maritime blue with billowing crests in relief.
Sucking on a honeysuckle flower, Erdosain crossed the estate toward the house.
He felt as if he were in the countryside, very far from the city, and the sight of the building cheered him.
Though low, it had two stories, with a ruined balcony on the second floor and a peeling set of Greek columns in the entrance hall, reached by a crumbling flight of steps bordered with palm trees.

The reddish roofs sloped obliquely, protecting the skylights and little windows of the garrets with their eaves, and between the jaunty foliage of the chestnut trees, above the crowns of the pomegranate trees spotted with scarlet asterisks, a zinc rooster could be seen turning its crooked tail to every wind.

All around, intricately, the garden rose, arranged like a little wood, and now in the quiet of the evening, beneath the sun that weighted the space with an atmosphere of pearly crystal, the rosebushes poured forth their overwhelmingly potent perfume, so penetrating that all the air seemed filled with a red and fresh atmosphere like a stream of water. Erdosain thought:

“Even if I had a silver boat with golden sails and ivory oars, and the ocean turned into seven smooth colors, and from the moon a millionairess blew me kisses with both hands, my sadness would be the same...
But there’s no need to say that.
Still, I’d live better here than there.
Here I could have a laboratory. ”
A poorly closed tap dripped into a barrel.

At the foot of a pergola post a dog dozed, and when he stopped to knock at the foot of the steps the gigantic figure of the Astrologer appeared at the door, wearing a yellow duster and with his top hat pulled down over his forehead, shadowing his broad, diamond-shaped face.
A few locks of curly hair escaped over his temples, and his nose, with the septum fractured in the middle, was extraordinarily twisted toward the left.
Beneath his heavy eyebrows lively round black eyes moved, and that face with its hard cheeks furrowed by rough lines gave the impression of having been sculpted in lead.
How heavy that head must have been!
“Ah!
It’s you?...
Come in.
I’m going to introduce you to the Melancholy Pimp. ”
Crossing the dark vestibule that stank of damp, they entered a study whose walls were covered with faded greenish paper patterned with branches.
The room was frankly sinister, with its very high ceiling crossed by cobwebs and the narrow window protected by a knotted iron grille.
In the inlaid surface of an old cabinet pushed into a corner, the bluish clarity broke into livid shadows.
Seated in an armchair upholstered in worn green velvet was a man dressed in gray; a blackened wave of hair slanted across his forehead, and he wore light-colored ankle boots.
The Astrologer’s yellow duster rippled as he approached the stranger.
“Erdosain, I’m going to introduce you to Arturo Haffner. ”

At another time the swindler would have said something to the man the Astrologer privately called the Melancholy Pimp, who, after shaking Erdosain’s hand, crossed his legs in the armchair, resting his bluish cheek on three fingers whose nails glittered.

And Erdosain examined that almost round face, relaxed in peace, which only betrayed the man of action by a mocking, restless spark at the bottom of the eyes, and by that habit of raising one eyebrow higher than the other while listening to the speaker.
Erdosain noticed at one side, between the jacket and the silk shirt the Pimp wore, the black butt of a revolver.
Undoubtedly, in life, faces mean very little.
Then the Pimp turned his head again toward a map of the United States of North America, to which the Astrologer moved, picking up a pointer.
And now standing still, with his yellow arm cutting across the Caribbean Sea, he exclaimed:
“The Ku Klux Klan had only in Chicago 150,000 adherents...
In Missouri, 100,000 adherents.
It is said that in Arkansas there are more than 200 ‘caves.’ In Little Rock, the Invisible Empire claims that all the Protestant pastors are members of the brotherhood.
In Texas it dominates absolutely in the cities of Dallas, Fort Worth, Houston, Beaumont.

In Binghamton, residence of Smith, who was Grand Dragon of the Order, there were 75,000 adepts, and in Oklahoma these men got the Chambers to pass a bill suspending Walton, the governor, for persecuting them, so that practically the state was, until recently, under the control of the Klan. ”
The Astrologer’s yellow duster looked like the robe of a Buddhist priest. The Astrologer continued:
“Do you know they burned many men alive?... ”
“Yes,” the Pimp assented; “I read the telegrams. ”
Erdosain was now studying the Melancholy Pimp.
That was what the Astrologer called him, because the pimp had tried to commit suicide many years before.
It had been an obscure affair.
Overnight, Haffner, who for a long time had been living off prostitutes, put a bullet in his chest, next to his heart.
The contraction of the organ at the precise instant the projectile passed saved him from death.
Later, as was natural, he continued his life, perhaps with a little more prestige because of that gesture that none of his fellow predators could explain. The Astrologer continued:
“The Ku Klux Klan gathered millions... ” The Pimp stretched and answered:
“Yes, and the Dragon... now there’s a real Dragon for you!... is being prosecuted for fraud... ” The Astrologer ignored the reply:
“What is there to prevent a secret society from existing here in Argentina that attains as much power as that one over there?
And I speak to you frankly.
I don’t know whether our society will be Bolshevik or Fascist.
Sometimes I am inclined to believe that the best thing is to prepare a Russian salad that not even God can understand.
I think no more sincerity can be asked of me at this moment.
Notice that for now what I intend to do is to create a bloc in which all possible human hopes are consolidated.
My plan is to direct ourselves preferably toward young Bolsheviks, students, and intelligent proletarians.

In addition, we shall welcome those who have a plan to reform the universe, clerks who aspire to become millionaires, failed inventors—not to take it personally, Erdosain—, the unemployed of any kind, those who have just undergone a trial and are left on the street not knowing which way to look... ”
Erdosain remembered the mission that had brought him to the Astrologer’s house, and said:
“I need to speak with you... ”
“Just a moment...
I’ll be right with you,” and he went on: “The power of this society will not derive from what the members want to give, but from what the brothels annexed to each cell produce.

When I speak of a secret society, I am not referring to the classic type of society, but to a supermodern one, where each member and adherent has interests and reaps profits, because only in that way is it possible to bind them more and more tightly to ends that only a few will know.
That is the commercial aspect.
The brothels will produce income sufficient to maintain the growing ramifications of the society.
In the mountains we shall establish a revolutionary colony.

There the novices will take courses in anarchist tactics, revolutionary propaganda, military engineering, industrial installations, so that these associates, the day they leave the colony, can establish a branch of the society anywhere...
Do you understand?
The secret society will have its academy, the Academy for Revolutionaries. ”
The clock hanging on the wall struck five.
Erdosain realized he could waste no more time, and exclaimed:
“Forgive me for interrupting you.
I have come on a serious matter.
Do you have six hundred pesos? ”
The Astrologer set down his pointer and folded his arms:
“What’s the matter with you? ”
“If I don’t put six hundred pesos back in the sugar company tomorrow, they’ll put me in prison. ”
The two men looked at Erdosain curiously.
He must have been suffering greatly to have blurted out his request like that. Erdosain continued:
“You must help me.
Over the course of several months I have embezzled six hundred pesos.
I was denounced in an anonymous letter.
If I don’t replace the money tomorrow, they’ll put me in prison. ”
“And how did you come to steal that money?... ”
“Like this... slowly... ”
The Astrologer stroked his beard, worried.
“How did it happen? ”
Erdosain had to explain again.
The merchants, upon receiving the merchandise, signed a voucher in which they acknowledged owing the amount purchased.
Erdosain, together with two other collectors, received at the end of each month the vouchers that had to be collected during the remaining thirty days.
The receipts that these men claimed not to have collected remained in his possession until the merchants decided to settle the debt. And Erdosain continued:

“Notice that the cashier’s negligence was such that he never checked the vouchers we said we had not collected, so that to an account that had been collected and embezzled we would enter it on the collection sheet with money that came from an account we collected later.
Do you see? ”
Erdosain was the vertex of the triangle formed by the three seated men.
The Melancholy Pimp and the Astrologer glanced at each other from time to time.
Haffner shook the ash from his cigarette and then, with one eyebrow higher than the other, continued to examine Erdosain from head to foot.
At last he ended by asking him this strange question:
“And did you find any satisfaction in stealing?... ”
“No, none... ”
“Then how do you go around with broken boots?... ”
“It’s that I earned very little. ”
“But what about what you stole? ”
“It never occurred to me to buy boots with that money. ”
And it was true.
The pleasure he had felt at first in freely disposing of what did not belong to him soon evaporated.
One day Erdosain discovered in himself the uneasiness that makes sunny skies look blackened with soot visible only to a sad soul.
When he verified that he owed four hundred pesos, the shock drove him toward madness.
Then he spent the money in a stupid, frantic way.

He bought sweets he had never craved, lunched on crabs, turtle soups, and frog fritters in restaurants where the right to sit beside well-dressed people is extremely expensive, drank costly liqueurs and insipid wines for his insensitive palate, and yet lacked the most necessary things for an ordinary life, such as underwear, shoes, ties...

He gave abundant alms and often left the waiters who served him substantial tips, all in order to erase the traces of that stolen money he carried in his pocket and which the next day he could remove with impunity.
“So it never occurred to you to buy boots?
” Haffner insisted.
“Really, now that you point it out, it seems curious to me too, but the truth is I never thought that with stolen money one could buy those things. ”
“Then what did you spend the money on? ”
“I gave two hundred pesos to a family of friends, the Espilas, to buy an accumulator and set up a small galvanoplasty laboratory to manufacture the copper rose, which is... ”
“I already know about that... ”
“Yes, I already told you about it,” replied the Astrologer.
“And the other four hundred? ”
“I don’t know...
I spent them in an absurd way... ”
“And now, what do you plan to do?... ”
“I don’t know. ”
“Don’t you know anyone who could lend you some?... ”
“No, no one.
Ten days ago I asked a relative of my wife, Barsut.
He told me he couldn’t... ”
“So they’ll put you in prison, then? ”
“Of course... ”
The Astrologer turned to the pimp and said:
“You already know I have a thousand pesos.
That is the basis of all my projects.
The only thing I can give you, Erdosain, is three hundred pesos.
Really, my friend, the things you do!... ”
Suddenly Erdosain forgot about Haffner and exclaimed:
“It’s the anguish, you know?...
That damned anguish that drags you along... ”
“What’s that?
” the Pimp interrupted.
“I said it’s the anguish.
One steals, one does stupid things because one is anguished.
You walk along the streets with the yellow sun that looks like a plague sun...
Of course.
You must have been through those situations.
To carry five thousand pesos in your wallet and be sad.
And suddenly a tiny idea suggests theft to you.
That night you can’t sleep for joy.
The next day you make the attempt trembling and it turns out so well that there’s nothing left but to continue... just like when you tried to kill yourself. ”
At these words Haffner sat up in the armchair and clasped his knees with his hands.
The Astrologer would have liked to silence Erdosain. It was impossible, and he continued:
“Yes, like when you tried to kill yourself.
I have imagined it many times.
You had grown tired of being a pimp.
Ah, if you only knew how interested I was in meeting you!
I used to say to myself: This must be a strange pimp.
Of course, out of a hundred thousand individuals who like you live off women, one finds a single one of your kind.
You asked me if I felt pleasure in stealing.
And you, do you feel pleasure in being a pimp?
Tell me: do you feel pleasure?...
But what the devil!
I didn’t come here to give explanations, you know?
What I need is money, not words. ”
Erdosain had risen, and now, trembling, he squeezed the brim of his hat between his fingers.
He looked indignantly at the Astrologer, whose top hat covered the state of Kansas on the map, and at the Pimp, who had slipped his hands between his belt and his trousers.
The latter settled back into his green-velvet armchair, rested his cheek on his plump hand, and smiling mockingly, said calmly:
“Sit down, friend, I’m going to give you the six hundred pesos. ”
Erdosain’s arms contracted.
Then, without moving, he looked at the Pimp for a long time.
The latter insisted, emphasizing the words.
“Sit down confidently, friend.
I’m going to give you the six hundred pesos.
That’s what men are for. ”
Erdosain did not know what to say.
The same sadness that had burst inside him when the man with the boar’s head told him in the office that he could go, the same sadness now enervated him.
So life was not so bad after all!
“Let’s do this,” said the Astrologer.
“I’ll give you three hundred pesos and you give him the other three hundred. ”
“No,” said Haffner.
“You need that money.
I don’t.
For that I have three women.
” And turning to Erdosain, he continued: “You see, friend, how things get arranged?
Are you satisfied? ”
He spoke with sly calm, with a certain phlegm of a countryman who always knows that his experience of nature will allow him to find a way out of the most complicated situation.
And only now did Erdosain perceive the burning perfume of the roses and the dripping of the tap into the barrel that could be heard through the half-open window.
Outside the paths undulated, lit by the sun, and the weight of the birds bent the branches of the pomegranate trees, constellated with scarlet asterisks.
Again the spark of malicious light shone in the Pimp’s eyes.
With one lip raised higher than the other he awaited the explosion of Erdosain’s joy, but as it did not come, he said:
“Have you been living like this for a long time?... ”
“Yes, a long time. ”
“Do you remember that I once told you that in that way, even though you didn’t confide anything in me, one cannot live?
” objected the Astrologer.
“Yes, but I didn’t want to talk about the matter.
I don’t know... those things one cannot explain why one keeps silent about them with the people one trusts most. ”
“When are you going to replace that money? ”
“Tomorrow. ”
“Good, then I’ll write you a check now.
You’ll have to cash it tomorrow. ”
Haffner went to the desk.
He took the checkbook from his pocket and wrote the sum firmly, then signed it.

Erdosain passed through that motionless minute’s journey with the unconsciousness of one who finds himself before the prospect of a dream, and which later, when remembered, serves to affirm that in certain circumstances life is steeped in an intelligent fatalism.
“Here you are, friend. ”
Erdosain took the check, and without reading it folded it in four, putting it in his pocket.
Everything had happened in a minute.
The event was more absurd than a novel, even though he was a man of flesh and blood.
And he did not know what to say.
He no longer owed the money, and the miracle had been worked by a single gesture of the Pimp.
This event was an impossibility according to the logic that governs ordinary procedures, and yet nothing had happened.
He wanted to say something.
Again he examined the appearance of the man lounging in the worn velvet armchair.
Now the revolver stood out beneath the gray cloth of the jacket, and Haffner, nonchalant, rested his bluish cheek on his three glittering-nailed fingers.
He wanted to thank the Pimp, but did not know with what words to do so.
The latter understood, and, addressing the Astrologer, who had sat down on a stool beside the desk, said:
“So one of the bases of your society will be obedience?... ”
“And industrialism.
Gold is needed to capture the conscience of men.
Just as there was religious and chivalric mysticism, industrial mysticism must be created.
To make a man see that it is as beautiful to be the head of a blast furnace as it once was to discover a continent.
My politician, my political pupil in the society, will be a man who will seek to conquer happiness through industry.
This revolutionary will know how to speak as well of a fabric-printing system as of the demagnetization of steel.
That is why I esteemed Erdosain as soon as I met him.
He had the same preoccupation as I. You remember how many times we spoke of the coincidence of our views.
To create a superb, beautiful, inexorable man who dominates the multitudes and shows them a future based on science.
How else is a social revolution possible?
The leader of today must be a man who knows everything.
We shall create that prince of knowledge.
The society will take charge of fashioning his legend and spreading it.
A Ford or an Edison has a thousand times more chance of provoking a revolution than a politician.
Do you believe that future dictatorships will be military?
No, sir.
The military man is worth nothing beside the industrialist.
He can be his instrument, nothing more.
That is all.
The future dictators will be kings of oil, of steel, of wheat.
We, with our society, will prepare that environment.
We shall familiarize people with our theories.
That is why a careful study of propaganda is needed.
To make use of the male and female students.
To beautify science, to bring it so close to men that suddenly... ”
“I’m leaving,” said Erdosain.
He was about to take leave of Haffner when the latter said:
“Then just a moment, listen. ”

The Astrologer and the pimp went out for an instant, then returned, and when saying goodbye at the gate of the estate Erdosain turned his head to look at the gigantic man, who with his arm bent was making gestures of farewell.
And once they had turned the corner by the villa, Erdosain said:
“You know I don’t have any way to thank you for this enormous favor you’ve done me?
Why did you give me this money? ”
The other man, who was walking with a slight roll of his shoulders, turned with an air of indifference and said:
“I don’t know.
You caught me in a good mood.
If a person had to do that every day... but like this...
Besides, imagine, I’ll get it back in a week... ”
The question slipped out of Erdosain.
“And how is it that someone with a fortune like yours stays in the ‘life’? ”
Haffner turned, aggressive at first, then:
“Look, friend, the ‘life’ isn’t for every man.
You know?
Why would I leave three women who bring in two thousand pesos a month without me lifting a finger?
Would you leave them?
No. So? ”
“And you don’t love them?
None of them attracts you in a special way? ”
Only after the question had left his mouth did Erdosain realize he had just said something stupid.
The pimp looked at him for a second and replied:
“Listen carefully.

If a doctor came to see me tomorrow and told me the Basque girl is going to die in a week whether I take her out of the brothel or not, I’d let the Basque girl—who’s given me thirty thousand pesos in four years—keep working those six days and drop dead on the seventh. ”
The pimp’s voice had grown hoarse.
There was something like a furious bitterness in his words, that same bitterness Erdosain would later recognize in the voices of all those taciturn idlers and bored scoundrels.
“Pity?
” the other continued.
“Friend, you mustn’t feel pity for a woman of the life.
There is no bitchier, harder, more bitter woman than a woman of the life.
Don’t be shocked; I know them.
The only way to handle them is with beatings.
You believe, like ninety percent of people, that the pimp is the exploiter and the prostitute the victim.
But tell me: what does a woman need with all the money she earns?

What the novelists have never said is that a woman of the life who doesn’t have a man is desperate to find one who will deceive her, who will break her heart from time to time and take all the money she makes, because she’s that stupid.
They’ve said woman is equal to man.
Lies.
Woman is inferior to man.
Look at savage tribes.
She’s the one who cooks, works, does everything, while the male goes hunting or to war.
The same thing happens in modern life.
The man, except for making money, does nothing.
And believe me, a woman of the life who isn’t relieved of her money despises the man.
Yes, sir, as soon as she starts to care for him, the first thing she wants is for him to ask her...
And what joy she feels the day you say to her: ‘Ma chérie, can you lend me a hundred pesos?’ Then that woman lets herself go, she’s happy.
At last the filthy money she earns is good for something, for making her man happy.
Of course, the novelists haven’t written that.
And people think we’re monsters, or exotic animals, the way the vaudeville writers have painted us.
But come and live in our world, get to know it, and you’ll see it’s exactly the same as the bourgeois world and our aristocracy.

The kept woman looks down on the cabaret woman, the cabaret woman looks down on the streetwalker, the streetwalker looks down on the brothel woman, and, curiously enough, just as the woman in a brothel almost always chooses a shady character for her man, the cabaret woman ends up with a rich boy or a worthless doctor to exploit her.
The psychology of the woman of the life?
It’s contained in the words a little woman once said to me, crying, after a friend of mine left her:
‘Encoré avec mon cul je peu soutenir un homme.’ People don’t know that, nor do the novelists.
A French proverb already says it: ‘Gueuse seule ne peut pas mener son cul.’”
Erdosain stared at him in astonishment. Haffner went on:
“Who takes care of her like a pimp?
Who looks after her when she’s sick, when she gets arrested?
What does the public know?
If you heard a woman on a Saturday morning tell her ‘marlu’: ‘Mon chéri, I did fifty more tricks than last week,’ you’d become a pimp, you know?

Because that woman says ‘I did fifty more tricks’ in the same tone a decent woman would use to tell her husband: ‘Darling, this month, by not buying myself a dress and washing my own clothes, I saved thirty pesos.’
Believe me, friend, woman—whether decent or not—is an animal made for sacrifice.
She was built that way.
Why do you think the Fathers of the Church despised woman so much?
Most of them had lived like great libertines and knew what kind of little animal she is.
And the woman of the life is even worse.
She’s like a child: you have to teach her everything.
‘You walk this way, you don’t go past that corner, you don’t greet that “fioca.
” Don’t start trouble with that woman.’ Everything has to be taught to her. ”
They walked beside the brambles, and in the gentle dusk the pimp’s words opened a parenthesis of strangeness in Erdosain.
He understood that he was beside a life substantially different from his own. Then he asked:
“And how did you get started in the ‘life’? ”
“At the time I was young.
I was twenty-three and had a chair in mathematics.
Because I am a professor,” Haffner added proudly, “a professor of mathematics.
I was living off my teaching post when one night in a brothel on Rincón Street I met a little French girl who took my fancy.
That was ten years ago.
Just around then I had received an inheritance of five thousand pesos from a relative.
Lucienne pleased me, and I offered to have her come live with me.
She had a pimp, the Marseillais, a brutal giant I used to see from time to time...
I don’t know if it was my smooth talk or because I was good-looking, but the fact is the woman fell in love, and one stormy night I took her out of the house.
It was like a novel.
We went to the Córdoba hills, then to Mar del Plata, and when the five thousand pesos ran out I told her:
‘Well, goodbye idyll.
It’s over.’ Then she said to me: ‘No, my dear, we will never leave each other again.’”
Now they walked beneath vaults of greenery, interlaced branches and apses of stems.
“I was jealous.
Do you know what it is to be jealous of a woman who sleeps with everyone?
And do you know the emotion of the first lunch she pays for with money from the ‘miché’?
Can you imagine the happiness of eating with crossed forks while the waiter looks at you and her knowing who you are?
And the pleasure of going out into the street with her hanging on your arm while the cops watch you?
And seeing that she, who sleeps with so many men, prefers you, only you?
That’s very beautiful, friend, when you’re on the game.

And she’s the one who worries about you getting another woman to exploit, she’s the one who brings her home saying: ‘We’re going to be sisters-in-law,’ she’s the one who trains the new girl so she only picks up ‘trips’ for you, and the more timid and ashamed you are, the more she enjoys destroying your scruples, sinking you into her filth, and suddenly... when you least expect it you find yourself buried up to your hair in the mud... and then you have to dance.

And while the woman is in the game you have to take advantage, because one day she gets a crazy fit, falls madly for another man, and with the same unconsciousness with which she followed you she sacrifices herself again.
You’ll ask me: why does a woman need a man?
Well, I’ll tell you right now: No brothel owner is going to deal with a woman.
He deals with her ‘marlu.’ The pimp gives a woman peace of mind to practice her life.
The cops don’t bother her.
If she gets arrested, he gets her out; if she’s sick, he takes her to a sanatorium and has her looked after, and he saves her from trouble and a thousand fantastic things.
Look, a woman who works on her own in this world always ends up the victim of a robbery, a swindle or some brutal attack.
On the other hand, a woman who has a man works calmly, peacefully, no one messes with her and everyone respects her.
And since she, for one reason or another, chose this life, it’s logical that with her money she can buy the happiness she needs.
Of course, all this is new to you, but you’ll get used to it.
And if not, tell me: how do you explain that there are ‘fiocas’ who have up to seven women?
The Italian Repollo in his good days had eleven women.
The Galician Julio had eight.
There’s hardly a Frenchman who doesn’t have three women.

And they know each other, and not only do they know each other, they know how to live together and they compete over who gives him more, because it’s a point of pride to be the favorite of a man who can silence the most arrogant detectives with a single look.
And the poor things are so crazy that you don’t know whether to pity them or smash their heads with a stick. ”
Erdosain felt crushed by the enormous contempt this man showed toward women.

And he remembered that on another occasion the Astrologer had told him: “The Melancholy Pimp is the kind of guy who, the moment he sees a woman, thinks: This one on the street would bring in five, ten or twenty pesos.
Nothing more. ”
And now Erdosain felt the man repelled him. To change the subject he said:
“Tell me...
Do you believe in the success of the Astrologer’s enterprise? ”
“No. ”
“And does he know you don’t believe? ”
“Yes. ”
“Then why do you go along with him? ”
“I go along with him in a limited way, and because I’m bored.
Since life has no meaning, it’s the same to follow any current. ”
“Life has no meaning for you? ”
“Absolutely none.
We’re born, we live, we die, and the stars keep moving and the ants keep working just the same. ”
“And do you get very bored? ”
“Moderately.
I’ve organized my life like that of an industrialist.
Every day I go to bed at midnight and get up at nine in the morning.

I do an hour of exercise, bathe, read the papers, have lunch, take a siesta, at six I have a vermouth and go to the barber’s, at eight I have dinner, then I go to the café, and in two years, when I have two hundred thousand pesos, I’ll retire from the trade and live definitively off my income. ”
And in reality, what will your role be in the Astrologer’s society?
If the Astrologer gets money, to guide him in the recruitment of women and the setting up of the brothel.
“But you, deep down, what do you think of the Astrologer? ”
“That he’s a maniac who may or may not succeed. ”
“But his ideas... ”
“Some are muddled, others clear, and frankly I don’t know how far that man is aiming.
Sometimes you think you’re listening to a reactionary, other times to a Red, and, to tell the truth, it seems to me that even he himself doesn’t know what he wants. ”
“And if he were to succeed?... ”
“Then not even God knows what might happen.
Ah, by the way, did you talk to him about cultivating Asiatic cholera bacilli? ”
“Yes... it would be a magnificent means of combat against the army.
Scatter a culture in every barracks.
You see?
Simultaneously, thirty or forty men could destroy the army and let the proletarian masses carry out the revolution... ”
“The Astrologer admires you a great deal.
He has always spoken of you as a man with great possibilities of success. ”
Erdosain smiled, flattered.
“Yes, one studies a bit in order to destroy this society.
But going back to what we were saying: what I can’t understand is your position with regard to us... ”
Haffner turned quickly, measured Erdosain with a glance as if surprised by his terms, and then, smiling mockingly, added:
“I’m not in any position.
Understand me clearly.
Helping the Astrologer doesn’t hurt me.
The rest, his theories, I take as conversation.
He is, for me, a friend who plans to open a business foreseen and tolerated by our laws.
That’s all.
Now, what he does with the money he earns from that business—whether he invests it in a secret society or in a convent—I personally don’t care.
So you see that my role in the famous society couldn’t be more innocent. ”
“And does it seem logical to you to think that a revolutionary society should be based on the exploitation of woman’s vice? ”
The Pimp pursed his lips.
Then, looking at Erdosain out of the corner of his eye, he explained:
“What you say makes no sense.
Present society is based on the exploitation of man, woman and child.
Go, if you want to understand what capitalist exploitation is, to the iron foundries of Avellaneda, to the meat-packing plants and the glass factories, match factories and workshops.
” He laughed unpleasantly as he said these things.
“We, the men of this world, have one or two women; they, the industrialists, have a multitude of human beings.
What should we call those men?
And who is more heartless, the owner of a brothel or the shareholders of a company?
And without going any further, didn’t they demand that you be honest on a salary of a hundred pesos while carrying ten thousand in your wallet? ”
“You’re right... but then, why did you give me the money? ”
“That’s a different matter. ”
“But that worries me. ”
“Well, that’s your problem. ”
And before Erdosain could answer him, the Pimp took a tree-lined diagonal path.
He walked hurriedly.
Erdosain looked at him for a moment, then set off after him and caught up with him beside a villa.
Haffner turned irritably, and now in a shrill voice exclaimed:
“Can one know what it is you want from me?...
What do I want?...
I want to tell you this: that I don’t thank you in the least for the money you gave me.
You know?
Do you want the check?
Here it is. ”
And indeed he held it out to him, but this time the Pimp examined it contemptuously:
“Don’t be ridiculous, will you?
Go and pay. ”
The wire fences rippled before Erdosain’s eyes.
He was visibly suffering, because he went pale until he was yellow.
He leaned against a post; he thought he was going to vomit.
Haffner, stopped in front of him, asked condescendingly:
“Is the dizziness passing? ”
“Yes... a little... ”
“You’re not well... you should see a doctor... ”
They walked a few steps in silence.
Since the excess of light bothered Erdosain, they crossed to the shaded side of the street.
They reached the railway station that way.
Haffner walked slowly along the platform. Suddenly he turned to Erdosain:
“Have you never felt cruel whims about people? ”
“Yes, sometimes... ”
“How strange... because just now I was remembering the mania I had for a while of inducing a blind girl into prostitution... ”
“And is she still alive?... ”
“Yes, now she’s pregnant.
You see?
A blind pregnant woman.
One of these days I’ll take you.
You’ll meet her.
An interesting spectacle, I warn you.
You see?
Blind and knocked up.
She’s mean, she’s always walking around with needles in her hands...
Besides she’s greedy as a sow.
It’ll interest you. ”
“And you intend... ”
“Yes, as soon as the Astrologer opens the brothel she’ll be the first one in.
We’ll keep her hidden: she’ll be the rare dish... ”
“You know you’re stranger than she is? ”
“Why? ”
“Because one can’t explain you.
While you were talking to me about the blind girl, I was thinking about what the Astrologer told me.
That you had a relationship with an honest woman, that chance brought this honest woman to your house and that you respected her.
What’s more, let me speak: that woman loved you, she was a virgin, why did you respect her? ”
“That’s not important.
A bit of self-control, nothing more. ”
“And the business with the necklace? ”

Erdosain knew, from the Astrologer, that the Pimp had asked a dancer for a material proof of affection; that she, in front of other women, had taken off a magnificent necklace given to her by a lover, an old textile importer.
The scene had been curious because the old man was in the vicinity.
Haffner received the necklace and, to everyone’s astonishment, weighed it, examined the carat of the stones, and then handed it back to her with a mocking smile.
“The necklace is simple,” Haffner replied.
“I was a little drunk.
That didn’t stop me from knowing that the gesture I was making would give me enormous prestige among that cabaret scum, especially among the women, who are a bit fanciful.
The curious thing is that half an hour later the old man who had given the necklace to René came to thank me humbly for not having accepted the gift.
You see?
From another table he had followed the scene trembling, and if he didn’t intervene it was for fear of causing a scandal.
But he had trembled for the fate of his necklace...
You see how much filth... but here comes the train to La Plata.
Dear friend, see you soon...
Ah!
Come to the meeting on Wednesday at the Astrologer’s house.
You’ll find others more interesting than me. ”
Erdosain crossed thoughtfully to the platform where the trains for Buenos Aires left.
Undoubtedly, Haffner was a monster.
He arrived home at eight o’clock in the evening.
“The dining room was lit...
But let me explain,” Erdosain recounted later.
“My wife and I had suffered so much poverty that the so-called dining room was simply an empty room without furniture.
The other room served as our bedroom.
You’ll ask how we could rent a house while being poor, but that was one of my wife’s whims.
Remembering better times, she could not resign herself to not having a ‘properly set up’ home.
“In the dining room there was no other furniture but a pine table.
