In one corner our clothes hung from a wire, and another corner was occupied by a trunk with tin corners that gave a sense of nomadic life that would end with one final journey.
Later, how many times I thought about ‘the sensation of travel’ that that cheap trunk, stowed in a corner, cast over my sadness as a man who knows he lives on the edge of prison.
“As I was telling you, the dining room was lit.
When I opened the door I stopped.
My wife was waiting for me, dressed to go out, seated beside the table.
A black tulle veil covered her rosy little face up to the chin.
To her right, beside her feet, was a suitcase, and on the other side of the table a man stood up when I entered—or rather, when surprise halted me on the threshold.
“The three of us remained like that for a second...
The captain standing, one hand resting on the table top and the other on the hilt of his sword, my wife with her head bowed, and I facing them, my fingers forgotten on the edge of the door.
That second was enough for me never to forget the other man.
He was large, of athletic build inside the green cloth of his uniform.
When he turned his eyes from my wife, his gaze recovered a curious hardness.
I do not exaggerate if I say he examined me with insolence, as one examines an inferior.
I kept looking at him.
His physical size contrasted with the oval smallness of his face, with the delicacy of his fine nose and the austerity of his tightly pressed lips.
On his chest he wore the insignia of a pilot aviator. “My first words were: “‘What is happening here?’
“‘This gentleman...’ but ashamed, she corrected herself.
‘Remo,’ she said, calling me by my name, ‘Remo, I am not going to live with you anymore.’
Erdosain had no time to tremble. The captain spoke:
“Your wife, whom I met some time ago... ”
“And where did you meet her? ”
“Why do you ask those things?
” Elsa interrupted.
“Yes, true,” the captain objected.
“You will understand that certain things should not be asked... ”
Erdosain blushed.
“Perhaps you are right... forgive me... ”
“And since you did not earn enough to support her... ”
Gripping the butt of the revolver in his trouser pocket, Erdosain looked at the captain.
Then, involuntarily, he smiled, thinking that he had nothing to fear, since he could kill him.
“I do not think what I am saying can amuse you. ”
“No; I was smiling at a stupid thought...
So she told you that too? ”
“Yes, and besides she spoke of you as a genius in misfortune... ”
“We talked about your inventions... ”
“Yes... about your project to metalize flowers... ”
“Why are you leaving, then? ”
“I am tired, Remo. ”
Erdosain felt fury curling his mouth into ugly words.
He would have insulted her, but thinking that the other man could smash his face with punches, he held back the insult and replied:
“You have always been tired.
In your parents’ house you were tired... here... there... even there in the mountains... do you remember? ”
Not knowing what to answer, Elsa lowered her head.
“Tired... what is it that you have tired, you?...
And all women are tired, I don’t know why... but they are tired...
You, captain, are you not tired too? ”
The intruder observed him for a long time.
“And what do you understand by tiredness? ”
“Boredom, anguish... have you not noticed that these seem to be the times of tribulation the Bible speaks of?
That is what a friend of mine calls them, the one who married a lame woman.
The lame woman is the whore of the Scriptures... ”
“I never realized that. ”
“But I have.
It will seem strange to you that I speak of sufferings in these circumstances... but it is so... men are so sad that they need to be humiliated by someone. ”
“I do not see such a thing. ”
“Of course, with your salary...
What salary do you earn?
Five hundred? ”
“More or less. ”
“Of course, with that salary it is logical... ”
“What is logical? ”
“That you do not feel your servitude. ”
The captain fixed a severe look on Erdosain.
“Germán, pay no attention to him,” Elsa interrupted.
“Remo is always going on about that story of anguish. ”
“Is that true? ”
“Yes... she, on the other hand, believes in happiness, in the sense of ‘eternal happiness’ that would be in her life if she could spend her days among parties... ”
“I detest poverty. ”
“Of course, because you do not believe in poverty... the horrible poverty is inside us, it is the poverty within... of the soul that eats into our bones like syphilis. ”
They fell silent.
The captain, visibly bored, examined his carefully polished nails.

Elsa stared fixedly through the diamonds of her veil at the emaciated face of that husband she had once loved so much, while Erdosain asked himself why there existed in him such an immense emptiness, an emptiness in which his consciousness dissolved without finding words that could bark his grief in an eternal way.
Suddenly the captain raised his head.
“And how do you plan to metalize your flowers? ”
“Easily...
You take a rose, for example, and submerge it in a solution of silver nitrate dissolved in alcohol.
Then you expose the flower to light, which reduces the nitrate to metallic silver, so that the rose ends up covered with an extremely fine metallic film, capable of conducting electricity.
Then it is treated by the usual galvanoplasty procedure of coppering... and, naturally, the flower is transformed into a copper rose.
It would have many applications. ”
“The idea is original. ”
“Didn’t I tell you, Germán, that Remo has talent? ”
“I believe so. ”

“Yes, perhaps I have talent, but I lack life... enthusiasm... something that is like an extraordinary dream... a great lie that pushes the realization forward... but, speaking of everything at once, do you two expect to be happy? ”
“Yes. ”
Once again silence fell.
Around the yellow lamp the three faces seemed like three wax masks.
Erdosain knew that in a few moments everything would end, and digging into his anguish, he asked the captain:
“Why did you come to my house? ” The other hesitated, then:
“I was interested in meeting you. ”
“Did it seem amusing to you? ”
I swear it did not. ”
“And then? ”
“Curiosity to know you.
Your wife has spoken to me a great deal about you lately.
Besides, I never imagined finding myself in such a situation... in reality, I could not explain why I have come. ”
“Have you seen?
There are inexplicable things.
For some time now I have been trying to explain to myself why I do not kill you with a shot, having the revolver here, in my pocket. ”
Elsa raised her head toward Erdosain, who stood at the head of the table... The captain asked:
“What is holding you back? ”
“In truth, I do not know... or... yes, I am sure it is because of this.
I believe that in the heart of each one of us there is a length of destiny.
It is like a divination of things through a mysterious instinct.
What is happening to me now, I feel it is contained within that length of destiny... something as if I had already seen it...
I do not know where. ”
“How? ”
“What are you saying? ”
“It was not because you gave me a reason... no...
I already told you... a remote certainty. ”
“I do not understand. ”
“But I understand myself.
Look, it is like this.
Suddenly it occurs to one that certain things must happen in life... so that life may transform itself and become new. ”
“And you? ”
“Do you believe that your life? ”
Erdosain, ignoring the question, continued:
“And what is happening now does not surprise me.
If you told me to go buy you a pack of cigarettes, by the way, do you have a cigarette? ”
“Help yourself... and then? ”
“I do not know.
Lately I have lived incoherently... stunned by anguish.
You see with what calm I am conversing with you. ”
“Yes, he always expected something extraordinary. ”
“And you too. ”
“How?
You, Elsa, too? ”
“Yes. ”
“But you? ”
“Go on, captain, I understand you.
You mean that the extraordinary thing for Elsa is happening now, isn’t it? ”
“Yes. ”
“Well, you are mistaken, isn’t that so, Elsa? ”
“Do you think so? ”
“Tell the truth, you are expecting something extraordinary that is not this, aren’t you? ”
“I don’t know. ”
“Have you seen, captain?
That was always our life.
The two of us would be silent beside this table... ”
“Be quiet. ”
“Why?
We were seated and without saying anything we understood what we were: two wretches with unequal desires.
And when we went to bed... ”
“Remo! ”
“Mr.
Erdosain! ”
“Stop the ridiculous gestures... aren’t you two going to bed together? ”
“We cannot continue talking in this way. ”
“All right, and when we separated we had this similar thought: and is the pleasure of life and love only this?...
And without saying anything we understood that we were thinking the same thing... but changing the subject... do you plan to stay here in the city? ”
Suddenly Erdosain had the cold sensation of travel.
He seemed to see Elsa at the railing, beneath the row of glassy portholes, contemplating the blue thread of the distance.
The sun fell on the yellow cleats of the masts and on the black gallows of the winches.
It was growing late, but they remained with their thoughts fixed on other climates, in the shade of the deck awnings, leaning on the white gangway.
The wind blew iodized on the waves and Elsa looked at the waters through whose changing lattice her shadow came alive.
At times her little pale face turned and then both seemed to hear a reproach rising from the depths of the sea.
And Erdosain imagined that it said to them:
“What have you done with the poor little boy?
” (“Because I, in spite of my age, was like a boy,” Remo told me later.
“You understand, a man who lets his wife be taken from under his nose... is a wretch... is like a boy, you understand? ”)
Erdosain pulled himself out of the hallucination.
That question which had arisen in him was digging against his will.
“Will you write to me? ”
“What for? ”
“Yes, of course, what for?
” he repeated, closing his eyes.
He felt himself now more than ever fallen into a depth no man had ever dreamed of.
“Well, Mr. Erdosain,” and the captain rose, “we are leaving. ”
“Ah, you are going!...
You are going already? ”
Elsa held out her gloved hand.
“Are you leaving? ”
“Yes...
I am leaving... you understand that... ”
“Yes...
I understand. ”
“It could not be, Remo. ”
“Yes, of course... it could not be... of course... ”
The captain, describing a circle around the table, picked up the suitcase, the very suitcase Elsa had brought on the day of their wedding.
“Mr.
Erdosain, goodbye. ”
“At your service, captain... but one thing... are you leaving... you, Elsa... you are leaving? ”
“Yes, we are leaving. ”
“Excuse me, I am going to sit down.
Allow me a moment, captain... just a moment. ”
The intruder repressed words of impatience.
He had a brutal desire to shout at that husband:
“Attention, stand at attention, imbecile,” but out of consideration for Elsa he restrained himself.
Suddenly Erdosain left the chair.
Slowly he went to a corner of the room.
Then, turning abruptly to the captain, he said in a very clear voice, in which one could guess the contained desire that it should be gentle:
“Do you know why I do not kill you like a dog? ”
The others turned, alarmed.
“Because I am cold. ”
Now Erdosain walked from one side of the room to the other, with his hands crossed behind his back.
They watched him, waiting for something.
At last the husband, smiling with a pale grimace, continued softly, his voice languid in a desperation of held-back sobbing:
“Yes, I was cold...
I am cold.
” Now his gaze had become vague, but he smiled with the same strange, hallucinated smile.
“Listen to me... this will have no explanation for you, but I have found the explanation. ”
His eyes shone extraordinarily and his voice grew hoarse through the effort he made to speak.
“Look... my life has been horribly offended... horribly bruised. ”
He fell silent, stopping in a corner of the room.
On his face remained the strange smile of a man living a dangerous dream.
Elsa, suddenly irritated, bit the tip of her handkerchief.
The captain, standing beside the suitcase, waited.
Suddenly Erdosain took the revolver from his pocket and threw it into a corner.
The Browning chipped the plaster of the wall, striking the floor heavily.
“What is this piece of junk good for!
” he murmured.
Then, with one hand in the pocket of his jacket and his temple leaning against the wall, he spoke slowly: “Yes, my life has been horribly offended... humiliated.
Believe me, captain.
Do not be impatient.
I am going to tell you something.
The one who began this ferocious work of humiliation was my father.
When I was ten years old and had committed some fault, he would say to me: ‘Tomorrow I will beat you.’
“It was always like that, tomorrow...
Do you understand?
Tomorrow...

And that night I would sleep, but I slept badly, with a dog’s sleep, waking at midnight to look frightened at the windowpanes and see if it was already day, but when the moonlight cut across the bars of the little window, I would close my eyes, telling myself: there is still a lot of time.
Later I would wake again upon hearing the roosters crow.

The moon was no longer there, but a bluish clarity entered through the glass, and then I would cover my head with the sheets so as not to see it, although I knew it was there... although I knew there was no human force that could drive away that clarity.
And when at last I had fallen asleep for a long time, a hand would shake my head on the pillow.
It was he who said to me in a harsh voice: ‘Come on... it is time.’ And while I dressed slowly, I could hear that man moving the chair in the patio.
‘Come on,’ he would shout again, and I, hypnotized, would go in a straight line toward him: I wanted to speak, but that was impossible before his terrible gaze.
His hand would fall on my shoulder, forcing me to kneel; I would rest my chest on the seat of the chair, he would take my head between his knees and, suddenly, cruel lashes would cross my buttocks.
When he let me go, I would run crying to my room.
An enormous shame would sink my soul into darkness.
Because darkness exists even if you do not believe it. ”
Elsa looked at her husband, startled.
The captain, standing with his arms crossed, listened bored.
Erdosain smiled vaguely. He continued:

“I knew that most boys were not beaten by their fathers and at school, when I heard them talk about their homes, an anguish so atrocious would paralyze me that if we were in class and the teacher called me, I would look at him stunned, without grasping the sense of his questions, until one day he shouted at me: ‘But you, Erdosain, are you an imbecile who does not hear me?’ The whole class burst out laughing, and from that day they called me Erdosain ‘the imbecile.’ And I, sadder, feeling more offended than ever, kept silent for fear of my father’s lashes, smiling at those who insulted me... but timidly.
Do you understand, captain?
They insult you... and you still smile timidly, as if they were doing you a favor by insulting you. ”
The intruder frowned.
“Later—permit me, captain—later they called me ‘the imbecile’ many times.

Then suddenly my soul would shrink along my nerves, and that sensation that the soul was hiding ashamed inside my own flesh annihilated all courage; feeling that I was sinking deeper and deeper and looking into the eyes of the one who insulted me, instead of knocking him down with a slap, I would say to myself: Does this man realize to what extent he is humiliating me?
Then I would go away; I understood that the others were only finishing what my father had begun.
“And now,” the captain replied, “am I also sinking you? ”
“No, man, not you.
Naturally, I have suffered so much that now courage is shrunk inside me, hidden.
I am my own spectator and I ask myself: When will my courage leap out?
And that is the event I am waiting for.
Some day something monstrous will explode in me and I will become another man.
“Then, if you are still alive, I will come looking for you and I will spit in your face.
The intruder looked at him serenely.
“But not out of hatred, but to play with my courage, which will seem to me the newest thing in the world...
Now you may withdraw. ”
The intruder hesitated a moment.
Erdosain’s gaze, intensely enlarged, was fixed on him.
He took the suitcase and left.
Elsa stopped, trembling, before her husband.
“Well, I am going, Remo... it was necessary that this should end this way. ”
“But you?...
“And what did you want me to do? ”
“I don’t know. ”
“And then?
Stay calm, I beg you.
I have already left your clothes ready.
Change your collar.
You always make one feel ashamed. ”
“But you, Elsa... you?
And our plans? ”
“Illusions, Remo... splendors. ”
“Yes, splendors... but where did you learn such a beautiful word?
Splendors. ”
“I don’t know. ”
“And our life will remain forever broken? ”
“What do you want?
Yet I was good.
Later I came to hate you... but why weren’t you the same?... ”
“Ah, yes... the same... the same... ”
Grief stunned him like a great sunny day in the tropics.
His eyelids were falling.
He would have liked to sleep.
The meaning of the words sank into his understanding with the slowness of a stone in water that is too thick.
When the word touched the bottom of his consciousness, dark forces twisted his anguish.
And for an instant, at the bottom of his chest, his weeds of suffering remained floating and trembling as in the mire of a puddle.
She continued with a voice pacified by an inner resignation:
“Now it is useless... now I am leaving.
Why weren’t you good?
Why didn’t you work?
” Erdosain had the certainty like her, and an immense pity made him fall onto the edge of the chair, his head crushed on the arm stretched across the table.
“So you are leaving?
You are really leaving? ”
“Yes, I want to see if our life improves, you know?
Look at my hands,” and removing the glove from her right hand she showed it bruised by the cold, bitten by lye, pricked by sewing needles, darkened by the soot of saucepans.
Erdosain stood up, rigid with hallucination.

He saw his unfortunate wife in the monstrous tumult of cities of Portland stone and iron, crossing dark diagonals in the slanting shadow of the skyscrapers beneath a threatening net of black high-tension cables.
A crowd of businessmen passed by protected by umbrellas.
Her little face was paler than ever, but she remembered him while the breath of strangers cut across her profile.
“Where will my little boy be? ”
Erdosain interrupted his projection of the future:
“Elsa... you know... come whenever you want... you can come... but tell the truth, did you ever love me? ”
Slowly she raised her eyelids.
Her pupils widened.
Her voice filled the room with human warmth.
It seemed to Erdosain that he was living now.
“I always loved you...
I love you now too... never, why did you never speak as you have spoken tonight?
I feel that I am going to love you all my life... that the other man beside you is the shadow of a man... ”
“Soul, my poor soul... what a life ours was... what a life... ”
A curl of a smile painfully wrinkled her lips.
Elsa looked at him ardently for an instant.
Then, with a voice serious with promises:
“Look... wait for me.
If life is as you always told me, I will come back, you know?, and then, if you want, we will kill ourselves together...
Are you happy? ”
A wave of blood rose to the man’s temples.
“Soul, how good you are, soul... give me that hand,” and while she, still startled, smiled timidly, Erdosain kissed it.
“You are not angry, soul? ”
She raised her head, grave with happiness.
“Look, Remo...
I am going to come, you know?, and if what you say about life is true... yes, I will come...
I am going to come. ”
“Are you going to come? ”
“With whatever I have. ”
“Even if you are rich? ”
“Even if I have all the millions on earth, I will come.
I swear it! ”
“Soul, poor soul!
What a soul you have!
Yet you never knew me... it doesn’t matter... ah, our life! ”
“It doesn’t matter.
I am happy.
Do you realize your surprise, Remo?
You are all alone at night.
You are alone... suddenly, click... the door opens... and it is me... me who has come!
You are wearing an evening suit... white shoes and you have a pearl necklace.
“And I came alone, on foot through the dark streets, looking for you... but you do not see me, you are alone... your head... ”
“Say it... speak... speak... ”
“Your head resting on your hand and your elbow on the table... you look at me... and suddenly... ”
“I recognize you and I say: Elsa, is it you, Elsa? ”
“And I answer you: Remo, I have come, do you remember that night?
That night is this night and outside the great wind is blowing and we have neither cold nor sorrow.
Are you happy, Remo? ”
“Yes, I swear I am happy. ”
“Well, I am going. ”
“Are you going? ”
The man’s face deformed in sudden grief.
“Well, go then. ”
“Until soon, my husband. ”
“What did you say? ”
“I tell you this, Remo.
Wait for me.
Even if I have all the millions in the world, I will return. ”
“Well... then goodbye... but give me a kiss. ”
“No, when I return... goodbye, my husband. ”
Suddenly, Erdosain, propelled by a spasm without a name, seized her brutally by the wrists.
“Tell me: did you sleep with him?
” “Let me go, Remo...
I did not think you... ”
“Confess, did you sleep with him or not? ”
“No. ”
In the doorframe the captain stopped.
An immense weakness relaxed the nerves of his fingers.
Erdosain felt himself falling and saw no more.
He never became aware of how he dragged himself to his bed.
Time ceased to exist for Erdosain.
He closed his eyes obeying the need for sleep that his aching entrails demanded.
Had he had the strength, he would have thrown himself into a well.
Gushes of despair crowded in his throat, suffocating him, and his eyes grew more sensitive to the darkness than an open sore to salt.
At times he ground his teeth to deaden the creaking of his taut nerves inside his flesh, which surrendered, with the limpness of a sponge, to the waves of shadow cast up by his brain.
He had the sensation of falling into a bottomless pit and he squeezed his eyelids shut.
He never finished descending—who knows how many leagues of invisible length his physical body had, which could not halt the sinking of his consciousness now heaped into a bristling mass of despair!
From his eyelids fell successive layers of denser darkness.
His center of pain struggled uselessly.
He could find no single fissure in his soul through which to escape.
Erdosain contained all the suffering of the world, the pain of the world’s negation.
In what corner of the earth could a man be found whose skin was bristling with more folds of bitterness?
He felt he was no longer a man, but an open sore covered with skin, which shuddered and screamed at every beat of his veins.
And yet he lived.
He lived simultaneously in the remoteness and in the appalling proximity of his own body.
He was no longer an organism containing suffering, but something more inhuman... perhaps that... a monster coiled in upon itself in the black belly of the room.
Each layer of darkness descending from his eyelids was a placental tissue that isolated him more and more from the universe of men.
The walls grew, their courses of bricks rose higher, and new cataracts of shadow fell into that cube where he lay coiled and throbbing like a snail in an oceanic depth.
He could not recognize himself... he doubted that he was Augusto Remo Erdosain.

He pressed his forehead between his fingertips, and the flesh of his hand seemed strange to him and he did not recognize the flesh of his forehead, as if his body were made of two different substances.
Who knows what had already died in him?
Only a consciousness foreign to what had happened to him endured for his sensibility, a soul no longer than the blade of a sword that vibrated like a lamprey in the turbid water of his life.
Even the consciousness of being occupied, in him, no more than a square centimeter of sensibility.
Yes, his whole body lived, was in contact with the earth, only through a square centimeter of sensibility.
The rest vanished into the darkness.
Yes, he was a square centimeter of a man, a square centimeter of existence prolonging, with its sensitive surface, the incoherent life of a ghost.
The rest had died in him, had merged with the placenta of darkness that armored his atrocious reality.
Stronger and stronger grew within him the revelation that he was at the bottom of a cube of Portland cement.
A sensation from another world!
An invisible sun forever illuminated the walls with an orange storm-light.
The wing of a solitary bird brushed a touch of sky blue above the rectangle of the walls, but he would remain forever at the bottom of that taciturn cube, lit by an orange storm-sun.
Then the capacity of his life was reduced to that single square centimeter of sensibility.
He could even “see” the beating of his heart, and it was useless to try to reject the appalling figure that weighed him down at the bottom of that abyss, black one moment and orange the next.
If he relaxed his will even a little, the reality it contained would have screamed in his ears.
Erdosain did not want to look and yet wanted to look... but it was useless... his wife was there, at the bottom of a room upholstered in blue.
The captain moved in a corner.
He knew, though no one had told him, that it was a tiny bedroom, hexagonal in shape and almost entirely occupied by a wide, low bed.

He did not want to look at Elsa... no... no... he wanted to, but even if they had threatened him with death he could not have stopped staring at the man who was undressing in front of her... in front of his lawful wife who was no longer with him... but with another.

Stronger than his fear was his need for more terror, for more suffering, and suddenly she, covering her eyes with her fingers, ran toward the naked man with stiff legs, pressed herself against him and no longer shunned the livid erect virility in the blue depth.
Erdosain felt himself flattened in a perfection of horror.
Had they passed him between the rollers of a steel mill, his life could not have been flatter.
Were not the toads that the cartwheel crushed on the road left like that—flattened and burning?

But he did not want to look, so little did he want to look that now he saw with clarity how Elsa leaned against the man’s square, hairy chest while his hands cupped the woman’s jaw to lift her face toward his mouth.
And suddenly Elsa exclaimed: “Me too, my darling... me too.

” Her face had flushed with desperation, her clothes swirled around the triangle of her milk-white thighs, and with eyes enraptured by the man’s rigid trembling muscle, she uncovered the mane of her sex, her erect breasts... ah!... why was he looking?
Uselessly Elsa... yes, Elsa, his lawful wife, tried with her small hand to encompass all that virility in a caress.

The man, beneath the howl of his desire, pressed his temples, covered his eyes with his forearm; but she, leaning over him, drove this white-hot iron into his ears: “You’re more beautiful than my husband!
How beautiful you are, my God! ”
If they had slowly twisted his head on his neck to screw that atrocious vision deep into his soul, he could not have suffered more.
He suffered so much that if the pain were to cease, his spirit would explode like a shrapnel shell.
How can a soul bear so much pain?
And yet he wanted to suffer more.
That they should split his back with an axe on a chopping block in several places...
And if they had thrown him in four pieces into a garbage bin he would have gone on suffering.
There was not a square centimeter in his body that did not bear that extreme pressure of anguish.
All the cords had snapped under the tension of the dreadful vise, and suddenly a sensation of repose balanced his limbs.
He no longer desired anything.
His life ran silently downhill, like a lake after the breaking of its dam, and, without sleeping but with his eyelids closed, the lucid faint was more anesthetic to his pain than a chloroform dream.
His heart beat noticeably.

With difficulty he moved his head to lift his scalp from the overheated pillow, and he remained there with no other sensation of living than that coolness at the nape of his neck and the opening and closing of his heart, which, like an enormous eye, lifted its drowsy lid to recognize the darkness, nothing more.
Nothing more than the darkness?
Elsa was so far from his memory that in that transitory hypnosis it seemed a lie that he had ever known her.
Who knows if she existed physically.
Before he could see her; now he had to make a great effort to recognize her... and he barely could.
The truth was that she was not she and he was not he.
Now his life ran silently downhill; he felt himself in a retreat of years, the child who watched a green tree shading the continual disappearance of a river among stones with red stains.
He himself was a cascade of flesh in the darknesses.
Who could say when he would finish bleeding out!
And only the closing and opening of his heart was noticeable, which like an enormous eye lifted its drowsy lid to recognize the darkness.
The streetlamp halfway down the block filtered through a crack a slash of silver that fell upon the tulle of the mosquito net.
His sensibility painfully recovered itself.
He was Erdosain.
He recognized himself now.
With a great effort he arched his back.
Beneath the door that closed off the entrance to the dining room a yellow strip was visible.
He had forgotten to turn off the light.
He owed... ah, no!
No, Elsa has left... he owes six hundred pesos and seven cents to the Limited Sugar Company... but no, he no longer owes it, since he has a check...
Ah, reality, reality!
The oblique parallelogram of light that came from the street to silver the tulle of the mosquito net was the notion that he lived as before, as yesterday, as ten years ago.
He did not want to see that line of light, just as when he was small he had not wanted to “see that brightness that was there, although he knew no human force could drive that brightness away.
” Yes, similar to when his father told him he was going to beat him the next day.
It was not the same now.
That other brightness had been bluish; this one was silver, yet as strident and as announcer of the true as the old light.
Sweat dampened his temples and the circle of his hair.
Elsa had gone and would she never come back?
What would Barsut say?
Suddenly someone stopped in front of the street door.
Erdosain understood that it was him and leapt out of bed.
As usual, Barsut knocked trying not to make any noise.
With his voice hoarse, Erdosain shouted at him:
“Come in.
What are you doing out there?
Come in! ”
Barsut entered, shifting his weight onto his heels.
“I’m coming,” Remo shouted while the other man stepped into the dining room.
By the time he entered, Barsut had already sat down, crossing his legs, with his back, as usual, to the door and his profile turned toward the southeast corner of the room.
“What are you doing? ”
“How are you? ”
He rested his elbow on the edge of the table, his cheek propped on his fist, and the light cast a coppery redness over the white flesh of his hand.
Beneath his eyebrows, which stretched toward his temples, his green eyes tempered their hard glassiness with a temperature of inquiry.

And Erdosain made out his face as though through a haze of lights flickering above: the receding forehead with temples sloping toward pointed ears, the bony nose of a bird of prey, the flat chin built to withstand tremendous blows, and the neat knot of the black tie rising from the starched collar. In a dull tone, the other man asked:
“And Elsa? ”
Erdosain recovered the clarity of his mind.
“She went out. ”

They fell silent and Erdosain remained staring at the right angle formed by the gray sleeve of the jacket against the white edge of the table, and at the cheek that the lamp illuminated with a copper red all the way to the bridge of the nose, while the other half of the face remained, from the roots of the hair to the dimple in the chin, in a darkness where the hollow beneath the eye deepened into a basin of shadow.
Barsut slowly swung one leg crossed over the other.
“Ah!
” Erdosain heard, and asked: “What did you say? ”
It was that Erdosain had only now registered the “ah” that had been uttered several seconds earlier.
“Elsa went out?... ”
Barsut straightened his head, his eyebrows rose to let more light into his eyelids, and with his lips slightly parted he breathed:
“She left? ”
Erdosain frowned, examined the other man’s shoes out of the corner of his eye, and, half-closing his eyelids, spying through that filtered gaze the anguish in Barsut, let fall slowly:
“Yes... she... left... with... a... man... ”
And winking his left eyelid like the pharmacist Ergueta, he tilted his head.
Beneath the bronzed line of his eyebrows his pupils waited fiercely. Erdosain went on:
“You see?
There’s the revolver.
I could have killed them both and yet I didn’t.
What a strange animal man is, isn’t he? ”
“And you let them take your wife right under your nose? ”

In Erdosain the ancient hatred, now exacerbated by the fresh humiliation, turned into a motive for cruel jubilation and, with a voice trembling in his throat and his mouth dry with rancor, he exclaimed:
“What does it matter to you? ”
A tremendous slap sent him reeling on the chair.
Later he remembered Barsut’s arm drawing back and advancing, kneading his flesh.
He covered his face with both hands, tried to escape that mass that kept advancing on him like an unleashed force of nature.
His head struck dully against the wall and he fell.
When he came to, Barsut was kneeling beside him.
He noticed that his collar was unfastened and that threads of water were running down to his throat.
From the bridge of his nose a throbbing pain rose along the bone, and every moment he felt as though he were about to sneeze.
His gums were bleeding slowly and beneath the swelling of his lips the surface of his teeth showed.
Erdosain rose with difficulty and dropped onto a chair.
Barsut was so pale that two flames seemed to leap from his eyes.
From cheekbones to ears, bundles of muscle traced two trembling arcs.
Erdosain had the sensation of swaying in an endless dream, but he understood when the other man took him by the arm and said:
“Look, spit in my face if you want, but let me talk.
I have to tell you everything. ”
“Sit down... there, like that.
” Erdosain had risen unconsciously.
“Listen to me, please.
You see, don’t you?
I could beat you to death...
I just lost control...
I swear... if you want I’ll beg your forgiveness on my knees.
What can I say, I’m like that.
Look... ah... ah... if people only knew. ”
Erdosain spat blood.
A band of heat embraced his forehead, entering through his temples and stabbing all the way to the nape of his neck.
His back hunched so sharply that he rested his head on the edge of the table. Seeing him like that, Barsut asked:
“Do you want to wash your face?
It’ll do you good.
Wait a moment, don’t get up.
” And he ran to the kitchen, returning with the basin full of water.
“Wash yourself.
It’ll do you good.
Want me to rub it in?
Look, forgive me, it was an impulse.
You too, why did you wink like you were mocking me?
Wash yourself, please. ”
In silence Erdosain stood up and plunged his face into the basin several times.
When he ran out of breath he lifted his face from the surface of the water.
Then he sat down and the air evaporated the moisture from his hair near the temples.
How tired he was!
Ah, if Elsa could see him!
How she would pity him!
He closed his eyes. Barsut drew his chair closer and said:
“I have to tell you everything.
If I didn’t I’d feel like a bastard.
You see, I’m speaking calmly.
Look, if you don’t believe me put your hand on my heart.
I’m being sincere.
Well, I...
I denounced you to the sugar company...
I was the one who sent the anonymous letter. ”
Erdosain did not even raise his head.
Him or the other one—what did it matter!
Barsut looked at him; he expected who knows what words, and said:
“Why don’t you say anything?
Yes, I denounced you.
Do you understand?
I denounced you.
I wanted to get you thrown in jail, to keep Elsa, to humiliate her.
You can’t imagine the nights I’ve spent thinking they would lock you up!
You had no way to come up with the money and they would inevitably denounce you.
But why don’t you say anything? ”
Erdosain raised his eyelids.
Barsut was there, yes, it was him, and he was saying all these things.
From cheekbones to ears, beneath the skin, the reflection of the muscles trembled imperceptibly.
Barsut lowered his eyes, rested his elbows on his knees as though he were sitting before a hearth, and in a slow voice insisted:
“I have to tell you everything.
Who else could I tell all these things that make the heart ache?
They say, and it’s true, that the heart doesn’t ache, but believe me, at times I say to myself: why go on living?
Where is life going if I am like this?
Do you understand?
You have to see all that I’ve pondered thinking these things.
Look, I probably shouldn’t even tell you.
How is it that a man does something vile to another person, then approaches him and tells him his most intimate secrets, and feels no remorse?
I’ve asked myself many times: why don’t I feel remorse?
What kind of life is this if we commit an atrocity and feel nothing?
Do you understand this?
According to what we studied in school, a crime eventually drives the criminal mad, so how is it that in reality you commit a crime and remain perfectly calm? ”
Erdosain continued staring fixedly at Barsut; now the image of that man was settling at the bottom of his consciousness.
The forces of his life wrapped the pale relief in a mesh so intense that the imprint being made in those instants would never again be erased.
“Look,” Barsut continued, “I knew you hated me, that if you could have killed me you would have, and that both gladdened and saddened me at the same time.
How many nights I went to bed thinking of ways to kidnap you!
It even occurred to me to send you a bomb in the mail, or a snake in a cardboard box.
Or to pay a driver to run you over in the street.
I would close my eyes and the hours would pass thinking about the two of you.
Do you think I loved her?
” Erdosain noticed later that throughout that night’s conversation Barsut avoided saying Elsa’s name.
“No, I never loved her.
But I would have liked to humiliate her, you know?
To humiliate her for no reason: to see you ruined so that she would beg me on her knees to help you.
Do you understand?
I never loved her.
If I denounced you it was for that, to humiliate her, who was always so proud with me.
And when you told me you had defrauded the sugar company, a savage joy churned my guts.
And before you had finished speaking I said to myself: well, now we’ll see where her pride ends. ” Erdosain let the question escape:
“But you loved her?... ”
“No, I never loved her.
If you only knew how she made me suffer!
Me love her, when she never even gave me her hand?
Every time she looked at me it seemed she was spitting in my face.
Ah, you were the husband, but you never really knew her!
What do you know about what kind of woman she is!
Look, she could watch you die and not make a single gesture of pity.
Do you understand?
I remember.
When the Astraldi firm went bankrupt and you were left in the street, if she had asked me for everything I had, I would have given it to her.
I would have given her my whole fortune just to hear her say ‘thank you.’ Nothing more than thank you.
For that word I would have been left with nothing.
One day when I tried to start a conversation she answered: Remo is man enough to earn for the two of us.
Ah, you don’t know her!
She would be capable of watching you die without making a gesture.
And I would think.
How many things, my God, pass through a man’s head!

I would throw myself on a bed and start imagining things... you had murdered a man... it was necessary to save you and then she would come to me begging for help and I, without saying a word about my sacrifices, would run here and there.
What a woman, Remo!
What a woman!
I remember when she used to sew.
I would have stayed beside her, you know? holding the seam for her, and I knew she was not happy with you.
I could see it in her face, in her weariness, in her smile. ”
Erdosain remembered the words Elsa had spoken an hour earlier:
“It doesn’t matter...
I’m happy.
Can you imagine your surprise, Remo?
You’re all alone at night, you’re alone...
Suddenly, creak... the door opens... and it’s me... me, who has come. ” Barsut continued:
“And of course I asked myself what it was that made her bear life at your side, beside a man like you... ”
“And I came on foot alone through the dark streets, looking for you, but you don’t see me, you’re alone, your head... ”
Erdosain felt his ideas whirling on the surface of his brain like a whirlpool of water.
The giant cone drove its spiral down to the root of his limbs.
A whirlpool whose soft friction drew from his soul a pained, new tenderness.
How good Elsa’s words were, what extraordinary content!
“I always loved you.
I love you now too... never, why did you never speak like tonight?
I feel that I’m going to love you all my life, that the other man beside you is the shadow of a man. ”
Erdosain now had the certainty that these words would save his soul forever, while Barsut heaped up an envious anguish:
“And I would have liked to ask her what she found at your side, to open your chest in front of her and prove to her until she was tired that you were a madman, a bastard, a coward...
I swear I say these words without anger. ”
“I believe you,” Erdosain replied.
“Right now, looking at you, I ask myself: with what eyes does a woman look at a man?
That is something we will never know.
Don’t you think?
To me you were a wretch whom one could brush aside with a backhand.
But to her, who were you?
That is the dark point.
Did you ever know?
Tell me frankly: in your heart did you ever know what kind of man you were to your wife?
What did she see in you to suffer so much at your side, and to put up with you the way she did? ”
How gravely Barsut spoke!
His hoarse questions demanded an answer.

Erdosain felt him nearby not as a man but precisely as a double, a specter with a bony nose and bronze hair who had suddenly become a piece of his own consciousness, since, as it had done on other occasions, it was now directing the same questions at him.
Yes, it was probable that in order to live in peace it would be necessary to exterminate him, and the “idea” revealed itself coldly within him.
“Like a sword entering a block of cotton,” Erdosain would say later.
Barsut did not remotely imagine that at that instant Remo had just condemned him to death.
Explaining to me later the circumstances of that conception, Erdosain told me:
“Have you ever seen a general on a battlefield?...
But to make my idea more accessible I’ll put it in the terms of an inventor: You search for a certain time for the solution to a problem.
You know, you are certain that the key, the secret, is inside you, but you cannot grasp it, so covered is the secret with layers of mystery.
And one day, at the most unexpected moment, suddenly the plan, the complete vision of the machine, appears before your eyes, dazzling you with its easy precision.
It is something marvelous!

Imagine a general on a battlefield... everything is lost, and suddenly, clear and precise, a solution appears to him that he had never dreamed of conceiving, and yet it was there, within reach of his hand, inside himself.

In that instant I knew that I had to have Barsut killed, and he, in front of me, piling up useless words, had no idea that I, with my swollen mouth and aching nose, was holding back a stupendous joy, a dazzlement similar to what one feels when what has been discovered is as fatal as a mathematical law.
Perhaps there also exists a mathematics of the spirit whose terrible laws are not as inviolable as those that govern combinations of numbers and lines.
Because it is curious.
That slap that was still making my gum bleed, like the die of a hydraulic press, stamped on my consciousness the definitive lines of a plan of death.
Do you see?
A plan is three general lines, three admissible straight lines, nothing more.

And in a tumult my delight piled up over that cold relief whose three synthetic lines contained this: kidnap Barsut, have him killed, and with his money found the secret society as the Astrologer wished.
Do you see?
The plan for the crime arose spontaneously in me while the other man spoke sadly of our two condemned souls.
The plan appeared in me as if it had been stamped on an iron plate under thousands of pounds of pressure.
“Ah!
How can I explain it?

Suddenly I forgot everything, held by a frozen contemplation full of joy, something like the dawn that discovers a habitual night-owl and relieves him of his fatigue on the morning that follows a night full of exhaustion.
Do you see?
To have Barsut assassinated by a man who urgently needed money to carry out a brilliant idea.

And this new dawn that beat inside me was so perfectly individualized that many times afterward I have asked myself what secret the soul of a man can hold that, successively, shows him new horizons, peeling away sensations that are a surprise even to himself because of their apparently illogical origin. ”
In the course of this story I have forgotten to say that when Erdosain became enthusiastic he would revolve around the “idea” with a multitude of words.
He needed to exhaust every possibility of expression, possessed by that slow frenzy that, through the phrases, gave him the consciousness of being an extraordinary man and not a wretch.
That he was telling the truth I had no doubt.
What often confused me was the question I asked myself: where did that man draw the energy to endure his own spectacle for so long?
He did nothing but examine himself, analyze what was happening inside him, as if the sum of details could give him the certainty that he was alive.
I insist.
A dead man who had the power to converse would speak no more than he did, in order to assure himself that he was not, apparently, dead.
Barsut, unaware of all that had just occurred in the other man, continued:
“Ah, you never knew her... you never knew her.
Look, listen to what I’m going to tell you.
One afternoon I went to see you, I knew you weren’t there, I wanted to find her, to see her, even if only for a moment.
I arrived sweating; I don’t know how many blocks I walked in the sun before I made up my mind.
“Just like me, in the sun,” thought Erdosain.

“And that’s even though you know I didn’t lack money for a car, and even when I asked for you, she, without moving from the threshold, answered: Excuse me, I won’t let you in because my husband is not here.
Do you see what a bitch? ” Erdosain thought:
“There’s still a train for Temperley. ” Barsut continued:
“And I, who saw you as such a poor specimen, said to myself: what could Elsa have seen in this wretch to fall in love with him? ”
In an utterly calm voice Erdosain asked him:
“And does it show on my face that I’m a wretch? ”
Barsut raised his head, surprised.
For a moment he kept his translucent greenish pupils fixed on his interlocutor.
The sheet of light that fell on both of them interposed a dreamlike distance.
And Barsut understood himself to be as much a ghost as the other, because, moving his head with difficulty, as though suddenly all the muscles of his neck had stiffened, he answered:
“No, looking at you closely you seem like a man seized by a fixed idea... who knows what. ” Erdosain replied:
“You’re a psychologist.
Naturally, I still don’t know what that fixed idea consists of, but it’s curious, it never occurred to me that you were thinking of taking my wife from me...
And the calm with which you say these things... ”
“You won’t deny that I’m being frank with you... ”
“Besides, I wanted to humiliate her... not to steal her from you, what for?
Since I knew she would never love me. ”
“And how did you guess that? ”
“That’s what I don’t know.
Because one does certain things that cannot be explained.
Because she treated you and you treated me without either of us being able to ‘stand’ the other.
I came because coming made you suffer and I suffered.
Every day I would say to myself: I won’t go anymore...
I won’t go anymore...
But as soon as the hour arrived I would get nervous.
It was as if someone were calling me from somewhere, and then I would dress hurriedly... and come... ”
Erdosain suddenly had a singular idea, and said:
“Speaking of everything at once...
I don’t know if you know that this morning at the sugar company they spoke to me about the anonymous letter.
If I don’t render accounts they’ll put me in jail tomorrow.
The only one guilty, and I think you won’t mind admitting it, of this happening is you, so you have to provide me with the money.
Where am I going to get that amount? ”
Barsut straightened up, astonished.
“But how?
After I turn out to be a cuckold and beaten, after Elsa leaves and I commit an infamy, I’m the one who has to give you the money?
Are you crazy?
What advantage is there for me in giving you six hundred pesos?... ”
“With seven cents... ”
Erdosain stood up.
“Is that your last word? ”
“But understand, how could I?... ”
“Well, my boy...
Patience.
Now do me the favor of leaving, I want to sleep. ”
“Don’t you want us to go out? ”
“I’m tired.
Leave me. ”
Barsut hesitated.
Then, rising and with his hat held by one brim, he left the room clumsily.

Erdosain heard the bang the door made when it closed, brooded with a frown for an instant, searched in his pocket for a railway timetable, looked at the schedule, then washed himself again, and in front of the mirror combed his hair.
His lip was purple, a red stain bordered his nose, and another circled his temple near the hairline.
He looked around searching for something, saw the revolver on the floor, picked it up and left.
But since he had left the light on, he returned and turned off the lamp.
Everything was dark now; like the trail of a light a gleam shone before his eyes and he went out.
For the second time that day he was going to the Astrologer’s house.
«To Be» through a crime
A section of the platform at Témperley station was weakly lit by the light spilling from the telegraph office door.
Erdosain sat down on a bench beside the switch levers, in the darkness.
He was cold and perhaps feverish.
Moreover, he had the impression that the criminal idea was a continuation of his own body, like a man of darkness that he could cast into the light.

A red disk glowed at the end of the semaphore’s invisible arm; beyond it, other red and green circles were nailed to the darkness, and the curve of the galvanised rail, bathed in those lights, submerged its bluish or carmine roundness in the shadows.
At times the red or green light would descend.
Then everything remained still, the chains no longer creaking in the pulleys and the scrape of the wires against the stones falling silent.
He grew drowsy.
“What am I doing here?
Why am I staying here?
Is it true that I want to kill him?
Or do I only want to have the will to feel the desire to kill him?
Is that necessary?
By now she must be writhing with him.
But what does that matter to me?

Before, when I knew she was alone at home while I was at the café, I suffered for her, I suffered because she was miserable at my side... now—obviously... they must have fallen asleep by now, her head resting on his chest.
God’s name!
And this is life?
To be lost, always lost!
But am I really the one I am?
Or am I someone else?
The sadness!
To live with strangeness!
That is what is happening to me.
The same as with him.
When he is far away I imagine him exactly as he is: a scoundrel, wretched.
He almost broke my nose.
But how magnificent!
It turns out in the end that the cuckold who got beaten is him and not me!
Really, life is a clown show!
And yet there is something serious in it.
Why does he disgust me when he is near? ”
Some shadows swayed before the telegraph office’s yellow windowpane.
“Kill him or not kill him?
What does this matter to me?
Does it matter to me to kill him?
Let us be honest.
Does it matter to me to kill him?
Or does nothing matter to me?
Is it all the same to me whether he lives?
And yet I want to have the will to kill him.
If a god came now and asked me: Do you want the strength to destroy humanity?
Would I destroy it?
Would I?
No, I would not destroy it.
Because the power to do so would rob the matter of all interest.
Besides, what would I do alone on the earth?
Watch the dynamos rusting in the workshops and the skeletons crumbling on top of the boilers?
It is true that he slapped me, but does that matter to me?
What a list!
What a collection!
The Captain, Elsa, Barsut, the Man with the Boar’s Head, the Astrologer, the Pimp, Ergueta.
What a list!
Where could so many monsters have come from?
I myself am off-centre, I am not who I am, and yet I need to do something in order to become conscious of my existence, to affirm it.
Exactly that, to affirm it.
Because I am like a dead man.
I do not exist for the Captain, nor for Elsa, nor for Barsut.
They can, if they wish, have me thrown in prison, Barsut can slap me again, Elsa can go off with another man right under my nose, the Captain can carry her off once more.
For everyone I am the negation of life.
I am something like non-being.
A man is not as action, therefore he does not exist.
Or does he exist despite not being?
He is and is not.
There are those men.
Surely they have wives, children, a house.
Perhaps they are wretches.
But if someone tried to invade their home, to snatch a cent from them or to touch their woman, they would turn into wild beasts.
And why have I not rebelled?
Who can answer this question for me?
I myself cannot.
I know that I exist in this way, as negation.
And when I say all these things to myself I am not sad; rather my soul falls silent, my head empties.
Then, after that silence and emptiness, the curiosity for murder rises from my heart.
Exactly that.
I am not mad, since I can think, I can reason.
The curiosity for murder rises in me, a curiosity that must be my final sadness, the sadness of curiosity.
Or the demon of curiosity.
To see how I am through a crime.
That, exactly that.
To see how my conscience and my sensibility behave in the act of a crime.
“Yet these words do not give me the sensation of the crime in the same way that a telegram about a catastrophe in China does not give me the sensation of the catastrophe.
It is as if I were not the one thinking the murder, but another.
Another who would be like me, a flat man, a shadow of a man, in the manner of the cinema.
It has relief, it moves, it seems to exist, to suffer, and yet it is nothing more than a shadow.
It lacks life.
Let God say whether this is not well reasoned.
Very well: what would the shadow-man do?
The shadow-man would perceive the event but would not feel its weight, because it lacked volume to contain any mass.
It is a shadow.
I too see the event, but I do not contain it.
This must be a new theory.
What would a criminal judge say if he knew it?
Would he realise how sincere I am?
But do those people believe in sincerity?
Outside of me, beyond the limits of my body, movement exists, but for them my life must be as inconceivable as living simultaneously on the Earth and on the Moon.
I am nothing to everyone.
And yet if tomorrow I throw a bomb or murder Barsut, I become everything, the man who exists, the man for whom infinite generations of jurists have prepared punishments, prisons and theories.

I, who am nothing, will suddenly set in motion that terrible mechanism of policemen, secretaries, journalists, lawyers, prosecutors, prison guards, police vans, and no one will see in me a wretch but rather the antisocial man, the enemy who must be removed from society.
That really is curious!
And yet only crime can affirm my existence, just as only evil affirms the presence of man on earth.

And I would be the Erdosain foreseen, feared, characterised by the penal code, and among the thousands of anonymous Erdosains who infect the world, I would be the other Erdosain, the authentic one, the one who is and will be.
Really, all this is curious.
Yet despite everything the darkness exists and the soul of man is sad.
Infinitely sad.
But life cannot be like this.
An inner feeling tells me that life must not be like this.

If I could discover the particular reason why life cannot be like this, I would prick myself, and like a balloon I would deflate all this wind of lies and from my present appearance there would remain a brand-new man, strong as one of the first gods who animated creation.
With all this I have gone off on a tangent.
Shall I see the Astrologer or not?
What will he say when he sees me arrive again?
Perhaps he is expecting me.
He is, like me, a mystery to himself.
That is the truth.
He knows as little about where he is going as I do.
The secret society.
The whole society is summed up in him in these words: secret society.
Another demon.
What a collection!
Barsut, Ergueta, the Pimp and I...
One could not have gathered such specimens on purpose.
And to top it all, the blind pregnant woman.
What a beast!
The station guard passed in front of Erdosain for the second time.
Remo realised he was attracting the man’s attention and so, standing up, he headed toward the Astrologer’s house.
There was no moon.
The arc lamps shone among the airy branches of the street corners.

From some villa came the sounds of a piano and as he walked his heart grew smaller and smaller, oppressed by the anguish produced in him by the spectacle of the happiness he guessed lay behind the walls of those houses cooled by the shadows, in front of whose carriage gates a motorcar stood waiting.
The Astrologer was getting ready for bed when he heard footsteps on the path leading to the house.
Since the dog did not bark, he half-opened the shutter.

A parallelogram of light sliced through the darkness all the way to the crown of the pomegranate trees, and through that yellow shaft he saw Erdosain advancing, the light striking him full in the face.
“How curious!
” thought the Astrologer.
“I hadn’t noticed until now that this fellow wears a straw hat!
What can he want?
” And after making sure he had the revolver at his waist (a movement that was instinctive with him), he unlocked the door and Erdosain came in.
“I thought you were already in bed. ”
“Come in. ”
Erdosain stepped into the study.
The map of the United States was still there with the black flags pinned over the territories where the Ku Klux Klan held sway.
The Astrologer had been working on a horoscope, for the open box of compasses lay on the table.
The wind coming through the grating stirred the papers, and after waiting for the other man to put some documents away in the cabinet, Erdosain sat down with his back to the garden.

Once seated, he remained staring at the other man’s broad face, the crooked nose springing from the turbulent forehead, the cauliflower ear, the enormous chest contained within dull black clothing, the copper chain crossing his waistcoat from side to side, the steel ring with a violet stone on his hand of deformed fingers and weather-beaten skin.
Now that the man was without his hat, one could see that his hair was curly, wildly tangled and short.
He had stretched out his legs and was resting the whole weight of his body on the arms of the chair.
In his unpolished boots he looked like a mountain man, perhaps a gold prospector.
Why shouldn’t the gold prospectors of Patagonia look like that?

Erdosain thought, and without understanding his own distraction he went on staring at the map of the United States and mentally repeating the words he had heard the Astrologer say that afternoon while pointing out the federal states to the Melancholy Ruffian with a pointer.
“The Ku Klux Klan is strong in Texas, Ohio, Indianapolis, Oklahoma, Oregon... ”
“What do you say, my friend... how...? ”
“Oh, that’s right!...
I’ve come to see you... ”
“I was just about to go to bed.
I’ve been working on the horoscope of an imbecile... ”
“If I’m bothering you I’ll leave. ”
“No, stay.
Have you been in a fight?
What’s the matter with you? ”
“Many things.
Tell me, if you could...
You won’t be surprised by the question?...
If, in order to found your lodge, that is, to get the twenty thousand pesos you need, if to get twenty thousand pesos you had to kill a man, what would you do? ”
The Astrologer sat up straight in his chair, his body now raised in astonishment at a right angle...
And although his head was held erect by the thoughts Erdosain had stirred in him, it seemed to weigh prodigiously on his shoulders.
He rubbed his hands together and scrutinized Remo’s face.
“Why would you ask me such a question? ”
“Because I’ve found the candidate who has twenty thousand pesos.
We can kidnap him, and if he refuses to sign us a check we’ll torture him. ”
The Astrologer frowned.
Faced with the enigmas contained in that proposal, his perplexity grew, and with the fingers of his left hand he began to twist the ring on the ring finger of his right.
The violet stone passed again and again in front of the bronze chain, and although he kept his face lowered, beneath the line of his eyebrows his horizontal pupils scrutinized Erdosain’s face.
And the crooked nose, in that position, took on the vigor of a defense with the chin sunk into the black fabric of his cravat.
“Let’s see, explain all that to me, because I don’t understand a single word. ”
He had now risen to his feet and his face seemed to defy a rain of blows.
“It’s simple and brilliant.
My wife left tonight to go and live with another man.
So he... ”
“Who is he?... ”
“Barsut, my wife’s cousin...
Gregorio Barsut came to see me and confessed that he was the one who denounced me to the sugar company. ”
So it was he who denounced you?... ”
“Yes, and what’s more... ”
“But why did he denounce you?... ”
“How should I know!...
To humiliate me...
Anyway, he’s half crazy.
A man who lives frantically.
He has twenty thousand pesos.
His father died in an insane asylum.
He’ll end up there too.
The twenty thousand pesos are the inheritance from an aunt on his father’s side. ”
The Astrologer clutched his forehead.
He was more perplexed than ever.
The matter interested him, but he did not understand it. He insisted:
“Tell me everything in detail, in order. ”
Erdosain began his story again.
He narrated everything we already know.
He spoke slowly, meticulously, for the nervous tension that had preceded the proposal he made to the Astrologer had disappeared from him.
Now he was sitting on the edge of the chair, his back arched, elbows resting on his knees, cheeks latticed by his fingers, his gaze fixed on the floor.
The yellow skin stretched over the flat bones of his face gave him the appearance of a consumptive.
A mass of iniquities poured from his throat, without interruption, dully, as if he were reciting a lesson stamped coldly onto the surface of his consciousness.
The Astrologer, lips covered by his fingers, listened to him with a strange look.
He had imagined many things, but not so many.

With a slowness born of excessive attention so as not to make a mistake, Erdosain piled up anxieties, humiliations, memories, sufferings, nights spent without sleep, terrible quarrels. Among other things he said:
“It may seem a lie to you that I, I who have come to propose the murder of a man, should speak to you of innocence, and yet I was twenty years old and just a boy.
Do you know what kind of sadness it is that makes one spend the night in a filthy bar, wasting time among stupid conversations and gulps of cane liquor?
Do you know what it is to be in a brothel and suddenly have to hold oneself back so as not to weep desperately?
You look at me astonished, of course; you saw a strange man, perhaps, but you didn’t realize that all that strangeness came from the anguish I carried hidden inside me.
Look, it even seems a lie to me to be speaking with such precision.
Who am I?
Where am I going?
I don’t know.
I have the impression that you are the same as me, and that is why I have come to propose the murder of Barsut.
With the money we will found the lodge and perhaps we will be able to shake the foundations of this society. ” The Astrologer interrupted him:
“But why have you always behaved like this?... ”
“That is precisely what I don’t know.
Why do you want to organize the lodge?
Why does the Melancholy Ruffian go on exploiting women and polishing his boots even though he has a fortune?
Why did Ergueta marry a prostitute and leave the millionairess?
Do you think I tolerated Barsut’s slap and the captain’s presence just like that?
Apparently I am a coward, Ergueta is mad, the Ruffian is a miser, you are obsessed.

Apparently we are all that, but deep down, inside, beneath our consciousness and our thoughts there is another life, more powerful and enormous... and if we endure everything it is because we believe that by enduring or behaving as we do we will finally reach the truth... that is, the truth of ourselves. ”
The Astrologer stood up, walked over to Erdosain and, placing a hand on his head, said thoughtfully:
“You are right, my son.
We are mystics without knowing it.
The Melancholy Ruffian is a mystic, Ergueta is a mystic, you, I, she and they...
The sickness of the century, irreligion, has shattered our understanding and so we seek outside ourselves what lies in the mystery of our subconscious.
We need a religion to save us from the catastrophe that has fallen upon our heads.
You will tell me that I am not saying anything new.
Agreed; but remember that on earth the only thing that can change is style, custom; the substance remains the same.
If you believed in God you would not have lived that diabolical life, if I believed in God I would not be listening to your proposal to murder a fellow man.
And the most terrible thing is that for us the time to acquire a belief, a faith, has already passed.
If we were to go to a priest, he would not understand our problems and would only manage to recommend that we recite an Our Father and confess every week. ”
“And one asks oneself what one ought to do... ”
“There it is.
What one ought to do.
In other times the refuge of a convent or a journey to unknown and marvelous lands would have remained for us.
Today you can have a sorbet in the morning in Patagonia and eat bananas in the afternoon in Brazil.
What ought one to do?
I read a great deal, and believe me, in all the European books I find this same background of bitterness and anguish that you tell me about your life.
Look at the United States.
Actresses have platinum ovaries implanted and there are murderers who try to break records for horrible crimes.
You who have walked about know it.
Houses, more houses, different faces and identical hearts.
Humanity has lost its festivals and its joys.
Men are so wretched that they have even lost God!
And a three-hundred-horsepower engine only manages to distract them when it is piloted by a madman who can smash himself to pieces in a ditch.
Man is a sad beast whom only prodigies can move.
Or butcheries.
Very well, with our society we will give them prodigies, plagues of Asiatic cholera, myths, discoveries of gold deposits or diamond mines.
I have observed you while talking with you.
You only come alive when the prodigious enters our conversation.
And the same thing happens to all men, scoundrels or saints. ”
“So, we kidnap Barsut? ”
“Yes.
Now we have to see how we can get hold of him and the money. ”
The wind stirred the foliage.
Erdosain remained for a few seconds looking at the strip of light that fell from the half-open window onto the pomegranate trees.
The Astrologer had moved his chair over to the cabinet so that his head rested against the ochre panel, and his fingers again played with the steel ring, turning it before his eyes.
“How shall we get hold of him?
It’s very easy.
I will tell Barsut that I have found out where the captain is with Elsa... ”
“Yes, that’s good.
But how did you find out?
That’s what the other man won’t stop asking you... ”
“By telling him that I went to the Personnel Office of the Ministry of War. ”
“Perfect... very good... perfectly clear... ”
Now the Astrologer had risen briskly and was looking at Erdosain with interest.
“And with the pretext that he should persuade Elsa to come back to me again, we bring him here. ”
“Admirable.
Let me think a little.
Everything you are setting out... of course... is very good.
Ah... tell me one thing, does he have relatives? ”
“Except for my wife, no. ”
“And where does he live? ”
“In a boarding house.
The landlady’s daughter is cross-eyed. ”
“What will they say when Barsut disappears? ”
“We can do this, which is admirable.
We send the landlady a telegram from Rosario, signed by him, saying that she should send the trunks to a certain hotel, where you will be living under the name of Gregorio Barsut. ”
“Exactly that.
You know you’ve studied this very well?
The plan is perfect.
It’s true that everything lends itself to it: the captain, the addresses at the Ministry, having no relatives, living in a boarding house.
It’s clearer than a chess move.
Very good. ”
Having said this he began to pace from one side of the room to the other.
Each time he crossed in front of the window grating, the garden grew darker or a shadow spilled across the cabinet that reached as far as the ceiling joists.
Erdosain had not been wrong when he said that the plan was as sharp “as if it had been stamped on an iron plate under thousands of pounds of pressure.
” And while in the room the Astrologer’s boots sounded dully with every step, Erdosain was already lamenting that the “plan” was so simple and so little novelistic.
He would have liked a more dangerous adventure, less geometrical.
“What the devil!
This has no charm!
Anyone could be a murderer like this! ”
“And Gregorio has no relations with the cross-eyed girl? ”
“No. ”
“Then why did you mention her? ”
“I don’t know. ”
“And aren’t you afraid of feeling remorse after ‘that’ happens? ”
“Look, I believe that only happens in novels.
In reality I have done bad and good actions and in neither case have I felt the slightest joy or the slightest remorse.
I believe that what has been called remorse is simply fear of punishment.
Here they don’t hang you, and only cowards... ”
“And you?... ”
“Allow me.
I am not a cowardly man.
I am a cold man, which is different.
Reason it out.

If I have impassively let my wife be taken from me and allowed myself to be slapped by a man who betrayed me, with how much more reason will I impassively witness the scene of his death, provided it is not a butchery? ”
“True.
It is very logical.
Everything about you is logical.
Do you know, Erdosain, that you are an interesting individual? ”
“My wife used to say the same thing.
That did not prevent her from going off with another man. ”
“And do you hate him? ”
“Sometimes.
It depends.
Perhaps in me physical repulsion is stronger than hatred.
In truth, not hatred, because we can never hate people we know are capable of doing exactly the same villainies that we do. ”
“Then why do you want to kill him? ”
“And why do you want to found the society? ”
“And do you believe that this crime will have any influence on your life? ”
“That is the curiosity I have.
To know whether my life, my way of seeing things, my sensibility, will change with the spectacle of his death.
Besides, I already feel the need to kill someone.
Even if only to amuse myself, you know? ”
“And you want me to pull the chestnuts out of the fire for you? ”
“Of course!... because for you in these circumstances, pulling the chestnuts out of the fire for me amounts to having twenty thousand pesos to set up the society and the brothels... ”
“And how did it occur to you that I was capable of doing ‘that’? ”
“How?
I have been observing you for a long time.
But the conviction that you were a man who would embark on a dangerous adventure came to me a year ago when I met you at the Theosophical Society. ”
“Let’s see... ”
“I remember it as if it were now.
A coal-woman, to your left, was talking about the perispirit with a shoemaker.
Haven’t you noticed what a predilection shoemakers have for the occult sciences? ”
“And? ”
“On that occasion you addressed a Polish gentleman who was in communication with the spirit of Sobieski. ”
“I don’t remember... ”
“I do.
The Polish gentleman, you yourself told me later, was a bricklayer’s laborer...

You and the Polish gentleman moved from Sobieski to a discussion about ‘the homing sense of pigeons’ and you answered: ‘For me the only importance the homing sense of pigeons has is to serve as intermediaries in a blackmail,’ and there you began to explain...
Well, when you finished speaking, between the astonishment of the Pole, the coal-woman and the shoemaker, I said to myself: this man is an audacious fellow at large... ”
“Ha ha!
What a boy you are! ”
“Perfect. ”
“You must take this into account: it is a mechanism that breaks down into three sub-mechanisms that must work harmoniously, although they are independent.
Look: the first mechanism is the kidnapping.
The second, your stay in Rosario, where you will ask for and receive the luggage under the name of Barsut.
The third, the murder and the procedure for making the body disappear. ”
“Shall we destroy the corpse? ”
“Of course.
With nitric acid or else with a furnace where...
If it’s a furnace you need a minimum of five hundred degrees to carbonize the bones as well. ”
“And where did you get those facts from? ”
“You know I am an inventor.
Ah, out of the twenty thousand pesos we can devote part to manufacturing the copper rose on a large scale.
I have already ordered its manufacture from a family of friends.
Possibly one of the boys will join the society.
Besides, the other day an electromagnetic modification for Stephenson’s steam engine occurred to me.
Well, what I have devised is a hundred times simpler.
Do you know what I need?
To go away for a while, to be in the mountains, to rest and study. ”
“And you could go to the colony we will organize... ”
“So you agree with the plan? ”
“Ah!
One thing.
The money, where did Barsut get it from? ”
“Three years ago he sold a property he inherited. ”
“And he keeps it in a savings bank... ”
“No, in a current account. ”
“So he doesn’t live on the interest? ”
“No, he spends it little by little.
At two hundred pesos a month.
He says that before he finishes that sum he will be dead. ”
“It’s curious.
And what sort of man is he? ”
“Strong.
Cruel.
The kidnapping will have to be studied very carefully, because he will defend himself like a wild beast. ”
“Very good. ”
“Ah!
Before I go.
Will you tell the Ruffian anything about this? ”
“No.
It’s a secret between us.
The Ruffian will take part only as organizer of the brothels.
You’re paying at the sugar company tomorrow, aren’t you? ”
“Yes. ”
“Now that I remember, I know a printer.
He will be the one to make the circular from the Ministry of War for us. ”
Erdosain paced about the room for a moment.
“The kidnapping is easy.
You go to Rosario and with a telegram ask for the trunks.
What happens is that when one finds oneself facing the commission of a crime... ”
“It won’t be the only one we commit... ”
“What?... ”
“Of course not.
Another of the things that worries me is keeping the secret within the society.
I had thought the following.
In every corner of the state there will be a revolutionary cell.
The central committee will be based in the capital.

Then this committee would be organized in the following way: provincial capital chief, member of the central committee, provincial district chief, member of the provincial capital committee, chief of the main town, member of the district head committee. ”
“Don’t you think that’s very complicated? ”
“I don’t know, it would be studied.

Other organizational details that have occurred to me are: each cell will have a radio transmitter and receiver, and it will also be obligatory that every ten associates acquire a car, ten rifles, two machine guns, and that every hundred members pay for the price of a war plane, bombs, etc., etc. Promotions will be by decision of the supreme council, elections at lower levels will be governed by qualified votes.
But it’s time to go to bed.
In a little while there’s a train... or do you want to stay and sleep here? ”
In reality Erdosain had nothing to do.
The clock had already struck three in the morning and the words the Astrologer had spoken passed through his understanding, almost blurred.
Nothing interested him.
He wanted to leave, that was all.
To go far away.
He shook the other man’s hand; the Astrologer saw him off on the steps and Erdosain, weighed down, crossed the orchard.
When he turned his head in the darkness, the lighted window placed a yellow rectangle suspended in the center of the gloom.
Up in the tree.
Dawn breaks.
Erdosain walks along the path that runs beside the broken pavement next to the market gardens.
The freshness of the morning reaches the furthest cells of his weary lungs.
Although overhead the sky is still black, and all that darkness descends to bring things closer to the eye, for those in the distance remain invisible on the horizon.
Along the channel of the alleys, greenish-grey bands slowly turn red. Erdosain walks on, thinking:
“This is as sad as the desert.
Right now she is sleeping with him. ”
Quickly the watery clarity of dawn fills the alleys with whitish vapors. Erdosain tells himself:
“Still, one must be strong.
I remember when I was a boy.
I used to think I saw great men with curly hair walking along the crests of the clouds, their upright limbs plated in light. ”
In truth they walked within the land of Joy that lay inside me.
Ah, and to lose a dream is almost like losing a fortune.
What am I saying?
It is worse.
One must be strong; that is the only truth.
And one must have no pity.
And even if one feels tired, one must say: I am tired now, I am sorry now, but I will not be tomorrow.
That is the truth.
Tomorrow.
Erdosain closes his eyes.
A perfume he cannot tell whether it is tuberose or carnation drenches the atmosphere with a mysterious festive embalming. And Erdosain thinks:
“Despite everything it is necessary to graft some joy onto life.
One cannot live like this.
It is not right.
Above all our misery there must float a joy, I don’t know, something more beautiful than the ugly human face, than the horrible human truth.
The Astrologer is right.
We must inaugurate the empire of the Lie, of magnificent lies.
To worship someone?
To carve a path through this forest of stupidity?
But how? ”
Erdosain continues his soliloquy, his cheekbones tinged with pink:
“What does it matter if I am a murderer or a degenerate?
Does that matter?
No. It is secondary.
There is something more beautiful than the vileness of all men put together, and that is joy.
If I were joyful, happiness would absolve me of my crime.
Joy is what matters.
And also to love someone... ”
The sky turns green in the distance, while the low darkness still envelops the trunks of the trees.
Erdosain frowns.
Vapors of memory detach themselves from his spirit, golden mists, shining rails that vanish across the field of an afternoon vaulted with sun.
And the face of the girl, a pale little face with greenish eyes and black curls escaping beneath a small cloth hat, rises from the surface of his spirit.
Two years ago.
No. Three.
Yes, three years.
What was her name?
María, María Esther.
What was her name?
The sweet little face now occupies with its warmth a darkened space of dream.
He remembers so many things!
He was sitting beside her, the wind moving her black curls; suddenly he stretched out his hand and between his fingertips took the burning chin of the girl.
Where is she now?
Under what roof does she sleep?
If he found her, would he recognize her?
Three years ago.
