He met her on a train, spoke with her for a few minutes each day for fifteen days, and then she disappeared.
That is all and nothing more.
And she did not know he was married.
What would she have said if she had known?
Yes, now he remembers.
Her name was María.
But does that matter at all?
No. There was something more beautiful in all of it: the sweet fever that fell from her eyes, at times green and at times brown.
And her silence.
Erdosain remembers railway journeys; he is seated beside the girl who has let her head fall upon his shoulder, he tangles his fingers in her curls and the fifteen-year-old girl trembles in silence.
If she knew now that he plans to kill a man, what would she say?
Possibly she would not even understand the word.

And Erdosain remembers with what schoolgirl shyness she would raise her arm and rest her hand on his rough, stubbled cheeks; and perhaps that happiness which is the one he lost is the one needed to erase from the human countenance so many traces of ugliness.
Erdosain now examines himself with curiosity.
Why does he think so many things?
By what right?
Since when do would-be murderers think?
And yet there is something in him that gives thanks to the Universe.
Is it humility or love?
He does not know, but he understands that in incoherence there is sweetness; it occurs to him that a poor soul, upon going mad, abandons with gratitude the sufferings of this earth.
And beneath this pity, an implacable force, almost ironic, twists his lip with a grimace of contempt.
The gods exist.
They live hidden beneath the envelope of certain men who remember life on the planet when the earth was still a child.
He too carries a god inside him.
Is it possible?
He touches his nose, sore from the punches he received from Barsut, and the implacable force insists on that affirmation: he carries a god hidden beneath his aching skin.
But has the Penal Code foreseen what punishment can be applied to a homicidal god?
What would the examining magistrate say if he answered: “I sin because I carry a god within me”?
Yet is it not true?
This love, this force he carries within him at dawn, beneath the dampness of the trees that drip dew in the darkness, is it not a virtue of the gods?

And once again there detaches itself from the surface of his spirit the relief of that memory: an oval pale little face with greenish eyes and black curls sometimes wrapped around her throat by the wind.
How simple it all is!
He need say nothing, so perfect is his rapture.
Though there would be nothing improbable in his having gone mad thinking of the schoolgirl beneath the trees that drip with moisture.
If not, how is it to be explained that his soul is so different from the one that possessed him during the night?
Or is it that in the night only somber thoughts can be conceived?
Even if that is so, it does not matter.
He is another man now.
He smiles beside the trees.
Is this not magnificently idiotic?

The Melancholy Ruffian, the Depraved Blind Woman, Ergueta with his myth of Christ, the Astrologer, all these incomprehensible phantoms who utter human words, who possess a carnal word, what are they beside him who, leaning against a post beside a privet hedge, feels the advance of life coming to touch his chest?
He is another man, and for the sole reason of having thought of the girl who in a railway carriage let her head fall upon his shoulder.
Erdosain closes his eyes.
The sharp smell of the earth sends a shiver through him.
A vertigo rises from his tired flesh.
Another man walks along the road.
A harsh whistle comes from the station.
Other men in caps or crooked hats cross in the distance.
In reality, what the devil is he doing there?
Erdosain winks one eyelid; he is aware that he is cheating God, that he is acting out the comedy of a man who has not been able to deflect God’s curse.
Nevertheless, at moments gusts of darkness pass before his eyes, and a kind of deaf intoxication gradually takes hold of his senses.
He would like to violate something.
To rape common sense.
If there were a haystack nearby he would set it on fire...

Something repulsive thickens his face: the sullen expressions of madness; suddenly he looks at a tree, leaps, catches a branch, clings to it and, bracing his feet against the trunk, helping himself with his elbows, manages to clamber up to the fork of the acacia.
His shoes slip on the glossy bark, the twigs whip his face elastically; he stretches out his arm and seizes a branch, poking his head out among the wet leaves.
The street below continues its slope toward an archipelago of trees.
He is up in the tree.
He has violated common sense, just because, without purpose, like someone who murders a passer-by who crosses his path, to see whether the police can discover him afterward.
Toward the east, against the greenish sky, funereal chimneys stand out; then, mountains of greenery like monstrous herds of elephants fill the lowlands of Banfield, and the same sadness is in him.
It is not enough to have violated common sense in order to feel happy.
Nevertheless, he makes an effort and says aloud:
“Hey! sleeping beasts: hey!
I swear that... but no...
I want to violate the law of common sense, quiet little animals...
No. What I want is to proclaim audacity, the new life.
I speak from atop the tree, I am not ‘in the palm tree,’ but in the acacia: hey! sleeping beasts. ”
Rapidly his strength ebbs.

He looks around almost surprised to find himself in such a position; suddenly the face of the distant girl bursts inside him like a flower, and immensely ashamed of the comedy he is performing, he climbs down from the plant.
He is defeated.
He is a wretch.
The days that followed the kidnapping of Barsut, Erdosain spent locked in a room at a boarding house, to which he had moved temporarily after settling his debt with the Limited Sugar Company.
He had developed a terror of the street.
He never thought about the planned kidnapping of Barsut, and he even stopped visiting the Astrologer.
He spent the day in bed, with his fists propped on the pillow and his forehead crushed against them.
At other times he remained for hours with his eyes fixed on the wall, up which it seemed to him a thin mist of sleep and despair crept.
During that period he could never reconstruct Elsa’s face.
“She had withdrawn so mysteriously from my spirit that it cost me a great effort to remember the features of her physiognomy. ”
Then he would sleep or brood.

He tried, though uselessly, to occupy himself with two projects he considered important: the electromagnetic exchange for steam engines, and a dog-dyeing shop that would launch onto the market dogs with electric-blue coats, green bulldogs, violet greyhounds, lilac fox terriers, lapdogs with three-color sunset photographs printed on their backs, little bitches with arabesques like Persian tapestries.
He was calm: one afternoon he fell asleep and had this dream:
He knew he was engaged to one of the infantas.
This event, accompanied by the fact that he was a footman to His Majesty Alfonso XIII, delighted him at once, for the generals surrounded him, asking him pointed questions.
A mirror of water gnawed at the trunks of trees forever blossoming in white, while the infanta, a tall girl, taking him by the arm, said to him with a lisp:
“Do you love me, Erdosain? ”

Erdosain, bursting into laughter, answered the infanta with coarseness: a circle of swords flashed before his eyes and he felt himself sinking; successive cataclysms tore the continents apart, but he had been sleeping for many centuries in a little lead chamber at the bottom of the sea.

Beyond the glazed little window, one-eyed sharks came and went, furious because they suffered from hemorrhoids, and Erdosain rejoiced silently, laughing with the little laughs of a man who does not wish to be heard.
Now all the fish in the sea were one-eyed, and he was Emperor of the City of the One-Eyed Fish.

An eternal wall encircled the desert at the shore of the sea; the green sky oxidized on the bricks of the wall, and on the walls of the red towers the waves dashed together myriads of fat, one-eyed fish, monstrous pot-bellied fish sick with marine leprosy, while a dropsical Black man shook his fist at an idol of salt.
At other times Erdosain evoked past days in which he had foreseen the present events, as he had told the captain that night.
Muffled sufferings, prowlings around a reality that now made him say:
“I was right.
I wasn’t mistaken. ”

Thus he remembered that one night, talking with Elsa, she, in a moment of sincerity, confessed to him that had she been single she would not have married; she would have taken a lover. Erdosain asked her:
“Are you really saying that? ”
From the other bed, stubborn, Elsa answered:
“Yes, man, I would have a lover...
Why get married? ”
Curious phenomenon: Erdosain suddenly had the sensation of the silence of death, a silence parallel as a coffin to his horizontal body.

Possibly at that instant everything unconscious in the love a man feels for a woman was destroyed inside him, and this would later allow him to face terrible situations that would have been unbearable had that phenomenon not occurred first.

It now seemed to him that he was at the bottom of a sepulcher; he thought he would never see the light again, and in that light, black and weightless silence that filled the room, the phantoms awakened by his wife’s voice moved.

Later, explaining those moments, he remembered that he remained motionless in bed, afraid of breaking the equilibrium of his enormous unhappiness, which weighed his horizontal body down forever on the surface of an implacable anguish.
His heart beat heavily.
It seemed to him that each systole and diastole had to overcome the pressure of an elastic mass of mud.
And it was useless for him to try, from there, to move his hands to reach the sun that lay higher up.
And his wife’s voice still repeated in his ears:
“I wouldn’t have married.
I would have had a lover. ”
And those words, which had needed only the space of two seconds to be spoken, would now go on resounding inside him for the rest of his life.
He closed his eyes.
The words would be with him all his life, rooted in his entrails like a growth of flesh.
And his teeth ground together.
He wanted to suffer even more, to exhaust himself with pain, to bleed out in a slow trickle of anguish.
And with his hands glued to his thighs, stiff as a corpse in its coffin, without turning his head, holding back the gallop of his breathing, he asked in a hissing voice:
“And would you have loved him? ”
“Why not?...
Who knows!...
Yes; if he was good, why not? ”
“And where would you have seen each other?
Because they wouldn’t have tolerated that in your house. ”
“In some hotel. ”
“Ah! ”
They fell silent, but already Erdosain saw her, in the firm misfortune of his life, walking along the sidewalk of a street paved with river pebbles.
She advanced along the wide pavement.
A dark veil covered half her face, and heading toward the place to which her deliberate desire led her, she moved with quick, sure steps.

And eager to torture what little hope he still had left, Erdosain continued, with a false smile that she could not distinguish in the darkness, and in a gentle voice so that Elsa would not notice the fury that shook his lips:
“You see?
That’s nice, in a marriage, to be able to talk about everything with the trust of siblings.
And tell me, would you have undressed in front of him? ”
“Don’t say stupid things! ”
“No; tell me: would you have undressed? ”
“Well... of course!
I wasn’t going to stay dressed! ”
If they had split his spinal column with an axe, he could not have been more rigid.
His throat dried up as if a wind of fire had entered it.
His heart barely beat; over his brains he felt a mist running that escaped through his eyes.

He was falling into silence and darkness, sinking into nothingness by a gentle descent, while the firm paralysis of his cubic flesh remained so that the sensation of grief would stamp itself more deeply.

He fell silent, and yet he would have liked to sob, to kneel before someone, to get up at that very moment, dress, and go sleep in the atrium of some house, on the threshold of an unknown city. Driven mad, Erdosain shouted:
“But do you realize... do you realize how horrible this is, how appalling what you’ve told me is?
I ought to kill you!
You’re a bitch!
I ought to kill you, yes, kill you!
Do you realize? ”
“But what’s wrong with you?
Are you crazy? ”
“You’ve destroyed my life.
Now I know why you never gave yourself to me, and you forced me to masturbate!
Yes, that!
You’ve turned me into a rag of a man.
I ought to kill you.
The first person who comes along can spit in my face.
Do you realize?
And while I steal and swindle and suffer for you, you... yes, you are thinking about that.
About giving yourself to a good man!
But do you realize?
A good man!
Just like that, a good man! ”
“But are you crazy? ”
Erdosain was dressing rapidly.
“Where are you going? ”
He threw his overcoat over his shoulders; then, leaning over the woman’s bed, he exclaimed:
“Do you know where I’m going?
To a brothel, to catch myself some syphilis. ”

The chronicler of this story does not dare to define Erdosain, so numerous were the misfortunes of his life that the disasters he later caused in the company of the Astrologer can be explained by the psychic processes he underwent during his marriage.
Even today, when I reread Erdosain’s confessions, it seems to me implausible that I should have witnessed such sinister unfoldings of shamelessness and anguish.
I remember.
During those three days he spent taking refuge in my house, he confessed everything.
We would gather in an enormous room empty of furniture, where little light reached.
Erdosain would remain seated on the edge of a chair, his back arched, elbows resting on his thighs, cheeks latticed by his fingers, his gaze fixed on the floor.
He spoke in a muffled voice, without interruptions, as if reciting a lesson engraved in the cold by infinite atmospheres of pressure upon the plane of his dark consciousness.
The tone of his voice, whatever the events, was even, methodical, isochronous, like the meshing of a clock.
If interrupted he did not grow irritated; he would simply begin the account again, adding the requested details, always with his head lowered, eyes fixed on the ground, elbows braced on his knees.
He narrated with a slowness born of excessive attention, so as not to create confusion.
Impassively he piled anxiety upon iniquity.

He knew he was going to die, that human justice was hunting him with ferocity, yet he, revolver in his pocket, elbows on his knees, face latticed in his fingers, gaze fixed on the dust of the huge empty room, spoke impassively.
He had grown extraordinarily thin in just a few days.
The yellow skin stretched over the flat bones of his face gave him the appearance of a consumptive.
The autopsy later revealed that the disease was already far advanced in him.
On the second afternoon of his stay in my house he told me:
“Before I got married, I used to think of fornication with horror.

In my mind, a man only married so he could always be beside his wife and enjoy the joy of seeing her at every hour; of speaking to each other, loving each other with their eyes, with words and smiles.
It’s true I was young then, but when I became Elsa’s fiancé I felt the need to renew all those things. ”
He went on speaking.
Erdosain never kissed Elsa, because he was happy letting the vertigo of loving her tighten around his throat, and because he also believed that “one must not kiss a young lady.
” And he mistook for spirituality what was nothing more than an appetite of his own flesh.
“We never used the familiar ‘you’ either, because I liked the distance the formal ‘you’ placed between us.
Besides, I believed one did not address a young lady with the familiar form.
Don’t laugh.
In my mind, a ‘young lady’ was the authentic expression of purity, perfection and candour.
Beside her I never knew desire, only the unease of a delicious rapture that filled my eyes with tears.

And I was happy because I loved with suffering, unaware of the aim of my desire, and because I believed that all that terrible organic convulsion which left me blissfully prostrate before her quiet gaze was spiritual love—a clean gaze that slowly penetrated the most quivering underlayers of my spirit. ”
While he spoke I looked at Erdosain.
He was a murderer, a murderer, and he spoke of the nuances of an absurd feeling! He continued:
“And on the night of the day we were married, once we were alone in the hotel room, she undressed quite naturally in front of the lighted lamp.
Blushing to my temples, I turned my head away so as not to look at her and so she would not discover my shame.
Then I removed my collar, jacket and boots and got under the sheets still wearing my trousers.
On the pillow, among her black curls, she turned her face and said, smiling with a strange little laugh:
‘Aren’t you afraid they’ll get wrinkled? Take them off, silly.’
Later, a mysterious distance separated Elsa from Erdosain.
She gave herself to him, but with repugnance, disappointed in who knows what.
And he would kneel at the head of her bed and beg her to give herself to him for one moment, but the woman, in a muffled voice of impatience, would answer him almost shouting:
‘Leave me alone! Can’t you see you disgust me?’
Checking a terror of catastrophe, Erdosain would sink back into his own bed.
“I wouldn’t lie down; I stayed sitting up, back almost propped against the pillow, staring into the darkness.

I knew there was no point in staring into the darkness, but I imagined that she, taking pity on seeing me like that, abandoned in the gloom, would finally feel compassion and say: ‘All right, come if you want.’ But she never, never said those words, until one night I shouted at her in despair:
‘So what do you think... that I’m going to keep masturbating forever?’ And then she, serenely, answered me:
‘It’s useless: I should never have married you.’”
And anguish appeared in him, so powerful that suddenly Erdosain would clutch his head, maddened by a physical pain.
It seemed to him that his brain mass had come loose from his skull and was slamming against its walls with the slightest movement of an idea.

He knew he was irretrievably lost, banished from the possible happiness that always, someday, smiles even on the palest cheek: he understood that destiny had aborted him into the chaos of that dreadful multitude of sullen men who stain life with their exhausted images, weighed down by every vice and suffering.

He no longer had any hope, and his fear of living grew stronger when he thought that he would never have illusions, when, staring stubbornly at a corner of the room, he recognized that it was all the same to him whether he worked as a dishwasher in a cheap eatery or as a servant in a brothel.
What did it matter to him!

Anguish had leveled him into the bosom of a silent multitude of terrible men who during the day drag their misery selling gadgets or Bibles, and at nightfall roam the urinals where they exhibit their genitals to the youths who enter the toilets driven by similar anxieties.
These convictions left him drowsy with gloomy meditations.
He felt screwed to an enormous block from which he would never escape.

Because this anguish had become so persistent that he suddenly discovered his soul was sad for the fate that awaited his body in the city, a body that weighed seventy kilos and that he only saw when he placed it in front of a mirror.

In other times, with his mind, he had surrounded himself with every comfort and pleasure, pleasures that, not being limited by matter, had neither duration nor boundaries, whereas his present sadness referred to his body, a suffering body, and at times Erdosain thought of it as if it no longer belonged to him, but with the remorse of never having made it happy.
This sadness, insofar as it concerned his poor flesh, became profound, as profound as the pain of a mother who could never satisfy her son’s desires.

For he had given his flesh, which would live so short a time, neither a decent suit nor a joy that might reconcile it with living; he had done nothing for the pleasure of his matter, while to his spirit had not been denied even the geography of countries for which men have not yet discovered machines to reach. And many times he would say to himself:
“What have I done for the happiness of this wretched body of mine? ”
Because the truth was that he felt, in certain moments, as alien to it as the wine is to the barrel that contains it.

Then he would remember that this body was the one that bottled his broodings, that nourished them with its tired blood; a miserable, badly dressed body that no woman deigned to look at and that felt the contempt and burden of the days, for which only his thoughts were responsible—thoughts that had never craved the pleasures his body silently, timidly demanded.
Erdosain felt pity and sadness toward his physical double, of which he was almost a stranger.

Then, like a desperate man throwing himself from the seventh floor, he would hurl himself into the delicious terror of masturbation, wanting to annihilate his remorse in a world from which no one could expel him, surrounding himself with the delights that were distant from his life, with all the most different and beautiful bodies, for which an immense sum of lifetimes and money would be needed to enjoy.
It was a universe of gelatinous ideas, broken into passageways where obscenity dressed itself in the most expensive silks and laces, velvets and guipures; a world gleaming in its twilight pulp.

The most beautiful women of creation moved through it, unknown smooth-skinned women who uncovered for him their apple-like breasts, offering to his mouth—soured by ignoble cigarettes—fragrant lips and words heavy with sensuality.

And they were at times tall, fine, polished maidens, at times corrupted schoolgirls, a feminine and diverse world from which no one could expel him, him, a poor devil whom the madams of even the most rundown brothels eyed with distrust as if he were about to cheat them out of the price of fornication.

He would close his eyes and enter the burning darkness, forgetting everything, like the opium smoker who, upon entering the filthy den where the Chinese proprietor smells of excrement, believes he is recovering heaven.
And for a moment he would slide furtively toward the clandestine pleasure, ashamed, yet with the impatience of a youth entering a brothel for the first time.
Desire buzzed like a horsefly in his ears, but no one could now tear him from the sensual darkness.
This darkness was a familiar house in which he suddenly lost all notion of ordinary life.
There, in the black house, the terrible pleasures were habitual to him—pleasures that, had he suspected them in the existence of another man, would have separated him from that man forever.

Although this black house was inside Erdosain, he entered it by making strange detours, tortuous maneuvers, and once he had crossed the threshold he knew it was useless to turn back, because along the corridors of the black house, down one exclusive corridor always packed with shadows, there advanced to meet him, with light feet, the woman who one day on the sidewalk, on a tram, or in a house, had stiffened him with desire.

As one takes from his wallet money that is the product of various efforts, Erdosain would take from the bedrooms of the black house a fragmentary and complete woman, a woman composed of a hundred women torn apart by a hundred desires always the same, renewed at the sight of similar women.

For this one had the knees of a girl whose skirt the wind lifted while she waited for the bus, and the thighs he remembered having seen in a pornographic postcard, and the sad, faded smile of a schoolgirl he had met long ago on the tram, and the greenish eyes of a little dressmaker whose pale mouth was ringed with pimples, who on Sundays at dusk would go out with a friend to dance in those recreation centers where shopkeepers push against the girls with their rebellious flies, girls who like men.

This arbitrary woman, kneaded from the flesh of all the women he had not been able to possess, showed him those compliances that prudent fiancées show who have already let their hands rest in their boyfriends’ laps without ceasing to be honest.
She came toward him.

Her buttocks were held by an orthopedic girdle that left her slightly curved breasts free, and her manners were irreproachable like those of an educated young lady who knows how to reason, which does not prevent her from letting her boyfriend lose his fingers in the half-open bodice.
Then he would fall into the abysses of the black house.
The black house!

From those times Erdosain retained an abominable memory; he had the sensation that he had lived inside a hell whose diabolical content accompanied him through the days, and even a few of those before his death, pursued by the law.

When he turned his memory toward that period he would grow soberly exalted, a red flame would shine before his eyes, and such was his painful fury that he would have wished, in a single leap, to go beyond the stars, to burn himself in a bonfire that would cleanse his present of all that terrible past, persistent and inevitable.
The black house!

It still seems to me that I have before my eyes the rigid face of the taciturn man who would suddenly lift his head toward the ceiling, then lower his eyes until they were level with mine and, smiling coldly, would add:
“Go on, tell men what the black house is.
And that I was a murderer.
And yet I, the murderer, have loved all beauties and have fought within myself against all the horrible temptations that rose hour after hour from my entrails.
I have suffered for myself, and for others, you understand?
Also for others... ”
The kidnapping took place ten days after Elsa’s escape.
On the fourteenth of August Erdosain received a visit from the Astrologer, but since he had gone out, on returning he found an envelope that had been slipped under the door.
It contained a forged circular from the Ministry of War informing Erdosain of the supposed address of Captain Belaunde and a curious postscript that read as follows:
“I shall wait for you until the twentieth, every morning between ten and eleven, in the company of Barsut.
Knock and enter without waiting.
Do not come to see me alone. ”
Erdosain read the Astrologer’s letter and remained pensive.
He had forgotten about Barsut.
He knew he had to kill him; then that resolve had been covered over by darkness, and the days that filled the interval, which he had spent in a stupor, had vanished forever.
“He had to kill Barsut.
” The explanation of the word “had” might be found in the very nature of Erdosain’s madness.
When I questioned him on the matter, he answered: “I had to kill him, because otherwise I would not have been able to live in peace.
Killing Barsut was a prerequisite for existing, just as breathing clean air is for others.
” Thus, as soon as he received the letter, he headed for Barsut’s house.
The latter lived in a boarding house on Uruguay Street, a dark and filthy apartment occupied by a fantastic assortment of people of every sort.
The landlady of that den practiced spiritualism, had a cross-eyed daughter, and was inexorable when it came to payments.
Any boarder who fell twenty-four hours behind was certain to find, upon returning at night, his trunks and belongings thrown into the middle of the patio.
He arrived at the other man’s house at dusk.
Gregorio was precisely in the middle of shaving when Erdosain entered his room.
Barsut stopped, pale, with the razor against his cheek; then, looking Erdosain up and down, he exclaimed:
“What the hell do you want here? ”
“Anyone else would have become indignant,” Erdosain commented later.
“I looked at him smiling ‘amicably,’ because at that moment I felt like his friend, and without saying a word I handed him the letter from the Ministry of War.
An inexplicable joy kept me restless; I remember sitting for a minute on the edge of his bed, then getting up and pacing nervously about the room. ”
“So she’s in Temperley.
And you want us to go look for her? ”
“Yes, that’s what I want.
And for you to go look for her. ”
Barsut murmured something Erdosain did not catch; then he began to rub the muscles of his arms with his hands and his skin flushed faintly.
He was about to shave off his mustache; he held the razor in the air, turned his head, and said:
“You know?
I thought you’d never have the courage to come see me. ”
Erdosain held the furrowed green gaze; the man really had the face of a tiger. After folding his arms, he replied:
“It’s true, I thought so too, but as you see, things change... ”
“Are you afraid to go alone? ”
“No.
What I have is an interest in seeing you in the adventure... ”
Barsut clenched his teeth.
With his chin dripping soapy lather and his forehead powerfully furrowed, he studied Erdosain and finally said:
“Look, I thought I was a bastard, but I think you... you’re worse than I am.
All right, let it be as God wills. ”
“Why do you say ‘as God wills’? ”
Barsut stopped in front of the mirror, planted his fists on his hips, and what he said did not surprise Erdosain, who with a serene expression listened to these words:
“Who’s to say this circular isn’t forged and that you’re not setting a trap to murder me? ”
“How strange the human soul is!
” Erdosain commented afterward.
“I heard those words and not a single muscle in my face twitched.
How had Gregorio guessed the truth?
I don’t know.
Or did he also have my own evil imagination? ”
He lit a cigarette and answered with these sole words:
“Do whatever you like. ”
But Barsut, who was in a talkative mood, replied:
“But why not?
Tell me: why not?
What would be so strange about you wanting to kill me?
It’s logical.
I tried to steal your wife, I denounced you, I beat you up.
What the devil!
You’d have to be a saint not to feel like killing me. ”
“A saint?
No, my boy, I’m not one.
But I swear I won’t kill you tomorrow.
Some day, yes, but not tomorrow. ”
Barsut burst into cheerful laughter.
“You know you’re something else, Remo?
Some day you’ll kill me.
How curious!
You know what interests me about all that?
The face you’ll make when you kill me.
Tell me, will you be serious or will you laugh? ”
The questions had been asked with friendly gravity.
“Probably I’ll be serious.
I don’t know.
I think so.
You’ll understand that killing someone else is no game. ”
“And you’re not afraid of prison? ”
“No, because if I killed you I’d take my precautions first, and I’d destroy your corpse with sulfuric acid. ”
“You’re a savage...
By the way, my memory is worse: did you pay at the sugar refinery? ”
“Yes. ”
“Who gave you the money? ”
“A pimp. ”
“You have few friends, but they’re good ones...
So, what time will you come for me tomorrow? ”
“At eight that man goes to headquarters... so... ”
“Look, I still can’t quite believe it’s true, but if Elsa is there I’m going to slap her so many times I warn you it’ll take her many years to forget them. ”
When Erdosain left he went to a post office and sent a telegram to the Astrologer.
That night he did not sleep.
He was extremely tired.
He was not thinking about anything either.
He tried to give me a definition of that state in these terms:
“The soul feels as if it had slipped half a meter out of the body.
An extraordinary muscular annihilation, an anxiety that never ends.
You close your eyes and it seems the body is dissolving into nothing; suddenly you remember a lost detail from among the thousands of days you have lived.
Never commit a crime, because more than horrible it is sad.
You feel you are cutting, one after another, the moorings that tied you to civilization, that you are about to enter the dark world of barbarism, that you will lose the helm.
I told the Astrologer that too, that it came from a lack of training in crime, but that isn’t it, no.

In reality you would like to live like everyone else, to be honest like everyone else, to have a home, a wife, to lean out the window and watch the passers-by, and yet there is not a single cell in your organism that is not impregnated with the fatality contained in those words: I have to kill him.
You will say I am rationalizing my hatred.
Why not rationalize it?
I have the impression that I am living in a dream.
I even realize that I talk so much to convince myself that I am not dead—not because of what happened but because of the state a thing like that leaves you in.
It is like skin after a burn.
It heals, but have you seen what it looks like?
Wrinkled, dry, tight, shiny.
That is how the soul is left.
And the shine that sometimes reflects off it burns your eyes.
And the wrinkles it has disgust you.
You know you carry a monster inside you that can break loose at any moment and you do not know in what direction.
“A monster!
Many times I have stopped to think about that.

A calm, elastic, indecipherable monster that will surprise even you with the violence of its impulses, with the satanic obliquities it discovers in the recesses of life and that allow you to discern infamies from every angle.
How many times have I paused inside myself, in the mystery of myself, and envied the life of the humblest man!
Ah, never commit a crime.
Look at me, how I am.
And I confess to you just like this, perhaps because you understand me...
“And the night?...
I got home late.
I threw myself on the bed fully dressed.
The emotion a gambler can feel, I felt it in the anxious beating of my heart.

In reality I was not thinking about the events that would follow the crime, but rather I kept on the edge of it the curiosity of knowing how I would behave, what Barsut would do, in what way the Astrologer would kidnap him, and the crime I had read about in certain novels now appeared interesting; I saw now that it was something mechanical, that committing a crime is simple, and that it seems complicated to us only because we lack the habit of it.
“So much so that I remember I stayed lying there with my gaze fixed on a corner of the dark room.
Fragments of ancient existence, but disconnected, passed as if pushed by a wind before my eyes.

I never managed to explain to myself the mysterious mechanism of memory, which in the exceptional circumstances of our lives suddenly gives an almost extraordinary importance to an insignificant detail, to an image that for years and years has been covered in our memory by the present of life.

We did not know those interior photographs existed and suddenly the thick veil that covers them breaks, and so, that night, instead of thinking about Barsut I let myself remain there, in that sad boarding-house room, in the attitude of a man who waits for the arrival of something, of that something I have spoken of so many times, and which in my view was supposed to give an unexpected turn to my life, completely destroy the past, reveal to me a man absolutely different from what I was.
“In reality the crime did not worry me much, but another curiosity: how would I manifest myself after the crime?
Would I suffer remorse?
Would I go mad, end up turning myself in?
Or would I simply live as I had until now, aching with that singular impotence that gave all the acts of my life an incoherence which you now say are the symptoms of my madness?

“The curious thing is that at moments I felt great surges of joy, a desire to laugh in order to simulate a paroxysm of madness that did not exist in me; but once the impulse was broken I would try to imagine in what way we would kidnap Barsut.
I was sure he would defend himself, but the Astrologer was not a man to enter an undertaking without precautions.

At other times I posed the problem of how Barsut had guessed that the circular from the Ministry of War was falsified, and I was astonished at having achieved that perfect presence of mind when, turning toward me his soapy face, he had said almost ironically:
‘Look how funny if the circular were falsified.’
“In reality he was a scoundrel, but I was not far behind him; the difference perhaps lay in the fact that he did not feel curiosity about his own base passions as I would feel it.
Besides, nothing mattered to me in those circumstances.
Perhaps I would be the one to kill him, perhaps the Astrologer; the fact was that I had thrown my life into a monstrous recess where demons played with my senses as with dice inside a cup.
“Distant noises arrived; weariness seeped into my joints; at moments it seemed to me that my flesh, like a sponge, was soaking up the silence and the repose.
Grim ideas occurred to me regarding Elsa; a taciturn rancor stiffened the muscles in my jaws; I even felt the pain of my poor life.

“Nevertheless, the only way to rehabilitate myself in my own eyes was by assassinating Barsut, and suddenly I saw myself standing beside him; he was tied with thick ropes and thrown on a pile of sacks; of him only the green profile of his eye and his pale nose were distinct; I leaned gently over his body, I brandished a revolver, I softly brushed the hair away from his temples and said to him in a very low voice: ‘You are going to die, you bastard.’
“The shape shuddered; I raised the revolver, pressed the barrel against the skin at the temple and again repeated in a very low voice: ‘You are going to die, you bastard.’
“The arms moved under the thick bonds; it was a desperate labor of terrified bones and muscles.
‘Do you remember, you bastard, do you remember the potatoes, the salad spilled on the table?
Do I still have that wretched face that worried you?’

“But suddenly I felt ashamed of saying those vulgarities to him, and then I said to him, or rather I said nothing; I took a sack and covered his head; under the dense burlap the head moved furiously; I tried to press it against the floor to ensure the effectiveness of the shot and the secure position of the revolver barrel, and the burlap slipped over the hair and all my efforts were useless to subdue the courage of that beast, which now snorted dully to escape death.

“If this dream faded, I imagined myself traveling through the Malay Archipelago aboard a sailing ship in the Indian Ocean; I had changed my name, I mumbled English, my sadness was perhaps the same, but now I had strong arms, the most serene gaze; perhaps in Borneo, perhaps in Calcutta or beyond the Red Sea, or on the other side of the Taiga, in Korea or Manchuria, my life would rebuild itself. ”

It is true that they were no longer the dreams of the inventor or of the man who discovered electric rays so powerful they could melt masses of steel as if they were wax lentils, nor would he preside over the glass table of the League of Nations.
At other moments terror advanced in Erdosain: he had the sensation of being shackled; terrible civilization had put him inside a straitjacket from which there was no escape.
He saw himself chained and wearing the striped prison uniform, slowly crossing in a penal column between snow dunes toward the forests of Ushuaia.
The sky above was white like a sheet of tin.

This vision inflamed him; blinded by slow fury, he got up and walked from one side of the room to the other; he felt like pounding the walls with his fists, he would have liked to pierce the walls with his bones; then he stopped at the door jamb, crossed his arms; once again sorrow climbed back up to his throat.
Whatever he did was useless; in his life there was one glaring, unique, absolute reality.
He and the others.
Between him and the others there stood a distance; it was perhaps the incomprehension of the rest, or perhaps his own madness.
In any case, that did not make him any less wretched.

And once again the past rose in fragments before his eyes; the truth is that he would have liked to escape from himself, to abandon forever that life which contained his body and which was poisoning him.
Ah, to enter a newer world with great roads through the forests, where the stench of wild beasts would be incomparably sweeter than the horrible presence of man.
And he walked, wanting to exhaust his body, to wear it out completely, to crush it with fatigue to such a degree that it would be impossible for it to shape a single idea.
At nine in the morning Erdosain went to fetch Barsut.
They left without saying a word.
Later Erdosain would reflect on that strange journey in which the other man moved toward his fate without offering the slightest resistance.
Referring to those circumstances, he would say:

“I walked beside Barsut as a man condemned to death walks toward the place of execution, all his strength abandoned; with one persistent sensation, that of emptiness occupying the hollows of my entrails.

“Barsut in turn was sullen; I understood that there, seated beside the window with his elbow resting on the sill, he was accumulating furies to unleash them against the invisible enemy his instinct warned him was hidden in the Temperley villa. ” Erdosain continued:

“At moments I told myself how curious it would have been for the other passengers to know that those two men, sunk into the leather padding of the seats, were: one the future murderer and the other his victim.

“And yet everything went on exactly the same; the sun shone out there in the fields: we had left behind the freezing plants, the stearin and soap factories, the glass and iron foundries, the cattle pens where the steers sniffed the posts, the avenues yet to be paved with their plains stained by plaster and furrows.

And now, beyond Lanús, began the sinister spectacle of Remedios de Escalada, monstrous red-brick workshops and their black maws, beneath whose arches locomotives maneuvered, and in the distance, between the tracks, one could see gangs of wretches beating gravel or carrying sleepers.

“Farther on, among a stunted vegetation of plane trees poisoned by soot and the stench of petroleum, ran the oblique path of the red chalets for the company employees, with their tiny gardens, their blinds blackened by smoke, and the roads sown with slag and cinders. ”
Barsut traveled absorbed in himself.
Erdosain, to explain the exact term, simply let himself be.
If at that moment he had seen a train advancing along the line in the opposite direction, he would not have blinked, so indifferent to him were life or death.
Thus the journey passed.
When they reached Temperley, Barsut shook himself as if waking with a shiver from a painful dream, and limited himself to saying:
“Which way is it? ”
Erdosain stretched out his arm, pointing vaguely into the distance they had to walk, and Barsut set off in that direction.
Now they crossed the streets in silence toward the Astrologer’s villa.
The tender blue of the morning fell upon the brambles of the oblique streets.
Stems, every shade of green foliage and trees, created shapeless vegetable buildings, crested with flexible plumes and bifurcated by labyrinths of red woodiness.

All this beneath an air that undulated gently, in such a way that those fantastic constructions of botanical chance seemed to float in an atmosphere of gold that had the glassy clarity of a concave crystal, retaining in its sphericity the deep stench of the earth.
“Lovely morning,” said Barsut.
And they spoke no more until they stood before the villa.
“This is it,” said Erdosain.
Barsut jumped backward and, looking at him with incredible sharpness, exclaimed:
“And how do you know it’s here if there’s no number? ”
Commenting later on this incident, Erdosain would say:

“It can be affirmed that there is an instinct for crime, an instinct that allows one to lie instantly without fear of falling into contradictions, an instinct that is like the impulse of self-preservation and that, at the sharpest moment of the struggle, allows one to find resources for salvation that are almost unbelievable. ”
Erdosain raised his eyes and with a composure unexpected in him and surprising afterward, answered:
“Because I came yesterday and walked around here.
I wanted to see if I could spot Elsa. ”
Barsut looked at him doubtfully.
He would have sworn that Erdosain was lying, but pride prevented him from retreating, and Erdosain, calling out, struck hard with the palms of his hands.
Covering half his face with the wide brim of a straw hat and in shirtsleeves, the Man Who Had Seen the Midwife stopped in front of the red-painted wire gate.
“Is the lady in?
” asked Barsut.

Bromberg, without answering, drew back the bolt and opened the gate; then he went down a path that curved toward the house among the eucalyptus trees, and the two men followed him. Suddenly a voice shouted:
“Where are you going? ”
Barsut moved his head.
Bromberg spun on his heels, and as if some spring in his arm had broken, it lengthened like a lightning bolt.
Barsut opened his mouth in a frenzy for air, the upper part of his body doubling instantly.
He was about to clutch his stomach with his hands, but Bromberg’s arm widened the angle of another blow, and under the cross to the jaw Barsut’s teeth clashed together.
He fell, and crushed among the grass he seemed to be dead, with his legs drawn up and his lips slightly parted.
The Astrologer appeared, and Bromberg, serious, almost sad, bent over the fallen man.
The Astrologer took him by the joints of the arms, fingers hooked under the armpits, and in this manner they carried him to the abandoned coach house.
Erdosain rolled back the ochre-painted sliding door; the smell of dry grass and a whirlwind of insects escaped from the black tarpaulin.
They carried the unconscious man into a stall: a thick chain was fastened to one of the pillars by a padlock.

The Astrologer secured the end of it above Barsut’s ankle, made several knots with the links, then fastened it with a padlock; the lock clicked as it opened, and Erdosain, straightening up over the fallen man, said, looking at the Astrologer:
“You see?
He doesn’t have the checkbook on him. ”
It was ten in the morning.
The Astrologer looked at his watch and said:
“I have time to catch the express that reaches Rosario at six.
Do you want to come with me as far as Retiro? ”
“What, you’re going to Rosario? ”
“Well, don’t I have to send the telegram to the owner of the boarding house?
Do you have the number? ”
“Yes, everything. ”
“It’s the best way to take possession of Barsut’s luggage without arousing suspicion.
He doesn’t have anything else at the boarding house? ”
“Yes, the trunk and two crutches. ”
“Perfect.
Let’s stop talking and get to the point.

At six I’ll be in Rosario, I’ll send the telegram to the old woman, you drop by tomorrow at ten and, acting the fool, ask if Barsut hasn’t arrived in Rosario yet, and since I won’t have arrived, you add that you know I’ve been offered an important job, etc., etc. What do you think? ”
“Very good. ”
At twelve the Astrologer boarded the train.

The trick devised by Erdosain and carried out by the Astrologer had succeeded, and the latter decided that the first meeting at which the “chiefs” would get to know one another should take place on Wednesday.
On Tuesday at four in the afternoon Erdosain received a visit from the Astrologer, who informed him that the chiefs would meet the following morning, Wednesday, at nine o’clock in Temperley.
The Astrologer stayed with Erdosain for a few minutes, and as he was going down the stairs, glancing anxiously at his watch, he said to him:
“Damn... it’s already four.
I’ve got a pile of places to go...
I’ll see you tomorrow at nine...
Oh, I’ve been thinking that the only one who could fill the post of Chief of Industries is you.
Well, we’ll talk about it tomorrow...
Ah!
Don’t forget to prepare... or rather, to draw up a project on hydraulic turbines, a simple model for a mountain power plant.
It would be for the colony and the electrometallurgical works. ”
“How many kilowatts? ”
“I don’t know... that’s for you to study.
There will be electric furnaces... anyway, you’ll manage.
Besides, the Gold Prospector has arrived; tomorrow he’ll give you more concrete details.
Get ready so the matter doesn’t catch you off guard.
Hell, it’s getting late... see you tomorrow...
” Adjusting his top hat, he hailed a passing driver and settled into the automobile.
The next day, as Erdosain walked along the pavements of Temperley, he observed with astonishment that it had been a long time since he had enjoyed such a feeling of calm.
He walked slowly.
Those vegetal tunnels gave him the sensation of a titanic and misshapen labor.
He gazed with delight at the paths of red gravel in the parks, whose scarlet sheets advanced all the way to the lawns—green tablecloths enamelled with violet, yellow and red flowers.

And if he lifted his eyes he met watery cisterns at the zenith that produced in him a vertigo of falling, for suddenly the sky vanished from his pupils and left in his eyes a blindness of blackness, while his mind cleared in a fleeting flutter of silver atoms that in turn evaporated, turning into terrible harsh, dry bluish tones, now high above, like caverns of methylene blue.

And the pleasure the morning awakened in him, the new delight, soldered together the fragments of his personality, shattered by the previous sufferings of the disaster, and he felt that his body was agile for any adventure.
“Augusto Remo Erdosain”—as though pronouncing his own name gave him a physical pleasure that doubled the energy the movement had infused into his limbs.
Along the slanting streets, beneath the cones of sunlight, he advanced, feeling the power of his brand-new personality: Chief of Industries.
The freshness of the botanical path enriched his consciousness with grandeur.
And this satisfaction weighted him solidly in the streets, like the lead ballast inside those celluloid dolls.
He thought he would show himself ironic at the meeting, and a malevolent contempt rose in him for the weak of the world.
The planet belonged to the strong, exactly, to the strong.
They would raze the world and present themselves to the rabble who glued their backsides to the armchairs of every office, armored in greatness, like solitary and cruel emperors.
Once more he imagined himself in an enormous hall with glass walls, whose center was occupied by a round table.
His four secretaries, papers in hand and pens behind their ears, approached to consult him, while in a corner, hats in their hands and gray heads bowed, stood the workers’ delegates.
And Erdosain, turning toward them, would simply say: “Either you return to work tomorrow or we’ll shoot you.
” That was all.
He spoke little and in a low voice, and his arm was weary from signing decrees.
What kept him on his feet was the ferocity of the times, which required the soul of a tiger to adorn the edges of every twilight with sinister executions.
He now advanced toward the Astrologer’s country house with his heart pounding with enthusiasm, repeating Lenin’s phrase to himself like a little tune full of voluptuousness:
“What the hell kind of revolution is this if we don’t shoot anybody! ”
When he reached the house and opened one of the doors, he saw the Astrologer coming to meet him, wearing a long gray smock and a straw hat.
They shook hands warmly while the Astrologer said:
“Barsut is calm, you know?
I don’t think he’ll put up much resistance about signing the check.
Those fellows have already arrived, but first we’ll see Barsut.
Let them wait, what the hell!
Do you realize my situation?
With that money the world is ours. ”
They had now entered the study and the Astrologer, twisting the ring with the violet stone and looking at the map of the United States, continued:
“We shall conquer the earth, we shall carry out our ‘idea’... we can set up a brothel in San Martín or in Ciudadela, and the colony of the Saints in the mountains.
Who is better suited to run the brothel than the Melancholy Pimp?
We’ll appoint him Grand Patriarch of Brothels. ”
Erdosain approached the window...
The rosebushes poured forth an extremely powerful, sharp perfume; all the air was filled with a red fragrance, fresh as a stream of water.
Horseflies with crystal wings fluttered around the scarlet blotches of the pomegranate trees.
Erdosain remained like that for a few seconds.
The spectacle carried him back to that identical afternoon when he had stood there, in the same place.
And yet he had no idea that the night was waiting for him with the surprise of Elsa’s departure.
The multiform greenery penetrated his eyes, but he did not see it.

There, at the bottom of his existence, with her cheek resting on the violet nipples of a square masculine chest, was his wife, languid, her gaze loose, her lips half-open for the obscene mouth of the other.
A bird passed before his eyes, and Erdosain, turning to the Astrologer, said in a voice that was forcedly gentle:
“Look, do whatever you like.
” Then he sat down, lit a cigarette and, observing the other man who was marking a circle on a blue map with a compass, asked: “But what do you plan to do?
Will the Melancholy Pimp agree to manage the brothels? ”
“Yes, there’s no worry on that score, and Barsut won’t put up much resistance. ”
“Is he still in the coach house? ”
“I thought it prudent to keep him sequestered.
I chained him in the stable. ”
“In the stable? ”
“It was the only solid place where I could keep him.
Besides, in a room above the coach house sleeps the Man Who Saw the Midwife... ”
“What’s that? ”
“I’ll tell you someday.
He saw the midwife and can’t sleep at night.
Well, I had thought that you... ”
“What, am I going to be the one who...? ”
“Let me speak.
That you should see him and try to persuade him to sign; in short, that you should explain our ideas to him... ”
“We’re going to have to make him sign by force... ”
“But how?
Naturally I am an enemy of violence, but you understand me.

Our idea stands above all sentimentality; that is what you must make Barsut understand; in short, that we would rather not find ourselves obliged to toast his feet or something worse... in order to get him to sign the check. ”
“And you are prepared? ”
“Yes, we are prepared because we cannot lose this only opportunity.
I was counting on your copper-rose invention, but that is slow.
It’s not convenient to ask the Melancholy Pimp for money.
If he doesn’t have it we’ll put him in a tight spot, and if he has it and doesn’t want to give it to us, we’ll lose a friend.
The fact that he was generous with you doesn’t mean he’ll be generous with us.
Besides, he’s a neurasthenic who doesn’t know what he’s capable of. ”
Erdosain looked through the squares formed by the window bars at the scarlet blotches on the green crowns of the pomegranate trees.
A yellow band of sunlight cut across the upper part of the wall.
An enormous sadness passed through his heart.
What had he done with his life?
The Astrologer noticed his silence and said:
“Look, Erdosain.
We have no choice but to face everything or give up.
Life is like that, sad... but what do you want us to do?
I too know that it would be pleasant to do things without sacrifices. ”
“It’s just that in this case the sacrifice is someone else... ”
“And we, Erdosain, we who are risking prison and indefinite loss of freedom.
Haven’t you read Plutarch’s Parallel Lives? ”
“Well, I’m going to give them to you so that, by reading them, you learn that a human life is worth less than a dog’s if, in order to give society a new direction, that life must be destroyed.
Do you know how many murders the triumph of a Lenin or a Mussolini costs?
People aren’t interested in that.
Why aren’t they interested?
Because Lenin and Mussolini triumphed.
That is the essential thing, what justifies every cause, just or unjust. ”
“And who is going to kill Barsut? ”
“Bromberg, the one who saw the midwife... ”
“You hadn’t told me... ”
“There was no reason to, because everything on that side was already settled.
” A gust of perfume spilled into the room.
The noise of water falling into the barrel became sharp.
“So we already know about the matter... ”
“You, me and Bromberg... ”
“Too many people for a secret... ”
“No, because Bromberg is my slave; he is a slave to himself, which is worse. ”
“Very well, but you are going to give me a signed document in which you and Bromberg confess to being the authors of the crime. ”
“And what do you want that for? ”
“To be sure you’re not deceiving me. ”
With a mechanical gesture the Astrologer adjusted his top hat, took his Mongolian face between his thick fingers, and walked to the center of the room.
Thus, with one elbow resting on the palm of the other hand, he said:
“I have no objection to giving you what you ask, but don’t forget this: I live exclusively to carry out my idea.
Extraordinary times are coming.
I could not explain to you all the prodigies that are going to occur because I have neither the time nor the desire to argue.
New times are undoubtedly coming.
Who will know them?
The chosen.
The day I find a man capable of replacing me and the enterprise is on its way, I shall retire to meditate in the mountains.
Meanwhile, everyone around me owes me absolute obedience.
You must understand this if you don’t want to follow the other man’s path... ”
“That is no way to talk. ”
“Yes, it is the way, because I am going to sign for you the document you ask of me. ”
“I don’t need it... ”
“Are you going to need money? ”
“Yes, about two thousand pesos for... ”
“Don’t tell me...
It will be given to you... ”
“Besides, I don’t want to have anything to do with the brothel business... ”
“Very good.
You will keep the accounts, but do you know what we need now?
It is to discover a vulgar symbol that will enthuse the rabble... ”
“Lucifer. ”
“No, that is a mystical... intellectual... symbol.
We must discover something coarse and stupid... something that enters the senses of the multitude like the black shirt...
That devil had talent.
He discovered that the psychology of the Italian people was the psychology of a barber and an operetta tenor...
Anyway, we’ll see; I already have a hierarchy in mind, something interesting... we’ll talk about it another day... it might work... ”
“The main thing is that we can sustain ourselves... ”
“That is taken for granted... the brothels will produce...
But are you going to see Barsut?
Do you know what you will tell him? ”
Erdosain went out in the direction of the coach house, where the stables were installed.
It was a large building with thick walls and an upper floor where there were numerous empty rooms, overrun by rats.
In one of them lived, or rather slept, the sinister Bromberg, whom Erdosain had seen on the day of the kidnapping.

He understood that he was now heading toward a collapse from which he could not imagine in what form his life would emerge damaged, and this uncertainty, together with his absolute lack of enthusiasm for the Astrologer’s projects, gave him the impression that he was acting falsely, gratuitously creating an absurd situation.
“Everything had gone bankrupt inside me,” he would say later; yet, overcoming his fatigue and indifference, he walked toward the coach house.
His heart beat violently at the knowledge that he was about to meet “the enemy.
” At moments he frowned and his rancor was evident.
He opened the padlock, slid back the chain and, suddenly irritated, pushed one of the leaves of the gate.
The prisoner was preparing to eat, his arms bare in the circle of yellow light that the kerosene lamp spread over a pine table.

Barsut was seated beneath the metal triangle of the manger, between the wooden walls of a stall, and when he saw Erdosain frowning he stopped for a second the oil cruet with which he was watering a piece of meat surrounded by potatoes; then, without uttering a word that might reveal his surprise, he plunged once more into his nourishing task.
Stretching out his arm and taking a pinch of salt between his fingers, he sprinkled the potatoes.
He maintained a somber composure although a hole in his pink undershirt revealed his black armpit.
His eyes fixed on the cold meat certified that Barsut gave more importance to his food than to Erdosain, who stood three paces away.
The rest of the stable remained in darkness.
Through the cracks in the walls entered oblique arrows of sun that left porous golden discs on the dusty floor.
Barsut did not deign to look at anything.

He pressed the bread against the table board, cut an energetic slice, served himself soda—not without first shooting a jet against the floor to clean the nozzle—and then leaned over to read a fat book beside his plate while he chewed a mixture of meat, bread and potatoes.

Erdosain leaned against a pillar that supported the roof, dizzy from the smell of dry hay, and with half-closed eyes made out Barsut, whose half-face was illuminated by the greenish clarity of the lampshade while his jaws moved in the raw light thrown by the lamp’s burner.
At that moment he turned his head and noticed a whip hanging on the wall.
Erdosain started.
It had a long handle and a short lash, and Barsut, who now followed his gaze, curled his lip contemptuously.
Erdosain looked successively at the man and at the whip and smiled again.
He walked to the corner and took down the riding crop.
Now Barsut had stood up and, with his eyes terribly fixed on Erdosain, thrust his body out of the stall.
The veins in his neck dilated extraordinarily.
He was going to speak, but pride prevented him from pronouncing a single word.
A dry crack sounded.

Erdosain had brought the crop down on the wood to test the flexibility of the leather; then he shrugged his shoulders and the slanting sunbeam that cut through the darkness was crossed by a black line, and the whip fell among the straw.
Erdosain walked silently about the stable.
He thought that that life was in his hands, that no one could take it from him, yet this feeling did not make him any happier.
Barsut, above the wooden partition, observed the sunlit field through the crack left by the gate.
Times had changed.
That was all. He looked at Barsut with rancor:
“Are you going to sign the check or not? ”
Barsut shrugged his shoulders and Erdosain did not ask again.

Perhaps one day, at that very hour, he would find himself in a dark cell while his memory evoked at that same instant the spectacle of a court with a brick-dust floor beside the river, and the rackets netting the sky of some girls playing tennis.
And unable to contain himself he exclaimed, addressing not so much Barsut as himself:
“Do you remember?
To you I had the face of a poor wretch.
Don’t speak.
And you didn’t know what I was suffering.
Neither you nor she.
Shut up.
Do you think your money interests me?
No, man.
The fact is I’m sad.
You and she have brought me to all this.
I don’t even know why I’m talking.
The only thing I know is that I’m tired.
But what’s the use of talking...
” And he was about to leave when the Astrologer entered.
Barsut examined his hands with a glance and the Astrologer, shifting the top hat on his head, took the lamp, put it out and, sitting down on a crate, said:
“I came to see you so we could settle this matter of the check.
You know that’s why we kidnapped you.

Of course I wouldn’t be speaking to you in this way if in the notebook we found in your pocket—which Erdosain wanted to burn and I prevented him from doing—I had not read a simply formidable thought: ‘Money turns a man into a god.
Therefore Ford is a god.
If he is a god he can destroy the moon.’”
That was a lie, but Barsut did not stir.
Erdosain observed the impenetrable rhomboid face of the Astrologer.
It was evident that the latter was performing a comedy in which Barsut did not believe, certain that the other was deceiving him.
The Astrologer continued:
“At first that thought of yours struck me as just another of the many stupidities that fill your ramblings...
Yet in the end I found myself involuntarily asking why money can turn a man into a god, and suddenly I realized that you had discovered an essential truth.
And do you know how I confirmed that you were right?
By thinking that Henry Ford, with his fortune, could buy enough explosive to blow a planet like the moon to pieces.
Your postulate was justified. ”
“Certainly,” growled Barsut, flattered in spite of himself.

“Then I realized that all classical antiquity, that all the writers of every age—except you, who had written this truth without knowing how to exploit it—had never conceived that men like Ford, Rockefeller or Morgan might be capable of destroying the moon... that they might possess that power... a power which, as I say, mythologies could only attribute to a creator god.
And you, implicitly, were establishing a principle: the beginning of the reign of the superman. ”
Barsut turned his head to examine the Astrologer.
Erdosain understood that the man was speaking in earnest.

“Now then, once I had reached the conclusion that Morgan, Rockefeller and Ford were, by virtue of the power conferred on them by money, something like gods, I realized that social revolution would be impossible on earth because a Rockefeller or a Morgan could destroy an entire race with a single gesture, the way you might destroy an anthill in your garden. ”
“Provided they had the courage to do it. ”
“Courage?
I asked myself whether it was possible for a god to renounce his powers...

I asked myself whether a copper or oil king would ever allow himself to be stripped of his fleets, his mountains, his gold and his wells, and I realized that to deprive oneself of that fabulous world one would need the spirituality of a Buddha or a Christ... and that they, the gods who held every force at their disposal, would never permit such expropriation.
Consequently, something enormous would have to happen. ”
“I don’t see it...
I wrote that thought guided by other motives. ”
“That matters little.
What is enormous is this: humanity, the multitudes of the vast continents, have lost religion.
I am not speaking of the Catholic one.
I mean every theological creed.
Then men will say: ‘What do we want life for?...’ No one will have any interest in preserving a merely mechanical existence, because science has severed all faith.
And at the moment that phenomenon occurs, an incurable plague will reappear on earth... the plague of suicide...

Can you imagine a world of furious people, their skulls dried out, moving through the undergrounds of gigantic cities and howling at the reinforced-concrete walls: ‘What have you done with our god?...’ And little girls and schoolgirls forming secret societies to devote themselves to the sport of suicide?
And men refusing to beget children whom the deluded Berthelot believed would feed on synthetic pills?... ”
“That is assuming a great deal,” said Erdosain.
The Astrologer turned toward him, astonished.
He had forgotten him.
“Of course, it will not happen as long as men do not perceive the true basis of their unhappiness.
That is what has actually happened with revolutionary movements of an economic character.

Judaism brought its nose close to the world’s Debit and Credit and said: ‘Happiness is bankrupt because man lacks money to meet his needs...’ when it should have said: ‘Happiness is bankrupt because man lacks gods and faith.’”
“But you are contradicting yourself!
Earlier you said...
” Erdosain objected.
“Be quiet.
What do you know?...
And thinking, I reached the conclusion that this was the metaphysical and terrible sickness of every man.
The happiness of humanity can rest only on metaphysical falsehood...

Deprive it of that falsehood and it falls back into economic illusions... and then I remembered that the only ones who could restore to humanity its lost paradise were the gods of flesh and blood: Rockefeller, Morgan, Ford... and I conceived a project that may appear fantastic to a mediocre mind...
I saw that the blind alley of social reality had only one exit... and that was to go backward. ”
Barsut, arms crossed, had sat down on the edge of the table.

His green pupils were fixed on the Astrologer, who, with his smock buttoned to the throat and his hair disheveled—for he had removed his hat—walked from one end of the coach house to the other, pushing aside with the toe of his boot the dry grass stalks that littered the floor.

Erdosain, leaning back against a post, observed Barsut’s face, which was slowly becoming impregnated with an ironic, almost malevolent attention, as though the Astrologer’s words deserved nothing but mockery.
The latter, as if listening to himself, walked, stopped, at times ran his fingers through his hair. He said:
“Yes, a moment will come when skeptical humanity, maddened by pleasures, blaspheming in its impotence, will grow so furious that it will be necessary to kill it like a rabid dog... ”
“What are you saying?... ”
“It will be the pruning of the human tree... a vintage that only they, the millionaires, with science at their service, will be able to carry out.
The gods, disgusted with reality, having lost all illusion in science as a factor of happiness, surrounded by tiger slaves, will provoke frightful cataclysms, will distribute fulminating plagues...

For some decades the work of the supermen and their servants will consist in destroying man in a thousand ways, until the world is almost exhausted... and only a remnant, a small remnant, will be isolated on some islet upon which the foundations of a new society will be laid. ”
Barsut had risen to his feet.
With a fierce frown and his hands thrust into his trouser pockets, he shrugged his shoulders and asked:
“But is it possible that you believe in the reality of these ravings? ”
“No, they are not ravings, because I would commit them even if only to amuse myself. ” And he went on:
“There are wretches who must believe in them... and that is enough...
But here is my idea: that society will be composed of two castes, between which there will be an interval... or rather, an intellectual difference of thirty centuries.

The majority will live scrupulously maintained in absolute ignorance, surrounded by apocryphal miracles, and therefore far more interesting than historical miracles, while the minority will be the absolute repository of science and power.
In this way the happiness of the majority is guaranteed, for the men of that caste will have dealings with the divine world in which today they do not believe.

The minority will administer pleasures and miracles for the flock, and the golden age, the age in which angels wandered along the paths of twilight and gods let themselves be seen in the clearings of the moon, will become a fact. ”
“But that is monstrous in itself.
That cannot be. ”
“Why not?
I know it cannot be, but one must proceed as if it were feasible. ”
“That monstrous disproportion... science... ”
“What science!
Do you even know what science is for?
Don’t you inwardly mock the wise and call them ‘infatuated with the perishable’? ”
“I see you have read that nonsense. ”
“Of course.
One must not contradict people for no reason.
And the monstrous disproportion you perceive in my society already exists in our own society, but in reverse.
Our knowledge, I mean our metaphysical lies, is in its infancy, while our science is a giant... and man, the suffering creature, bears within himself this frightful imbalance...
On one side he knows everything... on the other he knows nothing.

In my society the metaphysical lie, the practical knowledge of a marvelous god, will be the end... the whole that will fill the science of things, useless for inner happiness, will be in our hands merely a means of domination.
And let us not discuss this, for it is superfluous.
Almost everything has been invented, but man has not invented a maxim of government superior to the principles of a Christ or a Buddha.
No. Naturally I will not deny you the right to skepticism, but skepticism is a luxury of the minority...
To the rest we shall serve happiness well cooked, and humanity will joyfully swallow the divine swill. ”
“Do you think that is possible? ”
The Astrologer stopped for a moment.

Now he was turning the steel ring with the violet stone, removed it from his finger to examine its interior; then, approaching Barsut but with a gesture of strangeness, like a man whose imagination is far from reality, he replied:
“Yes, everything the human mind imagines can be realized in time.
Hasn’t Mussolini already imposed religious teaching in Italy?
I cite that as proof of the efficacy of the stick on the backs of peoples.
The point is to seize the soul of a generation...
The rest takes care of itself. ”
“And the idea? ”
“Here we come...
My idea is to organize a secret society that will not only propagate my ideas but will be a school for future kings of men.

I know you will tell me that many secret societies have existed... and that is true... all of them disappeared because they lacked solid foundations, that is, because they rested on a sentiment, on a political or religious ideal, to the exclusion of all immediate reality.

Our society, on the contrary, will be based on a firmer and more modern principle: industrialism; that is, the lodge will have an element of fantasy—if one wishes to call everything I have told you that—and another positive element: industry, which will result in gold. ”
His voice grew harsher.
A gust of ferocity produced a certain astigmatic distortion in his gaze.
He moved his shaggy head from right to left as if the sharpness of an extraordinary emotion pricked his brain, placed his hands on his kidneys and, resuming his pacing, repeated:
“Ah! gold... gold...
Do you know what the ancient Germans called gold?
Red gold... gold...
Do you realize?
Don’t open your mouth.
Satan.
Realize that never, never has any secret society attempted such an amalgamation.
Money will be the solder and the ballast that will give ideas the weight and violence necessary to drag men along.
We shall address ourselves especially to the young, because they are more stupid and enthusiastic.
We shall promise them the empire of the world and of love...

We shall promise them everything... do you understand me?... and we shall give them showy uniforms, splendid tunics... helmets with plumes of various colors... jewels... degrees of initiation with beautiful names and hierarchies...
And up in the mountains we shall erect the cardboard temple...
That will be to shoot a film...
No. When we have triumphed we shall erect the temple of the seven golden doors...
It will have columns of pink marble and the paths leading to it will be sanded with grains of copper.
Around it we shall build gardens... and there humanity will go to worship the living god we have invented. ”
“But the money... the money to do all that... the millions... ”
As the Astrologer spoke, his enthusiasm spread to Erdosain.
He had forgotten Barsut, though the latter stood before him.
Involuntarily he evoked a land of possible renewal.

Humanity would live in perpetual festival of simplicity, bouquets of strontium would stud the night with cascades of red stars, an angel with greenish wings would skirt the crest of a cloud, and beneath the botanical arcades of the forests men and women would glide, wrapped in white tunics, their hearts cleansed of the filth that infected his own.
He closed his eyes, and Elsa’s face slid through his memory, yet it awoke no echo, because the Astrologer’s voice filled the coach house with this savage reply:
“So you are interested in where we shall get the millions?
It is easy.
We shall organize brothels.
The Melancholy Ruffian will be the Grand Patriarch of Brothels... all the members of the lodge will have an interest in the enterprises...
We shall exploit usury... woman, child, worker, fields and madmen.
In the mountains—it will be in the Chilean Field—we shall set up gold-washing plants; the extraction of metals will be done by electricity.
Erdosain has already calculated a five-hundred-horsepower turbine.
We shall prepare nitric acid by reducing atmospheric nitrogen by the whirling electric-arc method and we shall obtain iron, copper and aluminum by means of hydroelectric power.
Do you see?
We shall lure the workers with deception, and those who refuse to work in the mines we shall whip to death.
Doesn’t that already happen today in the Gran Chaco, in the yerba mate plantations and in the rubber, coffee and tin operations?
We shall surround our properties with electrified cables and buy off all the police and commissioners of the South with a water-pear.
The thing is to begin; the Gold Seeker has already arrived.
He found placer deposits in the Chilean Field while wandering with a prostitute called the Mask.
We must begin.
For the comedy of the god we shall choose an adolescent...
Better still to raise a child of exceptional beauty, and he will be educated everywhere but in secret, and people’s imagination will multiply his prestige.

Can you imagine what the fools of Buenos Aires will say when the rumor spreads that away in the mountains of Chubut, in an inaccessible temple of gold and marble, there dwells an adolescent god... a fantastic ephebe who works miracles? ”
“You know, your ravings are interesting! ”
“Ravings?

Didn’t people believe in the existence of the plesiosaur discovered by a drunken Englishman, the only inhabitant of Neuquén whom the police do not allow to carry a revolver because of his terrifying aim?...
Didn’t the people of Buenos Aires believe in the supernatural powers of a Brazilian charlatan who undertook to cure Orfilia Rico’s paralysis by a miracle?
That really was a grotesque spectacle utterly devoid of imagination.

And countless simpletons wept copiously when the trickster raised the sick woman’s arm, which is still paralyzed, proving that men of this and every generation have an absolute need to believe in something.
With the help of some newspaper, believe me, we shall work miracles.
There are several papers that are desperate to sell themselves or exploit a sensational story.
And we shall give all those who thirst for marvels a magnificent god, adorned with tales we can copy from the Bible...
An idea occurs to me: we shall announce that the lad is the Messiah foretold by the Jews...
We must think about it...
We shall take photographs of the god of the forest...
We can print a cinematographic film with the cardboard temple in the depths of the woods, the god conversing with the spirit of the Earth. ”
“But are you a cynic or a madman? ”
Erdosain looked at Barsut with annoyance.
Was it possible that he was so imbecilic and insensitive to the beauty that adorned the Astrologer’s projects?
And he thought: “This brute envies the other man his magnificent madness.
That is the truth.
There will be no choice but to kill him. ”
“Both, and we shall choose a mean between Krishnamurti and Rudolph Valentino... but more mystical, a creature with a strange face symbolizing the suffering of the world.
Our films will be shown in the poor districts, in the suburbs.

Can you imagine the impression the spectacle will make on the rabble: the pale god resurrecting a dead man, the gold-washing plants with an archangel like Gabriel guarding the metal boats and deliciously attired prostitutes ready to be the wives of the first wretch who arrives?
There will be more applicants than we can handle to go and exploit the city of the King of the World and enjoy the pleasures of free love...
From that riffraff we shall choose the most uncultured... and down there we shall break their backs with sticks, making them work twenty hours in the washing plants. ”
“I thought you were a workerist. ”
“When I talk with a proletarian I shall be red.
Now I am talking with you, and to you I say: My society is inspired by the one organized at the beginning of the ninth century by a Persian bandit named Abdala-Aben-Maimum.
Naturally, without the industrial aspect I am injecting into mine, which necessarily guarantees its success.
