Maimum wished to fuse freethinkers, aristocrats and believers of two races as different as the Persian and the Arab into a sect in which he established various degrees of initiation and mysteries.
They lied shamelessly to everyone.

To the Jews they promised the coming of the Messiah, to the Christians that of the Paraclete, to the Muslims that of the Mahdi... so that a crowd of people of the most varied opinions, social positions and beliefs worked for a cause whose true purpose was known to very few.
In this way Maimum hoped to achieve complete dominion over the Muslim world.
Needless to say the directors of the movement were tremendous cynics who believed absolutely in nothing.
We shall imitate them.
We shall be Bolsheviks, Catholics, Fascists, atheists, militarists, in various degrees of initiation. ”
“You are the most shameless pimp I have ever met...
If you succeed... ”
Barsut experienced a singular pleasure in insulting the Astrologer.
The fact was he did not want to admit that he was inferior to the other man.
Besides, there was something that humiliated him profoundly; it may seem absurd, but it enraged him to think that Erdosain was a friend and enjoyed the intimacy of such a man. And he said to himself:
“How is it possible that this imbecile has become the friend of such a man?
” And for that reason he felt that inside him there was no bad reason that did not contradict the Astrologer’s words.
“We shall have it, since the bait of gold is there.
The results of our organization will be seen in the balance sheets of the businesses we undertake.
The brothels will be a source of money.
Erdosain has devised an apparatus that will make it possible to control daily the number of visits each girl receives.
This without counting donations, a new industry we intend to exploit: the copper rose that Erdosain has invented.
Now you can understand why we kidnapped you. ”
“What good does the explanation do me if I am a prisoner? ”

At that moment Erdosain observed in himself how singular it was that Barsut had not once threatened the Astrologer with reprisals for the moment he should be free, which made him say to himself: “One must be careful with this Judas; he is capable of selling us, not for money but out of envy. ” The Astrologer continued:
“Your money will serve us to set up a brothel, organize the small contingent and buy tools, install radiotelegraphy and other equipment for the gold-washing plant. ”
“And you do not admit that you may be mistaken? ”
“Yes...
I have already thought of that, but I proceed as if I were right.
Besides, a secret society is like an enormous boiler.
The steam it produces can drive a crane as easily as a fan... ”
“And you do not admit that you may be mistaken? ”
“Yes...
I have already thought of that, but I proceed as if I were right.
Besides, a secret society is like an enormous boiler.
The steam it produces can drive a crane as easily as a fan... ”
“And what is it you want to drive? ”
“A mountain of inert flesh.
We few want, we need the splendid powers of the earth.
Happy are we if with our atrocities we can terrify the weak and inflame the strong.
And for that it is necessary to create force, to revolutionize consciences, to exalt barbarism.
That agent of mysterious and enormous force that will arouse all this will be the society.
We shall institute autos-da-fé, we shall burn alive in the squares those who do not believe in God.
How is it possible that people have not realized the extraordinary beauty there is in that act... in burning a man alive?
And for not believing in God, do you realize? for not believing in God.
It is necessary, understand me, it is absolutely necessary that a somber and enormous religion should once again inflame the heart of humanity.
That everyone should fall to their knees at the passing of a saint, and that the prayer of the lowliest priest should kindle a miracle in the evening sky.
Ah, if you only knew how many times I have thought of it!
And what encourages me is knowing that the civilization and misery of the century have unbalanced many men.
These half-madmen who find no direction in society are lost forces.
In the most ignominious neighborhood café, between two simpletons and a cynic, you will find three geniuses.
These geniuses do not work, they do nothing...
I agree with you that they are tin geniuses...
But that tin is an energy which, properly used, can be the foundation of a new and powerful movement.
And that is the element I wish to employ. ”
“Manager of madmen?... ”
“That is the phrase.
I want to be manager of madmen, of the innumerable apocryphal geniuses, of the unbalanced who have no entry into spiritualist or Bolshevik centers...
These imbeciles... and I tell you this because I have experience... if properly deceived... sufficiently heated up, are capable of committing acts that would make your skin crawl.
Counter-litterateurs.
Neighborhood inventors, parish prophets, café politicians and philosophers of recreational centers will be the cannon fodder of our society. ”
Erdosain smiled.
Then, without looking at the chained man, he said:
“You do not know the unbearable insolence of those on the frontiers of genius... ”
“Yes, as long as they are not understood, isn’t that so, Barsut? ”
“I am not interested. ”
“It should interest you because you are going to be one of us.
This is my opinion.
If you dispute with a man on the frontier that he is not a genius, all the insolence and coarseness of the misunderstood creature rises up insulting before you.
But if you systematically praise a monster of self-love, that same individual who would have murdered you at the slightest contradiction becomes your lackey.
What one must know is how to supply them with a sufficiently dosed lie.
Inventor or poet, he will be your servant. ”
“Do you also think you are a genius?
” Barsut burst out furiously.
“I also think I am a genius...
Of course I do... but five minutes and only once a day... though it matters little to me whether I am or not.
Phrases matter little to those predestined to act.
It is those on the frontiers of genius who grow fat on useless words.
I have posed myself this problem which has nothing to do with my intellectual qualities.
Can men be made happy?

And I begin by approaching the unfortunate, giving them as the object of their activities a lie that makes them happy by inflating their vanity... and these poor devils who, left to themselves, would never have been more than misunderstood, will be the precious material with which we shall produce power... steam... ”
“You are beating about the bush.
I ask you what personal end you pursue in wanting to organize the society. ”
“Your question is stupid.
Why did Einstein invent his theory?
The world can perfectly well do without Einstein’s theory.
Do I perhaps know whether I am an instrument of the superior forces in which I do not believe a word?
I know nothing.
The world is mysterious.
Possibly I am nothing more than the servant, the lackey who prepares a beautiful house in which the Elect, the Saint, will come to die. ”
Barsut smiled imperceptibly.
That man speaking of the Elect with his cauliflower ear, his bristling mane and carpenter’s apron produced in him an ironic, indefinable impression.
To what extent was the scoundrel pretending?

And the curious thing was that he could not become angry with him; an imprecise sensation dominated the man; what he was saying was not unexpected, but rather it seemed he had already heard those phrases, with the same tone of voice, on some distant occasion, as if lost in the gray landscape of a dream.
The Astrologer’s voice became less imperious.
“Believe me, it always happens thus in times of unrest and disorientation.
A few anticipate with a presentiment that something formidable must occur...
Those intuitives—I belong to that guild of those who wait—feel it is their duty to excite the conscience of society... to do something even if that something is nonsense.
My something in this circumstance is the secret society.
Great God!
Does man perhaps know the consequence of his acts?

When I think that I am going to set in motion a world of puppets... puppets that will multiply, I shudder; I even come to think that what may happen is as alien to my will as the bestialities an electrician who had suddenly gone mad might commit on the switchboard would be to the will of the owner of a factory.

And in spite of that I feel the imperious need to set this in motion, to gather into a single bundle the deformed power of a hundred different psychologies, to harmonize them by means of selfishness, vanity, desires and illusions, having as a base the lie and as a reality gold... red gold... ”
“You are right...
You are going to triumph. ”
“Well, what is it you expect from me now?
” Barsut replied.
“I already told you before.
That you sign the check for seventeen thousand pesos.
You will be left with three thousand.
With that you can go to the devil.
The rest we shall pay you in monthly installments from what the brothels and the washing plants yield. ”
“And shall I leave here? ”
“As soon as we cash the check. ”
“And how do you prove to me that those are your truths? ”
“Certain things are not proved...
But since you ask me for a proof, I shall tell you: If you refuse to sign the check I shall have you tortured by the Man Who Saw the Midwife, and after you have signed the check I shall kill you... ”
Barsut raised his colorless eyes, and now his face with three days’ beard seemed wrapped in a copper mist.
Kill him!
The word made no impression on him.
At that moment it had no meaning for him.
Besides, life mattered so little to him...

For a long time he had been expecting a catastrophe; it had occurred, and instead of feeling pursued by terror he found within himself a cynical indifference that shrugged its shoulders at any fate. The Astrologer continued:
“But I should not like to come to that...
What I should like is to count on your personal help... that you should interest yourself in our projects.
Believe me, we are living in a terrible epoch.
Whoever finds the lie that the multitude needs will be the King of the World.
All men live in anguish...
Catholicism satisfies no one, Buddhism is not suited to our temperament spoiled by the desire for pleasure.
Perhaps we shall speak of Lucifer and the Morning Star.
You will add to our dreams all the poetry they need, and we shall address ourselves to the young...
Oh, this is very great... very great... ”
The Astrologer dropped onto the crate.
He was exhausted.
He wiped the sweat from his forehead with a checked handkerchief like those of peasants, and the three remained for a moment in silence. Suddenly Barsut said:
“Yes, you are right, this is very great.
Release me and I will sign the check. ”
He had thought that all the Astrologer’s words were lies, and that almost undid him. The Astrologer rose thoughtfully:
“Pardon me, I shall set you free after I have cashed the check.
Today is Wednesday.

Tomorrow at noon you can be free, but you will only be able to leave our house in two months”—he said this because he noticed that the other did not believe in his projects—“Do you need anything for this afternoon? ”
“No. ”
“Good, until later. ”
“But are you leaving like that?...
Stay... ”
“No.
I am tired.
I need to sleep a while.
I shall come tonight and we shall talk a little more.
Do you want cigarettes? ”
“All right. ”
They left the stable.
Barsut lay down on his bed of dry grass, and lighting a cigarette sent out a few puffs of smoke that, in the slanting ray of a sunbeam, unbraided their marvelous spirals of blue steel.
Now that he was alone his thoughts arranged themselves cordially, and he even said to himself:
“Why not help ‘that one’?
The project he has for the colony is interesting, and now I understand why that brute Erdosain admires him so much.
It is true that I shall be left in the street... perhaps yes, perhaps no... but one way or another it had to end.
” And he half-closed his eyes to meditate on the future.
The Astrologer, with his top hat pulled down over his eyes, turned to Erdosain and said:
“Barsut thinks he has deceived us.
Tomorrow, after cashing the check, we shall have to execute him... ”
“No, you will have to execute him... ”
“I have no objection... but what can we do?
Once free that envious man would denounce us at once.
And he thinks we are mad!
And indeed we should be if we left him alive. ”
They stopped beside the house.
Above, some chocolate-colored clouds advanced rapidly across the blue with their jagged relief.
“Who is going to assassinate him? ”
“The Man Who Saw the Midwife. ”
“You know it is not very pleasant to die with summer at the door... ”
“That’s how it is... ”
“And the check? ”
“You will cash it. ”
“Aren’t you afraid I might run away? ”
“No, not for the moment. ”
“Why? ”
“Because not.
You more than anyone need the society to succeed in order to relieve your boredom.
If you are my accomplice, it is precisely for that... out of boredom, out of anguish. ”
“It may be.
Tomorrow, at what time shall we meet? ”
“Well... at nine at the station.
I shall bring you the check.
By the way, do you have an identity card? ”
“Yes. ”
“Then there is nothing to fear.
Ah! one thing.
I recommend that you speak little at the meeting and coldly. ”
“Are they all there? ”
“Yes. ”
“Also the Gold Seeker? ”
“Yes. ”
Pushing aside the branches that lashed their faces, they advanced toward the bower.
It was a kiosk built of laths, and on the wooden diamonds the growths of a honeysuckle loaded with violet and white bellflowers fastened their green stems.
As he entered, the circle of men rose to their feet, but Erdosain stopped short in astonishment upon noticing an army officer among them, wearing a major’s uniform.
There stood the Gold Prospector, Haffner, an unknown man, and the Major.
The first two were leaning on the table.
Haffner was rereading some blank sheets of paper, while the Gold Prospector had a map spread out before him.
A heavy stone with a seal on it kept the wind from carrying the drawing away.
The Pimp shook Erdosain’s hand and the latter sat down beside him, immediately beginning to observe the Major, who had suddenly awakened all his curiosity.
Truly the Astrologer was a master of surprises.
Nevertheless, the unknown man made a bad impression on him.
He was a man of great height, livid, with jet-black eyes.
There was something repellent about him: his lower lip curled in a perpetual sneer of contempt, his long, hooked nose wrinkled above the brow by three transverse creases.

A silky mustache fell over his red lips, and his gaze barely rested on Erdosain; as soon as he was introduced he dropped into a hammock, remaining there with his head resting against the back, his sword between his knees and a lock of hair plastered to his flat forehead.
For several minutes everyone remained silent, observing one another with evident discomfort.
The Astrologer, seated to one side of the entrance to the bower, lit a cigarette and glanced sideways at the “chiefs,” as they would be called in a later meeting.
Suddenly he raised his head, looked at the other five men seated at the head of the table, and said:

“I don’t think it is necessary for us to repeat again what we all know and have agreed upon in private meetings... that is, the organization of a secret society whose upkeep will be carried out through moral or immoral businesses.
On this we are all in agreement, are we not?
What would you say (I like geometry) if we called the different radial chiefs of the society ‘cells’? ”
“That’s what they’re called in Russia,” said the Major.
“The members of each cell will not be able to know the members of another. ”
“How... the chiefs won’t know one another? ”
“The ones who will not know one another, I insist, are not the chiefs but the associates. ” The Gold Prospector interrupted:
“That way nothing will get done.
What is it that binds the members of the different cells together? ”
“But the society is the six of us. ”
“No, sir... the society is me,” objected the Astrologer.
“Speaking seriously, I will tell you that the society is everyone... always with restrictions as far as I am concerned. ” The Major intervened:
“I think the discussion is pointless, because as I understand it there will be a perfectly established hierarchy.
Each promotion will put the cell member in contact with a new chief.
There will be as many promotions as there are cell chiefs. ”
“How many cells are there at the moment? ”
“Four.
I will be in charge of everything,” the Astrologer continued.

“You, Erdosain, Chief of Industries; the Gold Prospector”—a young man at the corner of the table bowed his head—“will be in charge of Colonies and Mines; the Major will spread our society through the army, and Haffner will be Chief of the Brothels. ” Haffner stood up, exclaiming:
“Pardon me, I will not be chief of anything.
I am here as I could be anywhere.
The only thing I am doing for you people is giving you a budget and nothing more.
If I am in the way I can leave. ”
“No, stay,” the Astrologer corrected.
The Melancholy Ruffian sat down again and began to doodle with a pencil on the paper.
Erdosain admired his insolence.

But beyond all doubt the one who now concentrated everyone’s attention and curiosity was the Major, with the prestige of his uniform and the strangeness of his presence. The Gold Prospector turned toward him:
“What do you mean?
Do you have hope of infiltrating our society into the army? ”
Everyone had straightened up in their chairs.
This was the surprise of the meeting, the effect prepared in silence.
Undoubtedly the Astrologer had the makings of a true leader.
The pity was that he always kept the secret of his methods.
But Erdosain felt proud to share a complicity with him.
Now everyone had sat up in their seats to listen to the Major.
The latter looked at the Astrologer, then said:
“Gentlemen, I will speak to you in very weighty words.
Otherwise I would not be here. What is happening is this:
Our army is riddled with discontented officers.
It is not worth enumerating the reasons, nor would they interest you.

The ideas of ‘dictatorship’ and the military political events of recent times—I refer to Spain and Chile—have made many of my comrades think that our country could also be fertile ground for a dictatorship. ”
The most extraordinary astonishment opened every mouth.
This was the unexpected. The Gold Prospector replied:
“But do you believe that the Argentine army...
I mean... the officers, will accept our ideas? ”
“Of course they will accept them... provided you know how to present them.
I can already tell you that the number of officers disillusioned with democratic theories, including parliament, is far greater than you believe.
Do not interrupt me, sir.
Ninety percent of the deputies in our country are inferior in culture to a first lieutenant in our army.

A politician who has been accused of participating in the murder of a governor once said very aptly: ‘To govern a people you need no greater abilities than those of a ranch foreman.’ And that man spoke the truth with reference to our America.
” The Astrologer rubbed his hands with evident satisfaction.
The Major continued, with everyone’s eyes fixed on him:
“The army is a superior state within an inferior society, since we are the specific force of the country.

And yet we are subject to the decisions of the government... and who makes up the government?... the legislative and executive powers... that is, men chosen by shapeless political parties... and what representatives, gentlemen!

You know better than I that to be a deputy one must have had a career of lies, begun as a loafer in a political committee, compromising and living with scoundrels of every sort—in short, a life on the margins of the law and of truth.
I do not know if this happens in countries more civilized than ours, but here it is so.

In our chamber of deputies and senators there are individuals accused of usury and homicide, bandits sold to foreign companies, men of such crass ignorance that parliamentarianism here becomes the most grotesque comedy that could have debased a country.
Presidential elections are carried out with North American capital, after a promise to grant concessions to a company interested in exploiting our national wealth.
I do not exaggerate when I say that the struggle of political parties in our fatherland is nothing more than a brawl among merchants who want to sell the country to the highest bidder. ”
Everyone looked at the Major in stupefaction.
Through the diamond-shaped and bell-shaped openings one could see the blue sky of morning, but no one noticed it.
Erdosain told me later that none of those present at the Wednesday meeting had foreseen a scene of such high interest.
The Major passed a handkerchief over his lips and continued:
“I am glad my words interest you.
There are many young officers who think as I do.
We even have some new generals...
What is advisable, and do not be surprised at what I am going to tell you, is to give the society a completely communist appearance.
I tell you this because communism does not exist here, and one cannot call communists that bunch of carpenters who talk nonsense about sociology in a neighborhood where no one even removes his hat.
I wish to explain my thought clearly.
Every secret society is a cancer in the community.
Its mysterious functions upset the functioning of that community.
Very well, we, the cell chiefs, will give those cells a completely Bolshevik character.
” It was the first time that word had been pronounced there, and involuntarily everyone looked at one another.
“This appearance will attract numerous unbalanced people and, consequently, the multiplication of the cells.
Thus we will create a fictitious revolutionary body.
We will especially cultivate terrorist attacks.
An attack that enjoys moderate success awakens all the dark and ferocious consciences in society.
If in the space of a year we repeat the attacks, accompanying them with antisocial proclamations that incite the proletariat to the creation of ‘soviets’...
Do you know what we will have achieved?
Something admirable and simple.
To create revolutionary unrest in the country.

“I would define ‘revolutionary unrest’ as a collective uneasiness that does not dare to express its desires; everyone feels disturbed, inflamed; the newspapers foment the storm and the police help by detaining innocents, who, because of the sufferings they endure, become revolutionaries; every morning people wake up anxious for news, expecting an attack more ferocious than the previous one that will justify their suspicions; police injustices inflame the spirits of those who did not suffer them; there is never a lack of an exalted man who discharges his revolver into the chest of a policeman; workers’ organizations stir and decree strikes, and the words revolution and Bolshevism spread panic and hope everywhere.
Now then, when numerous bombs have exploded in the corners of the city and the proclamations have been read and revolutionary unrest is ripe, then we, the military, will intervene... ”
The Major moved his boots out of a ray of sunlight and continued:
“Yes, we, the military, will intervene.
We will say that in view of the government’s limited capacity to defend the institutions of the fatherland, capital, and the family, we are seizing the State, proclaiming a transitory dictatorship.
All dictatorships are transitory in order to inspire confidence.
Bourgeois capitalists, and especially conservative foreign governments, will immediately recognize the new state of affairs.
We will blame the Soviet government for forcing us to assume such an attitude and we will shoot a few poor devils convicted and confessed of manufacturing bombs.
We will suppress the two chambers and the national budget will be reduced to a minimum.
The administration of the State will be placed in the hands of military administration.
The country will thus attain a greatness never before seen. ”
The Major fell silent, and in the flowered bower the men burst into applause.
A dove took flight.
“Your idea is beautiful,” said Erdosain, “but the fact is that we will be working for you... ”
“Didn’t you want to be chiefs? ”
“Yes, but what we will receive will be the crumbs from the banquet... ”
“No, sir... you are mistaken... what has been thought... ” The Astrologer intervened:
“Gentlemen... we have not met to discuss orientations that do not interest us now... but to organize the activities of the cell chiefs.
If you are ready, let us begin. ”
A robust young man who until then had remained silent intervened in the discussion.
“Will you permit me? ”
“Of course. ”
“Well then, I believe the matter should be put this way: Do you or do you not want the revolution?
The details of organization must come later. ”
“That... that comes later... yes, sir. ”
The unknown man finally explained himself:
“I am a friend of Mr. Haffner.
I am a lawyer.
I have renounced the benefits my profession could give me because I will not compromise with the capitalist regime.
Do I or do I not have the right to think this way? ”
“Yes, sir, you do. ”
“Then I assure you that what the Major has said gives a new orientation to our society. ”
“No,” objected the Gold Prospector.
“It can be the basis of it without the exclusion of its other principles. ”
“Clearly. ”
“Yes. ”
The discussion was about to flare up again. The Astrologer rose:
“Gentlemen, you will argue another day.
Now it is a question of commercial organization... not of ideas.
Therefore we will suppress everything that departs from that. ”
“That is dictatorship,” exclaimed the lawyer.
The Astrologer looked at him for a moment, then said slowly:
“You feel you have the makings of a chief, I believe...
I think you do.
Your duty, if you are intelligent, is to organize another society far from us.
That way we will provoke the collapse of the present one.
Here you obey me, or you leave. ”
For an instant the two men examined each other; the lawyer stood up, fixed his eyes on the Astrologer, bowed with a strong man’s smile, and left.
The silence of all was broken by the voice of the Major, who said to the Astrologer:
“You have acted very well.
Discipline is the basis of everything.
We are listening. ”
Diamonds of sun laid their golden mosaic on the black earth of the bower.
In the distance the anvil of a blacksmith’s shop rang out; innumerable birds sent their warbling rolling among the branches.
Erdosain sucked at the white flower of the honeysuckle and the Gold Prospector, elbows on his knees, stared attentively at the ground.
The Ruffian smoked and Erdosain spied on the Mongolian countenance of the Astrologer, in his gray smock buttoned up to the throat.
A painful silence followed these words.
What was that intruder looking for there?
Erdosain, suddenly in a bad mood, stood up, exclaiming:
“There will be all the discipline you people want here, but it is absurd for us to be talking about military dictatorship.
The only thing that can interest us is soldiers joining a red movement. ”
The Major straightened up in his seat and, looking at Erdosain, said with a smile:
“Then you admit that I am playing my role well? ”
“Role?... ”
“Yes, man...
I am as much a major as you are. ”
“Do you all see now the power of the lie?
” said the Astrologer.
“I have disguised this friend as a soldier and already you yourselves believed, even though you were almost in on the secret, that we had a revolution in the army. ”
“Then?... ”
“This was nothing more than a rehearsal... since we will stage the comedy in earnest one day.
” The words sounded so threatening that the four men remained staring at the Major, who said:
“In reality I have not risen above sergeant”—but the Astrologer interrupted his explanations, saying:
“Friend Haffner, do you have the budget? ”
“Yes... here it is. ”
The Astrologer leafed through the sheets scrawled with figures for a few minutes and explained to those present:
“The most solid base of the economic part of our society is the brothels. ” The Astrologer continued:
“The gentleman has given me a budget referring to the installation of a brothel with ten girls.
Here are the expenses to be made. ” And he read: –10 used bedroom sets $2,000 –Monthly house rent $400 –Deposit, three months $1,200
–Installation, kitchen, bathrooms and bar $2,000 –Monthly bribe to the commissioner $300 –Bribe to the doctor $150
–Bribe to the political boss for the concession $2,000 –Monthly municipal tax $50 –Electric piano $1,500 –Manageress $150 –Cook $150 Total: $9,000
“Each girl pays 14 pesos per week for food expenses and must buy from the house the yerba, sugar, kerosene, candles, stockings, powder, soap and perfumes.
“Outside of all expenses we can count on a minimum income of two thousand five hundred pesos per month.
In four months we will have recovered the invested capital.
With fifty percent of the net receipts we will install other brothels, twenty-five percent will be destined to cover debts, and the remaining third will be used to support the cells.
Is the expenditure of ten thousand pesos authorized or not? ”
Everyone bowed their heads in approval, except the Gold Prospector, who said:
“Who is the auditor? ”
“He will be elected when everything is finished. ”
“Agreed. ”
“You too, Major? ”
“Yes. ”

Erdosain raised his head and looked at the pale face of the pseudo-sergeant, whose sly eyes had fixed on a white butterfly moving its wings in the greenery, and this time he could not help asking himself how it was possible that the Astrologer could move such actors. But the Astrologer interpreted him:
“You, Mr. Erdosain, how much do you need to set up the electroplating workshop? ”
“One thousand pesos. ”
“Ah!
You are the inventor of the copper rose?
” the Major said to him.
“Yes. ”
“I congratulate you.
I believe the sales will be successful.
Naturally one must metallize flowers in large quantities. ”
“That is so.
I have thought of adding the photography line.
It would cover the workshop expenses. ”
“That is up to your judgment. ”

“Besides, I already have a practical friend of mine for the electroplating”—as he said this he was thinking of the Espila family, who could well join the secret society, but the Astrologer interrupted his reflections, saying:
“The Gold Prospector is going to give us news of the area where we plan to install our colony”—and he stood up.
Erdosain was astonished when he considered the other man’s physique.
He had imagined him according to the canons of the cinema, an enormous man with a blond beard reeking of drink.
There was no such thing.
The Gold Prospector was a young man of his own age, skin stretched over the flat bones of his face and extremely pale, with lively jet-black eyes.
His enormous thoracic cage seemed to belong to a man twice as developed as he.
His legs were thin and bowed.
Between the leather belt and the cloth of his trousers one could see the butt of a revolver.
He had a clear voice, but everything about him had a strange air, as if the individual were composed of different human parts belonging to men of different conditions.
Thus, his face was that of a gambling-house man accustomed to squinting behind cards, his chest that of a boxer, and his legs those of a jockey.
And he had something of that mixture in the formless reality that emanated from his body.

Until the age of fourteen he had lived in the country, then he had shot a thief to death, and later fear of tuberculosis had driven him back to the plain and he had galloped days and nights over incredible distances.
Erdosain felt immediate sympathy for him.
The Gold Prospector unwrapped some stones.
They were pieces of gold-bearing quartz. Then he said:
“Here is the certificate of analysis from the Bureau of Mines and Hydrology. ”
The stones passed quickly from hand to hand.
Their eyes expressed an extraordinary voracity and the tips of their fingers brushed the quartz with delight, with its scales and compact grafts of gold.
The Astrologer, slowly rolling a cigarette, observed all the faces that had received a discharge of soul... a temptation tensed them as they examined the stones.
The Gold Prospector sat down again and said, addressing everyone:
“Down there is a lot of gold.
No one knows it.
It is in the Chilean Field.
First I was in Esquel... the machines from a failed operation are lying there, then I went to Arroyo Pescado...
I walked... down there, I don’t know if you know, the days are not counted and I entered the Chilean Field.
Jungle, pure forest of thousands of square kilometers.
The Mask was with me, a prostitute from Esquel who knew a trail to get in because she had been there before with a miner who was murdered on his way back.
Well, down there they kill a man for nothing.
She was syphilitic and she stayed behind in the forest.
The Mask.
Yes, I remember!
She had been wandering those parts for twenty years.
From Puerto Madryn she went to Comodoro, then to Trelew, then to Esquel.
She knew all the gold prospectors.

First we went as far as Arroyo Pescado... it is forty leagues farther south of Esquel... but there was only a little dust in the sands... on horseback we continued for fifteen days and between forest and forest we reached the Chilean Field. ”
With a clear voice and fixed on the subject of the narrator, the Gold Prospector told his odyssey in the south.
Listening to him, Erdosain had the impression of crossing, in the company of the Mask, gigantic black and glacial gorges, closed on the horizon by violet triangles of more mountains.

The high plateaus disappeared under the lofty advance of the perpetual forest of reddish trunks and black-green foliage, and they, hallucinated, continued onward beneath the deep space, smooth as a desert of celestial ice.
With slow gestures, indifferent to the astonishment his story aroused, the Gold Prospector told the adventure of months.
Everyone listened to him, absorbed.
Then, one morning he reached the black gorge.
It was a circle of black, crested basaltic stone, a rim plumed with dark stalagmites, where the blue of the sky became infinitely sad.
Wandering birds brushed the stone blocks in their flight, shaded by other circles of higher mountains...
And at the bottom of that great pit, a lake of golden water where threads of waterfalls, unbraided by the brambles, flowed back.
Never had the Gold Prospector been in such sinister places.
That depth of bronze water mirroring the black cliffs stopped him in astonishment.
The stone walls fell perpendicularly, mottled with greenish sarcomas, with long malachites, and in that bronze bottom his pale, bearded figure was reflected with his feet toward the sky.
At once it occurred to him that the water must be gold, but he rejected the hypothesis as absurd, because he had never read or heard anything like it, and he continued:

“But on the way back, finding myself one day in Rawson waiting in a dentist’s waiting room, it occurred to me to leaf through a magazine called ‘Medical Week’ that was on one of the tables in the lobby... and here the prodigy occurs.

I open the pamphlet at random and on the first page I look at I see an article titled: ‘Gold water, or colloidal gold in the therapeutics of erythematous lupus.’ I began to read and then I learned that gold is capable of remaining suspended in water in microscopic particles... and that this phenomenon which for me was brand new had been discovered by the alchemists who called it ‘gold water.’ They obtained it by the simplest procedure imaginable: throwing a red-hot piece of gold into rainwater.
Immediately I remembered the lake whose coloration I had attributed to vegetable substances.
I had been, without recognizing it, beside a lake of colloidal gold that perhaps how many centuries had taken to form by the passage of water beside the veins.
Do you realize now what ignorance is?
If chance had not thrown that magazine into my hands, I would have remained ignorant forever of the importance of that discovery... ”
“And did you go back?
” the Major interrupted.
“But of course.
I went back alone eight months ago; that was when I wrote to you... but I was starting from an error...

I have to study the metallic extraction of gold... besides there are veins there... it is a question of working... getting a diver’s suit, because the bottom of the water is golden and the water itself has no color. ” Haffner said:
“You know what you’re telling is interesting?
Even if there were no gold, that place is always more fun than this filthy city. ” The Major added:
“If the colony is installed in the Chilean Field, it will be necessary to have a telegraph station. ” Erdosain replied:
“If so, a portable station with a wavelength of 45 to 80 meters can be set up.
It would cost five hundred pesos and has a range of three thousand kilometers. ” The Major intervened again:
“The colony has my full preference because there we can install the asphyxiating gas factory.
You, Erdosain, know something about that. ”
“Yes, that aristol can be manufactured electrolytically, but I have not studied anything about it, although the asphyxiating gases and the bacteriological laboratory are what should concern us most.
Especially the laboratory for culturing bubonic plague and Asiatic cholera microbes.
We would have to get some ‘type’ bacteria; the advantage lies in the enormous cheapness of production. ” The Astrologer intervened:
“I think the most convenient thing would be to leave the organization of the colony for later.
For now we must limit ourselves to carrying out Haffner’s project.
Only when we have income will we organize the first contingent that will leave for the colony.
You, Erdosain, had spoken to me about a family? ”
“Yes, the Espilas. ” Haffner replied:
“What the devil!
It seems to me we’re doing nothing but talking nonsense.
Although it is true that in your society I am nothing more than a simple informant, it seems to me that something should be decided right now. ”
The Astrologer looked at him and replied:
“Are you prepared to give the money to do something?
No. Then?
Wait until we have capital, which cannot be many days before we will have it, and then you will see.
” Haffner stood up, and looking at the Gold Prospector, said:

“You know, comrade; when the colony matter is ready, let me know; and if you need people, all the better, I will provide you with a gang of rogues who will have no problem leaving Buenos Aires”—and putting on his hat, without shaking anyone’s hand and saluting them all with a gesture, he was about to leave when, remembering something, he exclaimed, addressing the Astrologer: “If you hurry to get the money, there is a magnificent brothel for sale.
It has an annex and a grill-room, and besides a lot of gambling goes on.
The owner is a Uruguayan and he asks 15,000 pesos cash, but with ten thousand and the other five on a year’s credit I think he will agree. ”
“Can you come here on Friday? ”
“Yes. ”
“Good, see me on Friday, I think we will settle the matter. ”
“Salú.
” Thus the Ruffian greeted them, and left.
After Haffner left, Erdosain, who felt like talking with the Gold Prospector, took his leave of the Astrologer and the Major.
Once again Erdosain was restless.
Before he withdrew, the Astrologer drew him aside and said:
“Don’t miss tomorrow at nine.
We have to cash the cheque. ”
He had forgotten about “that.
” Suddenly Erdosain looked around as if stunned by a blow.
He needed to talk to someone, to forget the dark duty that was now accelerating the beats of his veins under the burning midday sun.
The Gold Prospector had struck him as likeable. So he approached him and said:
“Would you care to come with me?
I’d like to talk with you about ‘down there.’”
The other man observed him with his sparkling little eyes and then said:
“Of course.
Delighted.
You’ve been very likeable to me. ”
“Thanks. ”
“Especially after what the Astrologer told me about you.
Do you know that your plan to make the social revolution with plague bacilli is formidable? ”
Erdosain raised his eyes.
Those praises almost humiliated him.
Was it possible that someone attached importance to the theories he thought up? The Gold Prospector insisted:
“That and the asphyxiating gases is admirable.
Can you imagine it?
Leaving a steel cylinder in the Police Department at the exact hour when that bandit Santiago is there!
Poisoning all the ‘narks’ like rats!
” And he let out such a thunderous guffaw that three birds flew off in a wide arc from a lemon tree.
“Yes, my friend Erdosain, you’re a colossus.
Plague and chlorine.
You know we’re going to revolutionize this city?
I can already picture that day: the shopkeepers scurrying out of their burrows like frightened viscachas while we clean the planet of filth with a machine gun.
Two hundred and fifty rounds per minute.
A piece of cake.
And then curtains of chlorine or phosgene...
Ah!
We ought to publish your projects in the papers, believe me... ”
Erdosain interrupted the panegyric with this question:
“So you found the gold, didn’t you?... the gold... ”
“I suppose you don’t believe in that novel about the placer deposits. ”
“What do you mean, novel?
So the gold...? ”
“It exists, of course it exists... but you have to find it. ”
Erdosain’s disappointment was so deep that the Gold Prospector added:
“Look, brother...
I spoke to you because the Astrologer told me I could. ”
“Yes, but I thought... ”
“What? ”
“That among so many lies, that would be one of the few truths. ”
“In the end it is true.
The gold exists... you just have to find it, that’s all.
You should be glad that everything is being organized so we can go look for it.
Or do you think those animals would move if they weren’t driven by extraordinary lies?
Ah!
How much I’ve thought about it.
That’s where the greatness of the Astrologer’s theory lies: men only shake themselves awake with lies.
He gives the false the consistency of the true; people who would never have walked a step to achieve anything, wrecks broken by every disillusion, come back to life through the power of his lies.
Could you want anything greater?
Notice that the same thing happens in reality and no one condemns it.
Yes, everything is appearance... realize that... there is no man who does not accept the small, stupid lies that govern the functioning of our society.
What is the Astrologer’s sin?
To replace an insignificant lie with an eloquent, enormous, transcendental lie.

The Astrologer, with his falsehoods, does not seem like an extraordinary man, and he isn’t... and he is; he is... because he draws no personal profit from his lies, and he isn’t because all he does is apply an old principle used by every swindler and reorganizer of humanity.
If one day the history of that man is written, those who read it and have a little cold blood will say: He was great, because he achieved with any charlatan.

And what seems novelistic and disturbing to us is nothing more than the anxiety of weak and mediocre spirits who only believe in success when the means to reach it are complicated, mysterious, and not simple.
And yet you ought to know that great acts are simple, like the proof of Columbus’s egg. ”
“The truth of the lie? ”
“Exactly.
What we lack is the courage for enormous undertakings.
We imagine that running a State is more complicated than running a modest household, and we load events with an excess of novelistic nonsense, of idiotic romanticism. ”
“But in your conscience do you feel—I mean, does reality give you the impression that we will succeed? ”
“Completely, and believe me... we shall at least be the masters of the country... if not of the world.
We have to be.
What the Astrologer is planning is the salvation of the souls of men exhausted by the mechanization of our civilization.
There are no more ideals.
There are no good or bad symbols.
The Astrologer was talking the other day about colonies founded in the old world by vagrants who didn’t feel at home in their own country.
We shall do the same, but giving the Society a sense of vigorous play... a game that seduces even the soul of shopkeepers when they go to the cinema to see a cowboy adventure.
What do you know, brother, about the messes we plan to stir up?...
In the last resort we’ll sow trinitrotoluene bombs to amuse ourselves a little with the terror of the rabble.
What do you think the old gangs and the toughs of the outskirts were?
Men who had found no channel in which to pour their energy.
So they vented it by beating up some dandy or some Turk.
Look...
Comodoro...
Puerto Madryn, Trelew, Esquel, Arroyo Pescado, Campo Chileno, I know all the roads and all the solitudes...
Believe me... we shall organize a splendid body of young men”—he had grown excited.
“You think there is no gold?
You remind me of children whose eyes at the table are bigger than their stomachs.
In our country everything is gold. ”
Erdosain felt himself swept along by the other man’s heat.
The Gold Prospector spoke convulsively, winking, raising first one eyebrow then the other, shaking Erdosain’s arm in a friendly way.
“Believe me, Erdosain... there is a lot of gold... more than you can imagine... but that is not the real point.
There is another: time that slips away.
Esquel, Arroyo Pescado, Río Pico...
Campo Chileno... leagues... roads of days and days... and you know, you know that to get a certificate for a horse worth less than ten pesos you walk for weeks; time is worth nothing...
Everything is big... enormous... eternal down there.
You have to convince yourself.
I remember when the Mask and I went along Arroyo Pescado.
Not only gold... red gold...
Down there the souls sickened by civilization are saved.
We shall send all our people to the mountains.
Look...
I am twenty-seven years old... and I’ve risked my hide with bullets several times”—he drew his revolver.
“See that sparrow?
”—it was fifty paces away; he raised the revolver to his chin, pressed the trigger, and at the sound of the shot the bird shot vertically off the branch.
“See?
That’s how I’ve risked my hide many times.
There’s no reason to be sad.
Look, I’m twenty-seven.
Arroyo Pescado, Esquel, Río Pico, Campo Chileno... all the solitudes will be ours... we shall organize the escort of the New Joy... the Order of the Knights of the Red Gold...
You think I’m exalted.
Not at all, man!
You have to have been there to understand.
And in those circumstances one conceives the need, the indispensable need for a natural aristocracy.
Defying solitude, dangers, sadness, the sun, the infinity of the plain, one feels like another man... different from the herd of slaves that agonizes in the city.
Do you know what the anarchist, socialist proletariat of our cities is?
A herd of cowards.
Instead of going off to break their souls in the mountains and the fields, they prefer the comforts and amusements to the heroic solitude of the desert.
What would the factories, the fashion houses, the thousand parasitic mechanisms of the city do if men went off to the desert... if each one of them pitched his tent down there?
Do you understand now why I am with the Astrologer?
We young men will create the new life; yes, we will.
We shall establish a bandit aristocracy.
The intellectuals infected with Tolstoy’s idiocy we shall shoot, and the rest will work for us.
That’s why I admire Mussolini.
In that land of mandolin players he established the use of the cudgel and that operetta kingdom was transformed overnight into the mastiff of the Mediterranean.
Cities are the cancers of the world.
They annihilate man, they mould him cowardly, cunning, envious, and it is envy that asserts his social rights, envy and cowardice.
If those herds were made up of courageous beasts they would have smashed everything to pieces.
To believe in the mass is to believe one can touch the moon with one’s hand.
Look what happened to Lenin with the Russian peasant.
But everything is already organized and there is nothing left but to say: in our century those who do not feel at home in the city should go to the desert.
That is what the Astrologer proposes.
He is quite right.
When the first Christians felt ill at ease in the cities they went to the desert.
There, in their own way, they built their happiness.
Today, on the other hand, the rabble of the cities bark in the committees. ”
“You know I like your simile of the desert? ”
“But of course, Erdosain.
The Astrologer says it: those who are not comfortable in the cities have no right to bother those who enjoy them.
For the discontented and uncomfortable of the cities there is the mountain, the plain, the bank of the great rivers. ”
Erdosain had not imagined such violence in the Gold Prospector.
The other guessed his thought, because he said:

“We shall preach violence, but we shall not accept into the cells the theorists of violence; rather, whoever wants to show us his hatred of the present civilization will have to give us proof of his obedience to the society.
Do you see now the purpose of the colony?
Isn’t gold also a beautiful illusion?
The effort will turn him into a superman.
Then powers will be granted to him.
Doesn’t the same thing happen with monastic orders?
Isn’t the army organized that way?
But, man, don’t stand there with your mouth open!
In the same commercial enterprises... for example, at Gath and Chaves, at Harrods, the employees have told me that the staff is governed by a discipline beside which military discipline is a toy.
So you see, Erdosain, that we invent nothing.
We replace a mean end with an extraordinary end, nothing more. ”
Erdosain felt humiliated before the Gold Prospector.
He envied the other man his violence; the other’s crude, indisputable truths irritated him, and he would have liked to contradict him, even as he told himself:
“I am less a character in a drama than he; I am the sordid, cowardly man of the city.
Why don’t I feel his aggressiveness and his hatred?
Yes, he is right.
And I smile at his words, prudently, as if afraid he might slap me, and it is because his violence frightens me, his courage angers me. ”
“What are you thinking about, brother?
” said the Gold Prospector.
The Gold Prospector shrugged his shoulders.
“You think you are a coward because circumstances have not forced you to risk your hide.
I want to see you the day your life hangs on the trigger of a revolver, whether you are a coward or not.
The fact is that in the city one cannot be brave.
You know that if you smash the face of some wretch the police procedures will bother you so much that you prefer to put up with it rather than take justice into your own hands.
That is the reality.
And one gets used to being resigned, to restraining one’s impulses... ” Erdosain looked at him:
“You know that’s remarkable? ”
“Don’t worry, partner.
You’ll soon see how you’re going to wake up... and you’ll find you have the soul of a brave man...
You just have to begin, that’s all. ”
At one in the afternoon the two men took leave of each other.

That same day, shortly before Erdosain reached the last turn of the spiral staircase, he noticed a woman standing on the landing, wrapped in a sealskin coat and a green hat, talking with the landlady of the boarding house.
An “there he comes” made him realize it was him they were waiting for, and when he stopped in the hallway, the stranger, turning her slightly freckled face toward him, said:
“Are you Mr. Erdosain? ”
“Where have I seen that face?
” Erdosain wondered as he answered the stranger in the affirmative. She then introduced herself:
“I am Mr. Ergueta’s wife. ”
“Ah!
So you’re the Cripple!
” But suddenly, ashamed of the blunder that had astonished the landlady into looking at the stranger’s feet, Erdosain apologized:
“Forgive me, I’m dazed...
You understand, I wasn’t expecting...
Would you like to come in? ”
Before opening the door to his room, Erdosain apologized once more for the disorder the visitor would find inside, and Hipólita, smiling ironically, replied:
“It’s quite all right, sir. ”
Yet Erdosain was irritated by the cold gaze that filtered through the woman’s transparent greenish-grey pupils.

And he thought: “She must be a perverse one,” for he had noticed that beneath the green hat, Hipólita’s red hair was smoothed down along her temples in two sleek bands that covered the tips of her ears.
He observed again her stiff red eyelashes and the lips that seemed swollen in the flushed softness of her freckled face.
And he told himself: “How different from the photograph! ”

She, standing before him, observed him as if saying to herself: “So this is the man,” and he, close beside the woman, felt her presence without grasping it, as though she did not exist or were many leagues away from him along some inner path.
Yet there she was, and something had to be said; since nothing else occurred to him, after turning on the light and offering the lady a chair while he took the sofa, he said:
“So you’re Ergueta’s wife?
Very well. ”
He still could not grasp what this life suddenly implanted in his bewilderment was doing there.

A gust of curiosity stirred his soul, but he would have preferred to feel otherwise, to feel familiar with the woman’s face, whose oval lines held something of the red of copper, like those rays of sunlight in a rainstorm that, in paintings of saints, burst forth in a thousand shafts from among a pinnacle of clouds. And he kept saying to himself:
“I am here, but my soul—where is it?
” And again he said: “So you’re Ergueta’s wife?
Very well. ”

She, who had crossed her legs, pulled the hem of her dress well below her knee; the fabric gathered between her pink fingers, and raising her head as though the movement cost her a great effort in the strangeness of an unfamiliar setting, she said:
“You must do something for my husband.
He has gone mad. ”

“My curiosity has received no great blow,” Erdosain told himself, and satisfied at remaining unmoved like one of those bankers in Xavier de Montépin’s novels, he added, with the inner glee of being able to play the part of the impassive man: “So he’s gone mad?
” But suddenly, realizing he could not sustain the role any longer, he said: “Do you realize, madam?
You give me extraordinary news, and yet I have remained impassive.
It pains me to be like this, empty of all emotion; I would like to feel something and yet I am like a paving stone.
You must forgive me.
I don’t know what’s happening to me.
You will forgive me, won’t you?
In the past, though, I wasn’t like this.
I remember I was as cheerful as a sparrow.
I’ve changed little by little.
I don’t know; I look at you and I’d like to feel that I’m your friend and I can’t.
If I saw you dying I probably wouldn’t even hand you a glass of water.
Do you realize?
And yet...
But where is he? ”
“At the Hospicio de las Mercedes. ”
“How strange!
Weren’t you living in Azul? ”
“Yes, but we’ve been here for two weeks... ”
“And when did ‘that’ happen? ”
“Six days ago.
I can’t explain it myself.
It’s like what you were saying earlier about me. ”
Forgive me if I’m wasting your time.
I thought of you because you knew him; he always spoke to me about you.
When was the last time you saw him? ”
“Before he got married...
Yes, he spoke to me about you.
He called you the Cripple... and the Whore. ”
It seemed to Erdosain that Hipólita’s soul was quietly enameling her pupils.
He felt certain he could talk about anything with her.
The woman’s soul stood motionless there, ready to receive him naturally.
She had rested her crossed hands on her skirt above her knee, and that posture made the moment of confidence easier.

What had happened that morning at the Astrologer’s house now seemed remote; only some scrap of tree and sky occasionally crossed his memory, and the sliding of those broken images left resting on his consciousness a slow, unjustified pleasure.
He rubbed his hands together with satisfaction and said:
“You won’t be offended, madam... but I think he was already mad when he married you... ”
“Tell me...
Do you know whether he used to gamble before he married me? ”
“Yes...
Besides, I remember he studied the Bible a great deal, because among other things he spoke to me about the new times, the fourth seal, and a whole lot of other things.
Besides, he gambled.
He always interested me because I saw in him a frantic temperament. ”
“Exactly.
A frantic one.
He once accepted a five-thousand-peso bet at a poker table. ”
He sold my jewels, a necklace a friend had given me... ”
“But how?...
Didn’t you give that necklace to the maid shortly before you married him?
That’s what he told me.
That you gave him the necklace and the silver dinner service... and the ten-thousand-peso check the other man gave you... ”
“But do you think I’m crazy!...
Why would I give my maid a pearl necklace? ”
“Then he lied. ”
“That’s what it seems to me. ”
“How curious!... ”
“Don’t be surprised.
He lied a lot.
Besides, in the last few days he was lost.
He worked out a martingale to apply to roulette.
You would have laughed if you’d seen him.
He made a book of numbers that no one understood except him.
What a man!

He couldn’t sleep for worrying; he neglected the pharmacy; sometimes, when the light was out and I was about to fall asleep, I’d hear a heavy thud on the floor; it was him jumping out of bed, turning on the light, writing down figures as if he were afraid they would escape him...
But so he told you I had given my pearl necklace to the maid?
What a man!
What he did was pawn it before we got married...
Well, as I was saying... last month he went to the Real de San Carlos... ”
“And, naturally, he lost... ”
“No, with seven hundred pesos he won seven thousand.
You should have seen how he arrived...
Silent...
I said to myself: There!
He lost... but the strange thing is that he was frightened by the luck he’d had... until then he himself had had a certain confidence in his martingale... ”
“Yes...
I understand...
He preferred to believe in it rather than test it. ”
“Of course, for fear of failure.
But as I was telling you... for several days he was like a madman.
I remember one afternoon during siesta time he said to me: ‘Well, my black one, you’ll have to resign yourself to being the queen of the world.’”
“Always the mania for grandeur... ”
“I warn you that after that I too partly believed in the success of the martingale.
He had played according to the numbers in his calculation chart, and then, to break the bank, he withdrew three thousand pesos from the bank...
They were in my name, I remember, and another six thousand five hundred...
He had paid some pharmacy bills...
We left for Montevideo... and he lost everything. ”
“How long did it take? ”
“Twenty minutes...
I thought he was going to faint on the way... but so he told you I had given my necklace to the maid?...
What a man! ”
“It must have been to give me a better idea of you.
And how was the trip? ”
“Nothing... he didn’t say a word.
That’s true, his eyes were glassy, his face looked undone, slack, you know?
As soon as we reached Buenos Aires he went to bed... it was a Monday.
He stayed in bed until nightfall, then went out; I don’t know why but I had a feeling in my heart that something was going to happen...

At ten o’clock at night he still hadn’t returned, so I went to bed; around one in the morning his footsteps in the room woke me; I was about to turn on the light when he gave a great leap, grabbed me by the arm—you know the terrible strength he has—and in my nightgown he pulled me out of bed and dragged me down the corridors to the door of the hotel. ”
“And you? ”
“I didn’t scream because I knew it would enrage him.
Once at the hotel door he stood looking at me as if he didn’t know me, his forehead a mass of wrinkles, his eyes wide.

A wind was blowing that bent the trees; I covered myself with my arms, and he, without saying a word, did nothing but stare at me, when a policeman stopped in front of us while from behind the porter, who had woken with the noise, grabbed him by the arms.
And he shouted so loudly they could hear him from the corner: ‘This is the whore... the one who loved the ruffians whose flesh is like the flesh of a mule...’”
“But how do you remember those words? ”
“Everything that happened is as if I were seeing it now.

He, between the leaves of the door, pulling inward; from outside the policeman pulling him, while the porter held him around the throat to weaken him, and I in the doorway waiting for it to end, because several people had gathered who, instead of helping the policeman, were amusing themselves by looking at me.
It’s just as well I always wore a long nightgown...
Finally, with the help of other policemen whom a waiter inside had summoned with cries for help, they managed to get him to the police station.
They thought he was drunk... but it was an attack of madness...
That was the doctor’s diagnosis.
He was raving about Noah’s ark... ”
“Perfectly... and how can I help you?
” Once again Erdosain felt that the important part of the character was reappearing in his life like a novelistic element that must be tended to as one tends to one’s tie in the disorder of a dance.
“Well, I was bothering you to see if you could help me for the time being.
I can count on absolutely nothing from his family. ”
“But didn’t you get married at his house? ”
“Yes, but when we came back from Montevideo after we were married, we went to visit one day... imagine... visiting a house where I had been a servant. ”
“How colossal! ”
“You can’t imagine the indignation of those people.
One day of his... but why tell so many petty things!... don’t you think?
Life is like that and that’s that.
They threw us out and we left.
Patience, bad luck. ”
“The strange thing is that you were a servant. ”
“It’s nothing unusual... ”
“It’s just that you don’t give that impression... ”
“Thank you... the fact is that when I left the hotel I had to pawn a ring... and I need to manage the little money I have... ”
“And the pharmacy? ”
“It’s being run by a qualified man.
I telegraphed him to send money... but he answered that he has orders from Ergueta’s family not to give me a cent.
“And what do you plan to do? ”
“That’s what I don’t know...
Whether to go back to Pico or wait here. ”
“What a mess!... ”
“Believe me, I’m already sick of it. ”
“Well, the fact is I don’t have any money today.
Tomorrow, yes, I will... ”
“You know?...
I want to keep those few pesos in reserve just in case... ”
“And while you look into something serious... if you like you can stay here.
There happens to be an empty room next door.
And what else do you want? ”
“To see if you can get him out of the asylum. ”
“How am I going to get him out if he’s mad?
We’ll see.
Well... you’ll stay and sleep here tonight.
I’ll manage on the sofa... although it’s likely I won’t sleep here. ”
Again the woman filtered between her red eyelashes her malevolent greenish gaze.
It was as if she were projecting her soul onto the relief of the man’s ideas in order to take an imprint of his intentions.
“Well, I accept... ”
“Tomorrow, if you like, I’ll give you money so you can go peacefully to live in a hotel if you don’t prefer to stay here. ”
But suddenly, irritated with Hipólita by a thought that had just slipped into his mind, he said:
“You know you must not love Eduardo... ”
“Why? ”
“It’s obvious.
You come here, you tell me about this whole drama with a calmness that astonishes... and naturally, then... what is one to think of you? ”
As he spoke these words, Erdosain had begun to pace in the cramped space of the room.

He felt uneasy, and out of the corner of his eye he examined the oval freckled face, with its fine red eyebrows beneath the green visor of the hat, and the lips as though inflamed, while the two copper-colored wings of hair clasped her temples covering her ears, and her transparent pupils shot out beams of gaze.
“She hardly has any breasts,” Erdosain thought.
Hipólita looked around; suddenly, smiling amiably, she asked him:
“What exactly were you expecting from me, my little son? ”
Erdosain felt irritated by that sudden, whorehouse “my little son” that was added to the low “patience, bad luck. ” At last he said:
“I don’t know... anyway, I imagined you less cold... there are moments when you give the idea of being a perverse woman...
I may be wrong, but... well... that’s your business... ” Hipólita stood up:
“My little son, I have never put on acts.
I came to you simply because I knew you were his best friend.
What do you want?...
That I start crying like a Magdalene if I don’t feel it?...
I have already cried enough... ”
She too had risen to her feet.
She looked at him fixedly, but the hardness of line that lay rigid beneath the epidermis of her face like an armor of will dissolved with fatigue.

With her head tilted slightly to one side, she reminded Erdosain of his wife... it could well be her... she was at the door of an unknown lodging... the captain, indifferent, watched her walk away forever and did not stop her... the street opened before her... perhaps she would end up in a hotel with dirty walls, and then, taking pity, he said:
“Forgive me...
I’m a little nervous.
You are at home here.
The only thing I regret is that you found me without money.
But tomorrow I will have some. ”
Hipólita sat down again and Erdosain, as he walked, took his own pulse.
The veins were beating rapidly.
Weary from the afternoon spent with the Astrologer and Barsut, he said bitterly:
“Life is heavy... isn’t it?... ”
The intruder silently watched the tip of her little shoe.
She raised her eyes and a fine wrinkle furrowed her freckled forehead. Then:
“You seem worried.
Is something the matter? ”
“Nothing... tell me... did you suffer much beside him?... ”
“A little.
He is violent... ”
“How curious!
I’d like to picture him in the madhouse and I can’t.
I can barely make out a piece of his face and an eye...
I warn you that I foresaw the disaster.
I met him one morning, he told me everything and suddenly I had the feeling that you would be unhappy at his side... but you must be tired.
I have to go out.
I’ll tell the landlady to serve your dinner here. ”
I don’t feel like eating. ”
“Well then, if you’ll excuse me.
Here is the screen.
Make yourself at home. ”
When Erdosain left, the Cripple enveloped him in a singular look, a fan-like look that cuts a man’s body obliquely from head to foot, gathering in tangent all the inner geometry of his life.
Once out on the street, Erdosain noticed that a fine drizzle was falling, but he kept walking, driven by a dull resentment, an ill humor at being unable to think.
Events were growing more complicated... and he, meanwhile, what was he amid those gears that kept blocking him, burrowing ever deeper into life, submerging him in a mire that left him in despair?

Besides, there was that other thing... that impotence of thought, of thinking with clean, sharp lines like the moves in a game of chess, and a mental incoherence that turned him sour against everyone.
Then his irritation turned against the bestial happiness of the shopkeepers, who stood at the doors of their little caves spitting into the slanting rain.

He imagined them plotting endless shady deals while their wretched wives could be seen from the back rooms, spreading tablecloths over rickety tables, dishing up vile stews that, once uncovered in their platters, sent gusts of paprika and tallow farting out into the street, along with the harsh reek of reheated breaded cutlets.

He walked with a scowl, furiously and slowly probing the ideas that must be hatching beneath those narrow foreheads, staring brazenly at the livid faces of the merchants, who from the hollows of their eyes spied with a spark of ferocity on the customers moving about in the shops across the way; and at moments Erdosain felt the urge to insult them, a desire to call them cuckolds, thieves, and sons of bitches, to tell them they had the false fatness of lepers and that if any of them were thin it was from envying the successes of their neighbors.

And in his heart he went on insulting them atrociously, imagining that those businessmen were already screwed into imminent bankruptcies by terrifying promissory notes, and that the misfortune that was hurling him to the bottom of despair would also hover over their filthy wives, who, with the same fingers that moments before had removed the rags they menstruated with, would now cut the bread that their husbands would devour between curses aimed at their competitors.

And without being able to explain it to himself he told himself that the most educated of those scoundrels possessed a sly and profound coarseness, all of them envious to the marrow and more ruthless and implacable than Carthaginians.

As he passed mattress shops, grocery stores, and dry-goods stores, he thought that those men had no noble purpose in existence, that they spent their lives scrutinizing with malicious pleasure the private lives of their neighbors, who were as vile as they were, rejoicing with words of false compassion at the misfortunes that befell them, gossiping left and right about how bored they were, and this suddenly filled him with such rancor that he at once accepted that the best thing he could do was leave, because otherwise he would have an incident with those brutes beneath whose emphatic mugs he saw rising the soul of the city, debased, implacable, and ferocious like themselves.
He had no definite purpose; he recognized that his spirit was soiled with disgust for life, and suddenly, seeing a tram heading for Plaza Once pass by, he leaped onto the platform in great bounds.
Once at the ticket window he bought a round-trip ticket to Ramos Mejía.
He was going there as he might have gone in any other direction.
Tired, bewildered by the certainty that he had thrown his soul into a pit from which he would never be able to emerge again.
And waiting for him, the Cripple.
Wouldn’t it have been better to be a ship’s captain and command a super-dreadnought?

The funnels would vomit torrents of smoke and on the bridge he would converse with the turret commander while in his heart the image of a woman would be painted, a woman who perhaps would not be his wife.
But why was his life like this?
And the lives of others too, also “like this,” as if the “like this” were a stamp of misfortune that, seen in another, had a more blurred outline.
What had become of the strong life that certain men contain in their vessels like the blood of a lion?
The strong life that suddenly makes an existence appear before us without any previous periods of preparation and that possesses the perfect ease of cinematic compositions.
Weren’t the photographs of heroes like that?
Who kept a photograph of the heroes?
Who kept a photograph of Lenin arguing in a little room in London, or of Mussolini wandering the roads of Italy?

And yet they were suddenly revealed on a balcony haranguing a bearded multitude, or among the truncated columns of recent ruins, wearing sport shoes and a jipijapa hat that did not belie the ferocity of the conqueror’s face.

In contrast, he felt there, localized in his own life, the tiny images of the Cripple, of the Captain, of his wife, of Barsut, all existences that, as soon as they moved away from his eyes, were restored to the minuscule dimension that distance confers on physical bodies.
He rested his head against the window glass.

The carriage slid forward and then stopped; at the second whistle of the guard the train started again, and it entered the switch points with a fierce grinding as the rails clashed metallically when parted by the edge of the wheels.
The green and red lights of the underground dazzled his eyes for an instant; then he closed them again.
In the night the train communicated its vibration to the rails, and the mass multiplied by speed imprinted on his thoughts the vertigo of a march equally implacable and dizzying.

Cracc... cracc... cracc... the wheels tore at each rail joint, and that dull, formidable monorhythm eased his resentment, made his spirit lighter, while his flesh surrendered to the drowsiness that speed imparts to the senses.
Then he thought that Ergueta was already mad.

He remembered the other man’s words when he was on the edge of misfortune: “Get lost, you little turd, get lost,” and pressing his head into the padded angle of the seatback, he thought of times gone by, closing his eyes to distinguish clearly the images of a memory.

This caused him a certain strangeness, for it was the first time he had noticed that in a memory certain figures have the normal dimension with which they were known in reality, while other figures or things are tiny like lead soldiers or merely present a profile, lacking depth.

Thus, beside the bulk of a Black man whose hand was lost in the backside of a boy, he saw a minuscule table, as if for dolls, on which the tiny heads of thieving men were crushed, while the ceiling, of real height, gave an even more extraordinary air of desolation to the gray scene of the memory.

A dark multitude moved there, inside his soul; then shadow, like a cloud, covered his sorrow with weariness, and beside the little table where the tiny adult thieves slept, there rose, gigantic and thick-necked like an ox’s skull, the relief of the owner of the eating-house, with his fingers clamped on the muscular balls of his arms.

And another memory showed him how exact his presentiment of imminent fall had been, when he had not yet even thought of defrauding the Sugar Company, but was already seeking in sinister places an image of his possible personality.
How many paths there were in his brain!

But now he was heading toward the one that led to the eating-house, the enormous eating-house that sank its taciturn cube like a butcher’s shop into the furthest folds of his cerebellum, and although the relief of that cube that was born in his forehead and ended at the nape of his neck was at twenty degrees, the minuscule tables with the adult little thieves did not slide across the floor as logic would have it, but the cube righted itself under the counterweight of an instantaneous habit, the habit of thinking about it, and his flesh, already accustomed to the speed multiplied by the mass of the electric train, surrendered to a vertiginous inertia; and now that the memory had overcome the inertia of all the cells, the eating-house appeared before his eyes like a perfectly cut quadrilateral.

It seemed to plunge its straight lines into the interior of his chest, so that he could almost admit that if he looked at himself in a mirror, the front of his body would present a narrow room, deepened toward the perspective of the mirror.
And he walked inside himself, on a pavement muddied with spittle and sawdust, whose perfect frame was beveled toward the infinity of adjacent sensations.
And he thought that if the Cripple had been beside him, he would have said to her, referring to a memory:
“I still wasn’t a thief. ”
Erdosain imagined that the Cripple was looking at him, and he, in a bored tone, continued:
“Next to the old Critica building, on Sarmiento Street, there was an eating-house. ”

Hipólita raised her eyes as if questioning him; suddenly, amid the infernal jolting of the carriages as they crossed the points at Caballito, Erdosain imagined that he was a character who had lived like a bandit but had now reformed, and so he went on speaking to his invisible interlocutor:
“And there the newspaper vendors and thieves would gather. ”
“Oh, really? ”
To keep the tumults formed by that rabble from smashing the shop windows completely, the owner kept the metal shutters lowered all the time.
Light entered the room through the blue-tinted transom panes, so that in that den with walls painted gray like those of a Turkish butcher’s shop, a darkness floated that turned the cigar smoke milky.

In that gloomy cube, its ceiling crossed by enormous beams and flooded by the kitchen’s mists of stew and tallow, the dark tumult moved, a “mob” of thieves, men with foreheads shaded by the visors of their caps and kerchiefs loosely knotted at the necklines of their undershirts.
From eleven to two in the afternoon they crowded around the greasy marble tables to suck rotten clam shells or play cards between glasses of wine.

In that stinking mist the faces wore villainous expressions; one saw mugs lengthened as if by the violence of strangulation, jaws hanging and lips loosened in funnel shape; Black men with porcelain eyes and brilliant teeth between the hemorrhoidal flesh of their lips, who would touch the boys’ backsides while grinding their teeth; pickpockets and “stoolies” with tiger profiles, sunken foreheads and rigid pupils.

A hoarse clamor poured from these sprawled clusters on the benches and leaning on the marble tops, among whom the “lancers” slipped past, neatly dressed, with loose collars, gray vests, and seven-peso bowlers.

Some had just come out of Azcuénaga and brought news of the new prisoners, passing on messages; others, to inspire confidence, wore tortoiseshell glasses, and all of them, on entering, cast the quickest of glances over the den.
They spoke in low voices, smiling convulsively, buying bottles of beer for strange companions, and went in and out several times in a quarter of an hour, called by mysterious errands.
The master of this cavern was an enormous man with an ox’s face, green eyes, a trumpet nose, and very tightly pressed thin lips.
When he grew angry his roars startled the rabble, who feared him.
He handled them with a dull violence.

If some wastrel made more noise than was tacitly tolerated, the owner would suddenly approach; the noisy one knew the other would hit him, but he waited in silence, and then the giant would discharge terrible short blows with the edge of his fist on the edge of the culprit’s skull.

A joyous silence accompanied the punishment; the wretch would be kicked out into the street, and the clamor would renew itself, more insulting and resonant, displacing clouds of smoke toward the glazed quadrilateral of the door.
Sometimes musicians would enter this den, usually an accordion and a guitar.
They would tune the instruments and a silence of expectation would curl each beast into its corner, while a sadness moved its invisible swell in that aquarium atmosphere.
The prison tango would rise plaintive from the boxes, and then the wretches would unconsciously keep time with their resentments and their misfortunes.
The silence seemed a many-handed monster raising a dome of sounds over the heads slumped on the marble.
Perhaps that was what they were thinking!

And that terrible, high dome driven into every breast multiplied the languor of the guitar and the accordion, divinizing the suffering of the whore and the horrible boredom of prison that stabs the heart when one thinks of the friends who are outside “struggling” for life.
Then in the most latrine-like souls, beneath the filthiest mugs, an unknown tremor would burst; then everything would pass and no hand would stretch out to drop a coin into the musicians’ cap.
“That’s where I used to go,” Erdosain was telling his hypothetical interlocutor.
“In search of more anguish, of the certainty of knowing I was lost, and to think about my wife who, alone in my house, would be suffering for having married a useless man like me.
How many times, cornered in that eating-house, I imagined Elsa fleeing with another man.
And I kept falling lower and lower, and that den was nothing but the foretaste of the worse things that were to happen to me later.
And many times, looking at those wretches, I would say to myself: Won’t I end up like one of these?
Ah, I don’t know how, but I have always had the presentiment of what would happen later.
I have never been wrong.
Do you see?
And there, in the cavern, I found Ergueta one day, meditating.
Yes, him.
He was alone at a table, and some of the newsboys looked at him in astonishment, though others must have thought he was simply a well-dressed thief. ”
