Erdosain imagined that the Cripple was now asking him:
“What?
My husband was there? ”
“Yes, and with his ‘dog-catcher’ face he was gnawing the knob of his cane while a Black man was lifting a boy’s backside.
But he paid no attention to anything.
It seemed he was nailed to the floor of the cavern.

It’s true he told me he had gone to wait for a tipster who was supposed to give him some ‘information’ for the next race, but the truth is he was there as if he had suddenly felt lost and had entered that place to look for a meaning to life.
That is perhaps the exact truth.
“To look for a meaning to life among the events lived by the rabble.

There I learned for the first time of his decision to marry a prostitute, and when I asked him about his pharmacy, he answered that he had left the qualified assistant in charge of it in Pico, because at first I had supposed he had come to gamble.
I don’t know if you know that they expelled him from a club for cheating.
It was even said that he had forged chips, but that matter was never cleared up.
He only spoke to me about you when I asked him about his fiancée, a millionaire girl from Cacharí who was very much in love with him.
“‘I cut that off some time ago,’ he answered me. “‘Why?’
“‘I don’t know... she bored me... I was fed up.’
“‘But why did you leave her?’ I insisted.
“A sour light convulsed his pupil.
In a bad humor he insisted, brushing away with a swipe the flies that were circling his mug of beer:
“‘How should I know!...
From boredom... because I’m a turd.
And the poor thing loved me.
But what was she going to do with me. Besides, there’s no remedy now...’
“‘Did Ergueta tell you that there was no remedy now?...’
“‘Yes, ma’am; he said it like this: “There’s no remedy now, because tomorrow I’m getting married. ”’”
The electric train left Flores behind.

Erdosain, slumped in his seat, remembered that he had looked seriously at the pharmacist, on whose face there spread that watchful movement of the muscles that gives the countenance a malevolent expression. “‘And who are you marrying?’
“Ergueta’s face went pale to the ears.
As he inclined his head toward Erdosain he winked one eyelid while the other eye, motionless, tried to gather all the surprise that would alter Erdosain within a second:
“‘I’m marrying the Whore.’ Then he lifted his head and only the whites of his eyes were visible.
I did not move.
“The pharmacist wore on his face an expression of rapture like the one seen in popular chromolithographs in which a saint appears kneeling with the edges of his hands resting on his chest.

“And Erdosain remembered that in those circumstances the Black man who had been touching the boy’s backside was now guiding the boy’s hands to his private parts, while a circle of newsboys raised an infernal clamor and the gigantic owner crossed the room with a plate of soup in one hand and another of red stew for a pair of thieves who were devouring it in a corner.
“Nevertheless, his resolution did not surprise him.

Ergueta had those desperate resolutions of frenetic natures that obey the empire of obsessions with slow fury, a deep explosion whose detonation they themselves did not hear, but whose increase in volume centuples the instinct.
Nevertheless, pretending great serenity:
“‘The Whore?...
Who is the Whore?’ I asked him.
“A wave of blood reddened his face.
Even his eyes smiled.
“‘Who is she, old man?...
An angel, Erdosain.
In my face, right in my face, she tore up a thousand-peso check that a lover had left her.
She gave the maid a pearl necklace worth five thousand pesos.
To the building’s porters she gave all the silverware.
“I will enter your house naked,” she told me.’
“‘But all that is a lie!’ he now felt Hipólita saying to him in his memory.
“I believed her at the time. And he went on telling me:
“‘If you only knew what that woman has suffered.
Once, it was the seventh abortion they were doing on her, she was so desperate that she went to throw herself out the window from the fourth floor.
Suddenly, what a marvel, old man... on the balcony Jesus appeared to her.
He stretched out his arm and did not let her pass.’
“Ergueta was still smiling.
Suddenly he reached into his pocket and handed Erdosain a portrait.
The delightful creature fascinated him.
“She was not smiling.
Behind her the spaces were crowded with palms and ferns.
Seated on a bench with her head slightly inclined, she was looking at a magazine that her knee supported, for she had crossed one leg over the other.
In this way, a short distance from the grass, the flare of her dress suspended a bell.
The high coiffure and the hair drawn back from her temples made the moon of her forehead clearer and broader.
At the sides of the fine nose the arc of the eyebrows was thin as befits eyes that are slightly oblique in a delicately oval face.

“And looking at her, Erdosain suddenly knew that beside Hipólita he would never feel any desire, and that certainty gladdened him so much that he thought of the delight of caressing with forked fingers the chin of the strange young woman and hearing the crunch of the sand beneath the soles of her little shoes. “Then he murmured:
“‘How beautiful she is!... She must have a great sensitivity!...’
“How different she was in reality!
“The electric train was now passing through Villa Luro.
Among mountains of coal and gasometers veiled by the mist the voltaic arcs shone sadly.
Great black gaps opened in the locomotive sheds, and the red and green lights, suspended irregularly in the distance, made the locomotives’ calls even more dismal.
“How different the Cripple was in reality!
Nevertheless, he remembered that he had said to Ergueta:
“‘How beautiful she is!... She must have a great sensitivity!...’
“‘Yes, she is like that; besides she is very delicate in her manners.
I like the adventure.
Look at the faces they’ll make, those who doubted my communism.
I’ve jilted a stuck-up girl, a virgin, to marry a prostitute.
But Hipólita’s soul is above everything.
She too likes adventure and noble hearts.
Together we will do great things, because the times have come...’
“Erdosain picked up the pharmacist’s phrase:
“‘So you believe the times have come?...’
“‘Yes, terrible things are going to happen.
Don’t you remember that once you told me that President Roosevelt had made a great eulogy of the Bible?’ “‘Yes... but a long time ago.’
“Erdosain answered with those words because in reality he never remembered having quoted anything of that nature to the pharmacist. The latter continued:
“‘Outside I have read the Bible quite a bit...’
“‘Which does not prevent you from “screwing around. ”’
“‘That’s none of your business,’ Ergueta interrupted harshly.
“Erdosain looked at him annoyed; the pharmacist smiled with his childish smile and while the owner set down another half-liter of beer on the marble, he said:

“‘Look at what mysterious words are written in the Bible: “And I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out; and I will make them a praise and a name in every land of confusion. ”’
“An extraordinary silence fell over the eating-house.
Only inclined heads could be seen or groups that gazed thoughtfully at the coming and going of the flies in the grease of the tables.
A thief was showing a companion a diamond ring and the two heads remained jointly inclined in observation of the stones.
“Through the half-open door of frosted glass a ray of sun entered like a bar of sulfur that cut the bluish atmosphere in two.

“The other repeated: ‘and I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out,’ insisting and winking maliciously as he repeated: ‘and I will make them a praise and a name in every land of confusion...’” “‘But Hipólita is not lame...’
“‘No, but she is the one driven out and I am the fraudulent one, the “son of perdition.
” I have gone from brothel to brothel, and from anguish seeking love.
I thought it was physical love and later, reading that book that illuminated me, I understood that my heart was seeking divine love.
Do you see?
The heart orients itself on its own.
You are deceived, you want to do your own will, and you fail... why you fail... is a mystery...
“‘Then one day, suddenly, without knowing how, the truth appears.
And look, I have lived.
“Son of perdition,” that is my life.
Before dying in Cosquín my father wrote me a terrible letter, between vomits of blood and reproaching me, you know?
And he did not sign the letter with his name, but put: “Your father The Damned.
” Do you see?’—and again he winked the eyelid, raising his eyebrows in such a way that Erdosain asked himself: “‘Isn’t this fellow crazy?’
“Then they left the eating-house.
Automobiles glided along Corrientes Street, sparkling under the sun; many people were going to work, and beneath the yellow awnings the women’s faces appeared rosy.
They entered the Ambos Mundos café.
Circles of pimps surrounded the tables.
They were playing cards, dice, or billiards.
Ergueta looked around, then, spitting, said aloud:
“‘All pimps.
They’ll have to be hanged without looking at their faces.’
“No one took it as referring to himself.
“Erdosain, without wanting to, remained pondering some of the other man’s words.
“‘He was seeking divine love.’ So Ergueta was leading a frenetic, sensual life.
He spent nights and days in gambling dens and brothels, dancing, getting drunk, getting into terrible fights with toughs and pimps.
A dull impetus drove him to perform the most brutal feats.
“One night Ergueta was in Flores square, in front of Niers’ confectionery.
There was the drunk Delavene, who had graduated as a lawyer a month before, and many other toughs from the Flores Club.
They were bothering passers-by.
Suddenly, seeing a Spaniard approach, Ergueta unbuttoned his fly and when the man reached him he wet him with a stream of urine.
The man was prudent and disappeared grumbling.
Then the pharmacist, looking at Delavene who was boasting excessively, said:
“‘Well...
I bet you wouldn’t piss on the first one who passes?’ “‘Want to bet I would?’
“Everyone rejoiced, because the Basque Delavene was a savage.
A man turned the corner and Delavene began to urinate.
The stranger stepped aside, but the ‘Basque,’ almost bumping into him, wet him.
“Something terrible happened.

“Without saying a word the offended man stopped; the gang watched, laughing and whistling; suddenly the stranger drew his revolver, a shot rang out, and Delavene fell to his knees, clutching his belly with both hands.
The Basque’s agony was long and painful.
“Before dying, he nobly admitted that he had provoked the drama, and when Ergueta was drunk and Delavene’s name was mentioned, he would kneel and with his tongue make a cross in the dust.
While rolling a cigarette, the pharmacist answered a question from Erdosain about Delavene:
“‘Yes, he was a noble heart... a unique friend.
I will pay for him one day’—but folding his thought back to a more current concern, he said—: ‘Ah, I have thought a lot these last times.
And I asked myself if it was right that a sterile, sick, vicious, and immoral man should marry a virgin...’ “‘Does Hipólita... know?’
“‘Yes, she knows everything.
Besides, a virgin deserves a virgin’s name.
A man who has a virgin soul and body.
That is how it should be one day.
Can you imagine a handsome, virgin, and strong male?’
“‘That is how it should be,’ Erdosain whispered.
“The pharmacist looked at his watch. “‘Do you have something to do?’
“‘Yes, in a little while I’m going home to see Hipólita.’
“‘This time I was astonished,’ Erdosain told the chronicler of this story later.
‘The Ergueta family home was sumptuous and the spirit of the people who moved there like snails was absolutely conservative and routine.’ Erdosain asked him:
“‘What?... You took her to your house?’
“‘And the stories I had to invent!...
She didn’t want to go; or rather, she agreed to go, but as what she is...’ “‘She was capable?...’
“‘So capable that only at the end could I convince her.
To my mother I said I had stolen her at the moment she was about to embark with her uncles for Europe... a lie bigger than a house.’ “‘And your mother?’
“Erdosain was going to ask him if his mother had believed such a lie, as if Hipólita carried written on her face the ordeals that had convulsed her life...
“‘And how did your mother receive the news?’
“‘She told me to bring her immediately.
When I presented her, she embraced her and said: “Has he respected you, daughter?
” And she, lowering her eyes, answered: “Yes, Mother.
” Which is true.
I warn you that Mother and my sister Sara are delighted with Hipólita.’
“At that moment Erdosain had the presentiment that those wretches had prepared a future disaster for themselves.

He was not wrong, and now, remembering in the electric train the certainty that had not failed, he said to himself as he passed through Liniers: ‘It’s curious, the first impressions never deceive one,’ and when he asked Ergueta when he was getting married, the latter answered:
“‘Tomorrow we leave for Montevideo.
We’ll get married there, in case we don’t get along.’—On pronouncing these words he winked his eyelid again, smiling cynically, and added—: ‘I’m not one to be caught napping, old man.’
“Erdosain was annoyed by that excess of precautions. Unable to contain himself, he said:
“‘What?...
You’re not even married yet and you’re already thinking about divorce?
What kind of communist feat is that?
Deep down you’re still the cheating gambler.’
“But the pharmacist was gloating with the sufficiency of a usurer who does not mind insults if they are directed at him at the moment of paying interest. Coarse, he replied:

“But the pharmacist was gloating with the sufficiency of a usurer who does not mind insults if they are directed at him at the moment of paying interest. Coarse, he replied: “‘One has to be sharp, old man.’
“Erdosain was astonished before so much coarseness.
“He thought of the delightful creature and imagined her enduring that brute beneath a sky darkened by great clouds of dust and set on fire by a yellow and dreadful sun.
She would wither like a fern transplanted to a stony place.
Now Erdosain examined the pharmacist again, but with rage.
“The gambler noticed the malevolence of his companion and said:
“‘It is necessary to do something against this society, old man.
There are days when I suffer in an unbearable way.
It seems that all men have become beasts.
It makes you want to go out into the street and preach extermination or put a machine gun on every corner.
Do you see?
Terrible times are coming.
“‘The son shall rise against the father and the father against the son.
It is necessary to do something against this cursed society.
That is why I am marrying a prostitute.
The Scriptures say well: “And thou, son of man, wilt thou judge the bloody city?
Show her all her abominations.
” And these other words, notice these other words: “And she doted upon their paramours, whose flesh is as the flesh of asses, and whose issue is like the issue of horses.
”’—And pointing to the ‘pimps’ who were playing around the tables, he said—: ‘There they are.
Go into the Royal Keller, the Marzzoto, the Pigall, the Maipú; everywhere you go you will find them.
Wasted forces.
Even that rabble is bored in the end.
When the revolution comes they will be hanged or sent to the front line.
Cannon fodder.
I could have been like them and I renounced it.
Now terrible times are coming.
That is why the book says: “And I will save her that halteth, and gather her that was driven out, and I will make her a praise and a name in every land of confusion. ”

“‘Because today the city is in love with its paramours and they have sunk the lame one and the one driven out, but they will have to humble themselves and kiss the feet of the lame one and the one driven out.’ “‘But do you love Hipólita or not?’
“‘Of course I love her.
At moments it seems to me she has come down from the moon by a ladder.
Wherever she is everyone will feel happy.’
“And for an instant Erdosain believed that she had come down from the moon so that all men would come to be enraptured by her tranquil simplicity. “The pharmacist continued:
“‘Now times of blood are coming, old man, of vengeance.
Inside their souls men are weeping.
But they do not want to hear the weeping of their angel.
And the cities are like prostitutes, in love with their paramours and their bandits. This cannot go on like this.’
“He looked at the street for a moment, and then with his attention fixed as on an inner sound, the gambler said with a pathetic voice in the café of boredom:
“‘A man will have to come, an angel, I don’t know.
He will kneel in the middle of Avenida de Mayo.
The automobiles will stop, the bank managers and the rich men in the hotels will lean out on the balconies and, moving their arms indignantly, will say to him:
“‘What do you want, you toad-faced man?

Don’t bother us—but he will rise—and when they see his sad little face and his eyes burning with fever, everyone’s arms will fall, and he will address the stuck-up ones, he will speak to them, he will ask them why they did wrong, why they forgot the orphan and crushed the man and have made a hell of life that was so beautiful.
And they will not know what to answer, and the voice of the last angel will resound in such a way that their skin will crawl, and even the biggest ruffians will weep.’
“The pharmacist’s big mouth was deformed by anguish.
It seemed he was chewing an elastic and bitter poison.
“‘Yes, it is necessary that Christ come again.
The most dog-like men, the most latrine-like cynics still suffer.
And if he does not come, who is going to save us?’
The train stopped at Ramos Mejía.
The station clock read eight o’clock at night.
Erdosain got off.
A dense mist weighed on the muddy streets of the town.
When he found himself alone on Centenario Street, blocked in front and behind by two walls of fog, he remembered that the next day they were going to murder Barsut.
It was true.
They would murder him.

He would have liked to have a mirror in front of his eyes so he could see his murderer’s body, so implausible did it seem to him that he (the I) was the one who, with such a crime, was going to separate himself from all other men.
The streetlamps burned sadly, pouring through the mire cataracts of cottony light that dripped on the paving stones, making the town invisible beyond two steps.
An enormous desolation filled Erdosain as he walked on, sadder than a leper.
He now had the sensation that his soul had detached itself forever from every earthly affection.
And his anguish was that of a man who carries in his conscience a sinister cage where, among bones of sins, elastic tigers stained with blood yawn, fixing their eyes on the projection of a leap.

And Erdosain, as he advanced, thought about his life as if it were someone else’s, trying to understand those dark forces that rose from the roots of his nails to crowd together, whistling, against the bars of his cage like the simoom.
Wrapped in the mist that carried a heavy drop of moisture into the last cell of his lungs, Erdosain reached Gaona Street, where he stopped to wipe the sweat from his forehead.
He knocked on a plank door, the only entrance in an enormous factory façade beside which a kerosene lamp hung.
Suddenly a hand opened the gate and the young man, muttering curses, followed the side of a long wall along a brick path that bent in the mud under his footsteps.
He stopped in front of the glass panes of an illuminated door, clapped his hands, and a hoarse voice shouted at him:
“Come in. ”
Erdosain entered.
An acetylene lamp lit, with its sooty flame, the five heads of the Espila family, who a moment before had been bent over their plates.
They all greeted him with smiling, cheerful voices, while Emilio Espila, a tall, skinny, shaggy-haired lad, ran toward him to shake his hands.

Erdosain greeted them in order: first old Mrs. Espila, bent by time and covered in black clothes; then the two young sisters, Luciana and Elena; then the deaf Eustaquio, a graying giant, thin as if tubercular, who, as was his custom, ate with his nose in his plate while his gray eyes watched the hieroglyph in a magazine, deciphering it as he chewed.
Erdosain felt somewhat revived by the cordial smiles of Luciana and Elena.
Luciana was long-faced and blond, with a turned-up nose and a mouth of long, fine, sinuous lips tinted pink.
Elena had a nunlike appearance, with her oval, wax-colored face, long skirts, and plump, pale hands.
“Would you like some supper?
” said the old woman.
Erdosain, noticing how sparse the serving dish was, answered that he had already eaten.
“Have you really had supper? ”
“Yes...
I’ll have a little tea. ”

They made room for him at the table, and Erdosain sat down between the deaf Eustaquio, who continued watching his puzzle, and Elena, who was dividing the rest of the stew between Emilio and the old woman.
Erdosain observed them with pity.
He had known the Espilas for many years.

Once the family had enjoyed a relatively comfortable position; then a series of disasters had plunged them into utter poverty, and Erdosain, who had happened to meet Emilio in the street one day, had begun to visit them.
He had not seen them for seven years and was astonished to find them all living in a hovel, they who in another time had had a maid, a drawing room, and an antechamber.
The three women slept in the room crammed with old furniture that served as a dining room during supper or lunch, while Emilio and the deaf man took shelter in a little zinc-plated kitchen.
To meet the household expenses they performed the most extraordinary tasks: they sold social directories, homemade ice-cream makers, and the two sisters did sewing.
One winter the poverty was so great that they stole a telegraph pole and sawed it up at night.
Another time they carried off all the posts of a wire fence, and the adventures they ran in order to scrape together money both amused and saddened Erdosain at once.
The impression he received the first time he visited them was enormous.
The Espilas lived in a large ramshackle house near Chacarita, a three-story barracks with iron-sheet partitions.
The building looked like an ocean liner, and children poured out of it as if the tenement were a phalanstery.

For several days Erdosain walked the streets thinking about the sufferings the Espilas must have endured in order to resign themselves to that catastrophe, and later, when he invented the copper rose, he told himself that to lift these people’s spirits it was necessary to graft a hope onto them, and with part of the money stolen from the sugar refinery he bought a used accumulator, an ammeter, and the various materials to set up a rudimentary electroplating workshop.
And he convinced the Espilas that they should devote themselves to this work in their spare hours, for if it succeeded they would all grow rich.
And he, whose life was completely devoid of comfort or hope, he, who had felt lost for a long time, managed to instill in them hopes so intense that the Espilas agreed to begin the experiments.

Elena devoted herself very seriously to studying electroplating, while the deaf man prepared the baths and became skilled at connecting the ammeter cables in series or in parallel and at handling the resistance.
Even the old woman took part in the experiments, and when they succeeded in copper-plating a tin sheet no one doubted that they would soon grow rich if the copper rose did not fail.
Erdosain also spoke to them of making gold lace, silver veils, copper gauze, and even sketched a project for a metallic necktie that astonished them all.
His plan was essentially simple.
They would make shirts with metallic fronts, cuffs, and collars by taking fabric, soaking it in a saline solution, and subjecting it to a galvanic bath of copper or nickel.
Gath & Chaves, Harrods, or San Juan might buy the patent from them.

And Erdosain, who only half believed in these applications, came one day to think that he had gone too far in making these people dream, because now, although they owed money to everyone and were almost dying of hunger, the least they dreamed of was acquiring a Rolls-Royce and a chalet that, if it were not on Avenida Alvear, held no interest for them as property.

Erdosain bent over his cup of tea, and then Luciana, who was slightly flushed, answered Emilio’s smug smile with a signal, but he, extraordinarily toothless and therefore able to speak only with a heavy lisp, said:
“You know... the rose is a fact... ”
“Yes, thank God we’ve managed to produce it.
” But Luciana jumped up impatiently, opened a drawer in the washstand, and Erdosain smiled with enthusiasm.
Between the fingers of the blond girl rose the copper rose.
In the miserable hovel the marvelous metallic flower unfurled its vermilion petals.
The flicker of the acetylene lamp made a red transparency play across it, as if the flower were animated by a botanical life already burned by the acids and that constituted its soul.
The deaf man lifted his nose from the plate of escarole and, in a booming voice, exclaimed after examining both the puzzle and the rose:
“No doubt about it, old man...
Erdosain... you’re a genius... ”
“If this time we get rich... ”
“God grant it,” murmured the old woman.
“But Mama... don’t be so skeptical... ”
“Did it cost you a lot of work? ”
Elena, with smiling gravity and a scientific air, explained.
“Look, Remo, the first rose drew too much amperage and it burned... ”
“And the bath didn’t precipitate? ”
“No... we did warm it up a little, though... ”
“To give this one its bath we glued it... ”
“You know... a bath of fine, smooth glue... ”
Remo examined the copper rose again, admiring its perfection.
Each red petal was almost transparent, and beneath the metallic film one could barely distinguish the veined shape of the natural petal, which had blackened the glue.
The flower was light in weight, and Erdosain added:
“How light!...
It weighs less than a five-cent coin... ”
Then, noticing a yellow shadow that covered the pistils of the flower and streaked as it climbed the petals, he added:
“Still, when you take the flowers out of the bath you must wash them thoroughly in plenty of water.
You see these yellow streaks?
That’s the cyanide from the bath attacking the copper.
” All the heads formed a circle around him and listened with religious silence.
He continued: “Copper cyanate is formed, which must be avoided, because otherwise it will prevent the nickel bath from taking.
How long did it last? ”
“One hour. ”
When he raised his eyes from the rose his gaze met Luciana’s.
The girl’s eyes seemed velvety with a mysterious warmth and her lips smiled, revealing her bright teeth.
Erdosain looked at her in surprise.
The deaf man was examining the rose and all the heads pressed close to him followed the yellow cyanide streaks with attention.
Luciana did not lower her eyelids.

Suddenly Erdosain remembered that the next day he would take part in the murder of Barsut, and an enormous sadness made him drop his eyes; then, suddenly hostile toward these hopeful people who had no idea of his sufferings and the anguish he had been enduring for months, he stood up and said:
“Well, goodbye. ”
Even the deaf man looked at him in dismay.
Elena left her chair and the old woman remained with her arm motionless, holding a plate she was about to set in front of Eustaquio.
“What’s the matter, Remo? ”
“But, old man, Erdosain... ” Elena observed him gravely:
“Is something wrong, Remo? ”
“Nothing, Elena... believe me... ”
“Are you angry?
” asked Luciana, her eyes full of that mysterious and sad warmth.
“No, nothing...
I felt an enormous desire to see you...
Now I have to go... ”
“Are you sure you’re not angry? ”
“No, madam. ”
“It’s the worries...
I understand... ”
“Shut up, you fool... ”
The deaf man decided to abandon the puzzle and insisted on what he had said before.
“I warn you that you have to take this seriously, because you’re going to get rich. ”
“But is nothing wrong with you? ”
Erdosain picked up his hat.
He felt an enormous repugnance at uttering useless words.
Everything was settled.
What was the point of talking, then?
Nevertheless he made an effort and said:
“Believe me...
I love you all very much... as before...
I’m not angry... calm down...
I have more ideas...
We’ll open a dog dye-works and sell dogs dyed green, blue, yellow, and violet...
You see I have ideas to spare...
You are going to escape this horrible poverty...
I’m going to get you out... you see, I have ideas to spare. ”
Luciana looked at him with pity and said:
“I’ll walk you out,” and so they went out together into the street.
The mist fitted a cube into the alley in which the mantles of the kerosene lamps glowed sadly.
Suddenly Luciana took Erdosain’s arm and said to him in a very soft voice:
“I love you, I love you so much! ”
Erdosain looked at her ironically; his pain had transfigured itself into cruelty. He looked at her:
“I already know. ” She continued:
“I love you so much that to please you I’ve studied what a blast furnace is and the Bessemer converter.
Do you want me to tell you what the harnesses are and how the cooling system works? ”
Erdosain enveloped her in a cold glance, thinking: “This woman is unwell. ” She continued:
“I was always thinking about you.
Do you want me to explain the analysis of steels and how copper is smelted, look, and the washing of gold and what muffles are? ”

Erdosain, obstinately pressing his lips together, walked down the alley thinking that human existence was absurd, and once again unjustified rancor welled up in him toward the gentle girl who, pressed against his arm, said:
“Do you remember that time you spoke of your ideal being to be the foreman of a blast furnace?
You drove me crazy.
Why don’t you speak?
So I started studying metallurgy.
Do you want me to explain the difference between an irregular distribution of carbon and a perfect molecular one?
Why don’t you speak, dear? ”

The muffled roar of a train that passed in the distance was heard; the milky quality of the mist turned to darkness a short distance from the lamps, and Erdosain would have liked to speak, to explain his misfortunes to her, but that dull and embittered malice kept him rigid beside the girl, who insisted:
“But what’s the matter with you?
Are you angry with us?
And yet it’s to you we’ll owe our fortune. ”
Erdosain looked her up and down, squeezed the girl’s arm, and said hoarsely:
“You don’t interest me. ”
Then he turned his back on her, and before she could turn toward him he walked off at a rapid pace and disappeared into the mist.
He understood that he had gratuitously insulted the girl, and this conviction gave him so cruel a joy that he murmured between his teeth:
“I hope they all burst and leave me in peace. ”
At two in the morning, Erdosain was still walking between walls of wind through the downtown streets, looking for a brothel.
A dull murmur throbbed in his ears, yet driven by the frenzy of instinct he walked in the shadow cast by the tall façades onto the pavement.
A horrible sadness filled him.
At that moment he had no direction.
Like a sleepwalker he moved forward, his eyes fixed on the nickel-plated arrows on the policemen’s helmets that caught the shafts of light falling from the voltaic arcs at the street corners...
An extraordinary impulse hurled his body forward in long strides...
He had come from Plaza Mayo this way, and now, along Cangallo, he was leaving the Once station behind.
A horrible sadness filled him.
His mind, fixed on a single fact, kept repeating:
“It’s useless, I’m a murderer.

” But suddenly, when the red or yellow cube of a brothel entrance appeared, he would stop, hesitate a moment bathed in the reddish or yellowish haze, then tell himself, “It’ll be another one,” and continue on his way.

Silently, a car rolled past him and vanished at high speed, and Erdosain thought of the happiness he would never have and of his lost youth; his shadow raced ahead across the flagstones, then shrank, and, beginning as a trampled thing, leapt onto his back or swayed on the gleaming grate of a storm drain...
Yet with every step his anguish grew heavier, as if it were a mass of water, tiring the verticality of his limbs with its tide.
In spite of this, Erdosain imagined that, by the grace of his providence, he had entered a singular brothel.

The madam opened the bedroom door for him; he threw himself fully dressed onto the bed... in a corner a kettle of water boiled on a kerosene burner... suddenly the half-naked boarder entered... and stopping, astonished by a reason known only to her and him, the whore exclaimed:
“Ah!
Is it you?...
You!...
You’ve finally come!... ” Erdosain answered her:
“Yes, it’s me...
Ah, if you only knew how long I’ve been looking for you! ”
But since this could never happen, his sadness bounced back like a lead ball against a rubber wall.

And he knew full well that his longing to be suddenly pitied by an unknown whore would always, throughout the unfolding of the days, be as ineffective as that ball in piercing the thick life around him. Once more he repeated to himself:
“Ah!
Is it you?
You...
Ah!
You’ve finally come, my sad love...

” but it was all useless; he would never find that woman, and a merciless energy born of despair swelled his muscles, spread through the seventy kilos of his weight, moving it nimbly through the darkness, while inside the cube of his chest an enormous sadness made the beats of his heart heavy.
Suddenly he found himself in front of the great door of the boarding house where he lived; then he decided to go in.
His heart beat impatiently.
On tiptoe he crossed the gallery and, approaching the door of his room, opened it noiselessly.
Then, with hands stretched out in the darkness, he moved toward the corner where the sofa stood and slowly curled up there, careful not to make the springs creak.
Later he could find no explanation for this attitude.
He stretched his legs on the sofa and for a few minutes remained with the nape of his neck resting on the lattice of his hands.
And there was more darkness in his soul than in that moment of gloom, which would become a papered cube if he lit the lamp.
He wanted to fix his mind on something objective, but found it impossible.
This caused him a certain childish fear; for a few instants he sharpened his attention, but no sound reached him and then he closed his eyes.
His heart labored with dull thuds, driving the mass of his blood, and a watery coldness bristled the hair on his back.
With stiff eyelids and rigid body he waited for something to happen.
Suddenly he understood that if he remained in that posture he would scream with fear, and drawing his heels in, with his legs crossed like a Buddha, he waited in the darkness.
His annihilation was intense, yet he could call no one, nor could he weep.
And yet it was impossible to remain like that all night, squatting.
He lit a cigarette and a great chill immobilized him.
The Cripple was standing beside the edge of the folding screen, examining him with her poisonous cold gaze.
Her hair, parted in two smooth wings, covered her ears with its red panels, and the woman’s lips were pressed tight.
Everything about her showed an excess of attention, but Erdosain was afraid. At last he managed to say:
“You! ”
The match was burning his fingernails... and suddenly an impulse stronger than his shyness lifted him.
In the darkness he walked toward her and said:
Weren’t you asleep? ”
He felt her stretch out her arm; the woman’s hand took his chin between her fingers and Hipólita said in a deep voice:
“What’s the matter that you don’t sleep? ”
“Are you caressing me, ma’am? ”
“Why aren’t you sleeping? ”
“You’re touching me?...
But how cold your hand is!...
Why is your hand so cold? ”
“Light the lamp. ”
Under the vertical light, Erdosain stood contemplating her.
She sat down on the sofa. Erdosain murmured timidly:
“Would you like me to sit beside you?
I couldn’t sleep. ”
Hipólita made room for him, and beside the intruder, Erdosain could not contain the force that raised his hands, and with his fingertips he caressed her forehead.
“Why are you like this?
” he asked her.
The woman looked at him serenely.
Erdosain contemplated her for an instant with mute desperation; and at last he took her delicate hand.
He was about to raise it to his lips, but a strange force collided with his sensibility, and sobbing he collapsed onto the woman’s lap.
He wept convulsively in the shadow of the erect intruder and of her gaze fixed on the convulsions of his head.

He wept blindly, his life twisted by a hoarse fury, holding back cries whose incomplete lacerations renewed his horrible pain, and the suffering poured out of him inexhaustibly, flooding him with more grief, a grief that rose in sobs in his throat.
Thus he agonized for several minutes, biting his handkerchief so as not to scream, while her silence was a softness against which his exhausted spirit leaned.
Then the screaming suffering was exhausted; tears filled his chest and he found consolation in lying fallen like that, with wet cheeks, on a woman’s lap.

An enormous weariness overwhelmed him, the figure of his distant wife finally erased itself from the surface of his grief, and while he remained thus, a twilight calm came to resign him to all the disasters that had been prepared.
He lifted his reddened face, streaked by the folds of the fabric and damp with tears.
She looked at him serenely.
“Are you sad?
” she asked.
“Yes. ”
Then they fell silent and a violet flash of lightning lit the recesses of the dark patio.
It was raining.
“Shall we drink some maté? ”
“Yes. ”
In silence he prepared the water.
She gazed abstractedly at the windowpanes where the rain drummed, while Erdosain readied the herb.
Then, smiling through his tears, he said:
“I’ll brew it my way.
You’ll like it. ”
“Why were you sad? ”
“I don’t know... anguish... it’s been a long time since I’ve lived in peace. ”

Now he drank the maté in silence, and in the room with the wallpaper peeling in one corner, the figure of the woman became more perfect, wrapped in her otter coat, with her red hair combed in two wings that covered the tips of her ears. With a childish smile, Erdosain added:
“When I’m alone... sometimes I drink. ”

She smiled in a friendly way with one leg crossed over the other, her back slightly inclined, an elbow resting in the palm of her hand and the fingers of the other holding the maté, whose nickel-plated straw she sucked slowly.
“Yes, I was anguished,” Erdosain repeated; “but how cold your hands are!...
Do you always have them so cold? ”
“Yes. ”
“Will you give me your hand? ”
The intruder straightened her back and almost regally held it out to him.
Erdosain took it with care and brought it to his lips, and she looked at him for a long time, the coldness of her pupils melting into a sudden warmth that flushed her cheeks.
Then Erdosain remembered the chained man, and without this being able to overcome the pale joy that was in him, he said:
“Look... if you asked me now to kill myself, I would do it.
I’m so happy.
” The warmth that an instant before had convulsed the waters of his eyes was lost again in the coldness of her gaze.
The woman examined him with curiosity.
“I’m telling you seriously.
I’m going... it’s better... ask me to kill myself... tell me, don’t you think certain people would do better to leave? ”
“No. ”
“Even if they do the worst things? ”
“That’s in God’s hands. ”
“Then it’s not worth talking about it. ”

Once more they drank the maté in silence, a silence that came so he could enjoy the spectacle of the red-haired woman wrapped in her otter coat, with her transparent hands clasping her knee above the green silk dress.
And suddenly, unable to contain his curiosity, he exclaimed:
“Is it true you were a servant? ”
“Yes... what’s strange about that? ”
“How odd! ”
“Why? ”
“Yes, it’s odd.
Sometimes it seems to me that in another life I’m going to find what’s missing in this one.
And one imagines that there are people who have discovered the secret of happiness... and that if they told us the secret we too would be happy. ”
“My life, however, is no secret. ”
“But have you never felt the strangeness of living? ”
“Yes, that I have. ”
“Tell me. ”
“It was when I was a little girl.
I worked in a beautiful house on Avenida Alvear.
There were three girls and four servants.

And I would wake up in the morning and could never quite convince myself that it was I moving among those pieces of furniture that didn’t belong to me and those people who only spoke to me so that I would serve them.
And at times it seemed to me that the others were firmly nailed into life and into their houses, while I had the sensation of being loose, only lightly tied to life by a string.
And the voices of the others sounded in my ears as when one is asleep and doesn’t know whether one is dreaming or awake. ”
“It must be sad. ”
“Yes, it’s very sad to see others happy and to see that the others don’t understand that one will be unhappy for the rest of one’s life.
I remember that at siesta time I would go into my little room and instead of mending my clothes I would think: Will I be a servant all my life?
And it was no longer the work that tired me, but my thoughts.
Haven’t you noticed how stubborn sad thoughts are? ”
“Yes, they never go away.
How old were you then? ”
“Sixteen. ”
“And you hadn’t yet gone to bed with any man? ”
“No... but I was furious... furious at being a servant for the rest of my life... besides, there was something that impressed me more than anything.
It was one of the boys.
He was engaged and very Catholic.
I caught him caressing his cousin, who was his fiancée, more than once; now I realize she was a sensual girl, and I wondered how it was possible to reconcile Catholicism with those filthy things.
Involuntarily I ended up spying on him... but he, who was so attentive with his fiancée, was perfectly correct with me.
Later I realized I had desired him... but it was too late...
I was in another house... ”
Always with the weight of my ideas.
What did I want from life?
At the time I didn’t know.
Everywhere they were kind to me.
Later I heard people speak ill of the rich... but I never saw that wickedness.
They lived that way.
What need did they have to be bad, isn’t that so?
They were the young ladies and I the servant. ”
“I remember one day I was on the streetcar accompanying one of my mistresses.
Two young men were talking in the seat.
Have you noticed that there are days when certain words sound in the ears like drums... as if one had always been deaf and for the first time heard people speak?
Well.
One of the young men was saying: ‘An intelligent woman, even if she were ugly, if she went into the bad life would get rich and if she didn’t fall in love with anyone could be the queen of a city.
If I had a sister, I would advise her like that.’ On hearing him, I froze in my seat.

Those words instantly melted my shyness and when we reached the end of the journey it seemed to me that it had not been the strangers who had spoken those words, but I, I who until that moment had not remembered them.
And for many days the problem of how to be a woman of the bad life occupied me. ” Erdosain smiled:
“How wonderful! ”
“The first month’s wages I earned I spent on a pile of books that talked about the bad life.
I was wrong, because almost all of them were pornographic books... stupid... that wasn’t the bad life, but the bad life of pleasure...
And, believe me, none of my friends could explain to me, in substance, what the bad life was. ”
“Go on... now it doesn’t surprise me that Ergueta fell in love with you.
You are an admirable woman. ”
Hipólita smiled, blushing.
“Don’t exaggerate...
I’m just a sensible woman, nothing more. ”
“Tell me, you delightful creature. ”
“How childish you are!...
All right.
” Hipólita closed the lapels of her coat over her breast and continued: “I worked as before, all day, but the work became strange to me...

I mean that while I was scrubbing or making a bed, my thought was far away and at the same time so deep inside me that at moments it seemed that if that thought grew any larger it would burst my skin.
But the problem was not solved.
I wrote to a bookstore asking if they had any manual for becoming a woman of the bad life and they didn’t answer, until one day I decided to see a lawyer so he could clarify the point for me.

I went to the courts and wandered through a lot of streets, looking at one brass plate, then another, then another, until, turning down Juncal Street, I stopped in front of a luxurious house, spoke to the porter and he took me to the presence of a doctor of laws.
I remember it as if it were today.
He was a thin, serious man, his whole face that of a perverse bandit, but when he smiled his soul seemed that of a little boy.
Later, thinking about it, I came to the conclusion that that man must have suffered a great deal. ”
She sucked the maté at length, then, handing it back, said:
“How hot it is in here!
Would you open the window? ”
Erdosain opened one leaf.
It was still raining. Hipólita continued:
“Without losing my composure, I said to him: ‘Doctor, I’ve come to see you because I want to know what the bad life is.’ The other man looked at me astonished.
After reflecting for a few moments, he said: ‘With what purpose do you wish to know?’ I calmly explained my intentions and he listened to me attentively, frowning, pondering my words.

At last he said: ‘In a woman the bad life is called the sexual acts performed without love and for profit.’ That is, I replied, that through the bad life one frees oneself from the body... and remains free. ”
“You answered him that? ”
“Yes. ”
“How strange! ”
“Why? ”
“And then? ”
“Almost without saying goodbye, I went out into the street.
I was happy, I was never happier than that day.
The bad life, Erdosain, was that: to free oneself from the body, to have one’s will free to do all the things one felt like doing.
I felt so happy that I gave myself to the first good-looking man who passed and who desired me with pretty words. ”
“And then? ”
“What a surprise!
When the man...
I already told you he was a handsome fellow, fell like an ox after satisfying himself.
The first thing that occurred to me was that he was ill...
I never imagined that.
But when the other explained to me that it was natural in all men, I couldn’t contain my desire to laugh.
So the man, whose strength seemed immense like that of a bull... in short, have you never seen a thief in a room full of gold?
At that moment I, the servant, was the thief in the room full of gold.
And I understood that the world was mine...
Later, before launching myself into prostitution, I decided to study... yes, don’t look at me astonished, I read everything...
I had come to the conclusion, reading novels, that men attributed extraordinary capacities for love to the cultured woman...
I don’t know if I explain myself well...
I mean that culture was a disguise that gave value to the merchandise. ”
“Did you find pleasure in possession? ”
“No... but going back to the first thing: I read everything. ”
Erdosain felt himself enthused by the woman’s cynicism, and tenderly he said to her:
“Will you give me your hand? ”
She gave it to him, serious.

Erdosain took it with care; then he brought it to his lips and she looked at him for a long time; but Remo suddenly remembered the chained man; he would be awake now in the stable, and without this being able to overcome the sweetness that was drowsing his senses, he said:
“Look, if you... if you asked me now to kill myself, I would do it with delight. ”
She looked at him for a long time through her red lashes.
“I’m telling you seriously.
Tomorrow... today... it’s better... ask me to kill myself... tell me, don’t you think certain people should leave the earth? ”
“No... that isn’t done. ”
“Even if they become bandits? ”
“Who can judge another? ”
“Then let’s not talk about it anymore. ”
Once more they sucked the straw in silence.
Erdosain understood the sweetness of many things. He looked at her, then said:
“What a strange creature you are! ”
She smiled, flattered, and a festival entered his soul.
“Shall I put in more herb? ”
“Yes. ”
Suddenly Hipólita looked at him seriously.
“Where did you get that soul you have? ”
Erdosain was going to speak of his sufferings, but he restrained himself out of modesty and said:
“I don’t know... many times I thought about purity...
I would have liked to be a pure man,” and growing enthusiastic, he continued: “Many times I felt the sadness of not being a pure man.
Why?
I don’t know.
But can you imagine a man with a white soul, in love for the first time... and that everyone was the same?
Can you imagine what an enormous love there would be between a pure woman and a pure man?

Then, before giving themselves to each other, they would kill themselves... or no; it would be she who would offer herself to him one day... then they would commit suicide, understanding the uselessness of living without illusions. ”
“Nevertheless, that isn’t possible. ”
“But it exists.
Haven’t you seen how many shopkeepers and dressmakers commit suicide together?
They loved each other... they can’t marry... they go to a hotel... she gives herself and then they kill themselves. ”
“Yes, but they do it unconsciously. ”
“Perhaps. ”
“Where did you have supper last night?
” Erdosain spoke of the Espilas, explaining to her the fall of those people into misery.
“And why don’t they work? ”
“Where would they get work?
They look for it and don’t find it.
That’s the terrible thing.
It even seemed to me that misery had destroyed in them the desire to live.
Deaf Eustaquio has talent for mathematics... he knows infinitesimal calculus; but that’s no use to him.

He also knows Don Quixote by heart... but there must be something unhinged in his understanding... this fact will paint it for you: at sixteen they sent him to buy herb and he went to a pharmacy instead of a grocery store.
After many explanations he said that herb was a medicinal product... that that was how he had studied it in botany. ”
“He has no practical sense. ”
“Exactly.
Besides, he’s a brooding gambler... he’s capable of missing a meal to solve a riddle and when he has a few cents he goes into the pastry shops to stuff himself with sweets. ”
“How strange! ”
“On the other hand, Emilio is a good boy.

He has... so he’s told me, the certainty that that psychic state of theirs, apathetic and strange, is a hereditary consequence, and on that basis he rules his whole life, moves with the slowness of a tortoise.
He’s capable of taking two hours to dress... it seems that he does all his things in an atmosphere of extraordinary indecision. ”
“And the sisters? ”
“The poor things do what they can... they sew... one looks after a hydrocephalic child in a friend’s house, with a head bigger than a melon. ”
“How horrible! ”
“What I can’t understand is how they got used to all that.
That’s why after visiting them I felt the great need to give them illusions... and since I spoke quite well, I succeeded.
And they devoted themselves to the copper rose. ”
“What is that? ”
Erdosain explained his inventor’s broodings to her.
It had been at the beginning, shortly after he got married, when he dreamed of growing rich with a discovery.
His imagination occupied the nights with extraordinary machines, incomplete pieces of mechanisms turning their lubricated gears...
“But then you are an inventor?... ”
“No... not now... that had importance for me.
There was a time when I had the hunger... the terrible hunger for money... possibly I was sick with a madness that has changed...

Now, when I spoke to them about that, it wasn’t because the matter interested me economically, but because I needed to see them full of illusions, I needed to see with my own eyes those poor girls dreaming of silk dresses, of a handsome boyfriend, and of a car at the door of a chalet they would never have.
And now I’m sure they believe in all that. ”
“Have you always been like this? ”
“No, sometimes.
Hasn’t it ever happened to you to feel at a given moment the desire to perform works of mercy?
I remember now another fact.
I’ll tell it to you because you asked me before what soul was mine.
I remember.
A year ago.
It was a Saturday, at two in the morning.
I remember I was sad and I entered a brothel.
The room was full of people waiting their turn.
Suddenly the bedroom door opened and the woman appeared... imagine... a round little face of a sixteen-year-old girl... sky-blue eyes and a schoolgirl’s smile.
She was wrapped in a green coat and was rather tall... but her little face was that of a schoolgirl...

She looked around... it was already late; a horrible black man, with cardboard lips, stood up, and then she, who had enveloped us all in a promise, retreated sadly toward the bedroom, under the hard gaze of the madam. ”
Erdosain stopped for a moment, then, in a purer and slower voice, continued:
“Believe me... it’s very shameful to wait in a brothel.
One never feels sadder than in there, surrounded by pale faces that try to hide with false smiles, with evasions, the terrible carnal urgency.

And there is something else humiliating... one doesn’t know what it is... but time runs in the ears, while the sharpened ear listens to the creaking of a bed in there, then a silence, later the noise of washing... but before anyone occupied the black man’s place, I left my chair and went to the other.
I waited with my heart giving great blows, and when she appeared in the doorway I stood up. ”
“Always that... one after another. ”

“I stood up and entered, the door closed again; I left the money on the washstand, and when she was about to open her robe, I took her by the arm and said: ‘No, I haven’t come in to go to bed with you.’”
Now Erdosain’s voice had acquired a vibrant fluidity.

“She looked at me and surely the first thing she thought was whether I might not be some pervert; but looking at her seriously, believe me, I was moved, I said to her: ‘Look, I came in because you made me feel sorry for you.’ Now we had sat down beside the console of a gilded mirror, and she, with her schoolgirl’s little face, examined me gravely.
I remember!...
As if it were now.
I said to her: ‘Yes, you made me feel sorry for you.
I already know you’ll earn two or three thousand pesos a month... and that there are families who would consider themselves happy to have what you throw away on shoes...
I already know that... but you made me feel an enormous pity, seeing all the beauty you outrage in yourself.’ She looked at me in silence, but I didn’t smell of wine.

‘Then I thought... it occurred to me right after the black man came in, to leave you a beautiful memory... and the most beautiful memory that occurred to me to leave you was this... to come in and not touch you... and afterward you will always remember that gesture.’ Notice that while I was speaking, the prostitute’s robe had opened above her breasts, while on her crossed leg... suddenly she, looking at herself in the mirror, realized it and hurriedly lowered the dress over her knees, closing the neckline.

That gesture made a strange impression on me... she looked at me without saying a word... who knows what she was thinking... suddenly the madam knocked with her knuckle on the door, she looked in that direction with distress, then her little face turned toward me... she looked at me for a moment... she stood up... she took the five pesos and forcing them into my pocket while saying: ‘Don’t come back because if you do I’ll have the porter throw you out.’”
We were standing...

I was already going to leave by the other door, and suddenly, with her gaze fixed on mine, I felt her arms knot around my neck... she looked at me still in the eyes and kissed me on the mouth... what can I tell you about that kiss!... she passed her hand over my forehead and when I was already in the doorway, she said to me: “Goodbye, noble man. ”
“And you never went back? ”
“No, but I have the hope that someday we will meet... who knows where, but she, Lucién, will never forget me.
Time will pass, she will roll through the most miserable brothels... she will become monstrous... but I will always be in her as I had proposed, as the most precious memory of her life. ”
The rain beat on the windowpanes of the door and on the tiles of the patio.
Erdosain sucked his maté slowly.
Hipólita stood up, went to the windowpanes and looked for a moment at the black patio. Then she turned and said:
“You know you are a strange man? ”
Erdosain pondered for an instant.
“I’m sincere with you...
I don’t know what will become of my life... but, believe me, it wasn’t in my hands to be a good man.
Other dark forces twisted me... threw me down. ”
“And now? ”
“Now I’m going to do an experiment.
I’ve found an admirable man who is firmly convinced that lying is the basis of human happiness and I’ve decided to support him in everything. ”
“And does that make you happy? ”
“No... it’s been a long time since I felt that I will never again be happy. ”
“But do you believe in love? ”
“What’s the use of talking about that!
” but suddenly he glimpsed what was the motive of all the incoherences he had been saying for a few minutes, and said: “What would you think of me if tomorrow...
I mean any day... if any day you found out that I had murdered a man? ”
Hipólita, who had sat down, slowly raised her head and, leaving it resting on the back of the sofa, looked at the ceiling for a long time.
Then, half-closing her eyelids, she said, filtering a cold gaze between her red lashes:
“I would think that you were immensely unhappy. ”
Erdosain left his armchair, put the heater, the herb and the maté away in the wardrobe drawer, and then Hipólita said to him:
“Come here... to my feet. ”
An enormous sweetness was in him.
He sat down on the carpet so that his side rested against her legs, laid his head on her knees, and Hipólita closed her eyes.
It was good like that.
He rested on the woman’s lap, and the warmth of her limbs passed through the fabric, warming his cheek.

That situation moreover seemed very natural to him; life acquired that cinematographic aspect he had always pursued, and it did not occur to him to think about Hipólita, stiff on the sofa, thinking about him, that he was weak and sentimental.
The tick-tock of the clock spaced in the interval of its gears a drop of sound that fell successively like a lentil of water into the cubic silence of the room. And Hipólita said to herself:
“All his life he will do nothing but complain and suffer.
What use is a boy like that to me?
I would have to support him.
And the copper rose must be nonsense.
What woman is going to wear heavy metal ornaments on her hat that turn black?
All men are like that, however.
The weak ones, intelligent and useless; the others, brutes and boring.
I still haven’t found among them one worthy of cutting the throats of the others, or of being a tyrant.
They arouse pity. ”
She thought like this frequently, as reality faded the puppets that her imagination had for a moment colored with arrogant liveliness.
She could point to them with her finger.

This erect puppet, perfumed and severe, who on working days made a reputation with his bearing and silence, was a lascivious wretch; that other one, small and well-mannered, always gentle, discreet and sensible, was the victim of atrocious vices; that one brutal as a carter and strong as a bull, more inexperienced than a schoolboy, and so all of them passed before her eyes knotted by the same and inextinguishable desire, all had for an instant laid their heads on her bare knees, while she, alien to the clumsy hands and to the transitory frenzies that stiffened the sad puppets, thought, harsh, the sensation of living like a thirst in the desert.
“That was how it was.
Men were moved only by hunger, lust and money.
That was how it was.

Anguished, she told herself that the only one who had interested her was the pharmacist, capable of rising for a few instants above his vehement flesh, but the terrible game had dissolved his mechanism, and now he lay more broken than the other dolls.
What a life hers was!

In other times, when she was a helpless young girl, she thought she would never have money nor a house furnished with beautiful furniture, nor gleaming tableware, and that impossibility of wealth saddened her as much as today knowing that no man of those who could go to bed with her had the drive to become a tyrant or conqueror of new lands. ”
–Yes, she had dreamed!
There were days when she imagined a sensational encounter, some man who would speak to her of jungles and keep a tame lion in his house.
His embrace would be tireless and she would love him like a slave; then she would take pleasure in shaving her armpits for him and painting her breasts.
Disguised as a boy she would roam with him through ruins where centipedes sleep and villages where Black people have their huts in the forks of trees.
But nowhere had she found lions, only flea-ridden dogs, and the most adventurous gentlemen were crusaders of the fork and mystics of the pot.
She withdrew in disgust from these stupid lives.

In the course of the days the rare novelistic characters she had met were not as interesting as they were in novels; rather, the very traits that made them vivid in fiction were precisely the hateful aspects that rendered them repulsive in life.
And yet she had given herself to them.
But once sated, they drew away from her as if they felt humiliated at having shown her the spectacle of their weakness.
Now she submerged herself in the sterility of a life as flat as a geographically explored desert.
Just as it was impossible to transmute lead into gold, so it was impossible to transform the soul of man.
How many times had she fallen naked into the arms of a stranger and said to him: “Wouldn’t you like to go to Africa?
” The other would start as if a rattlesnake had hissed beside him.
And then she had the impression that those bodies armed with bones and wound round with muscle were weaker than those of tender infants, more easily frightened than children in the forest.
Women were hateful to her.
She saw them collapse under the sensuality of males only to display everywhere the ugliness of their swollen bellies.
They had a capacity solely for suffering; this was a world of weary people, ghosts barely awake who stank of earth with their gravid drowsiness, like the lazy and gigantic monsters of the first ages.
Hence her soaring soul felt crushed by the uselessness of her fellow beings.

For Hipólita would have liked to move in a less dense universe, a world as light as a soap bubble where matter was not subject to gravity, and she imagined the laughing happiness of traveling every path on the planet, metamorphosing it at will and giving the days the reality of a game that would compensate for the one her childhood had lacked.
Everything had been denied her when she was small.
She remembered that one of the chimeras of her infancy was to dream that she would be the happiest creature in the world if she lived in a room covered with wallpaper.

She had seen in the windows of hardware stores painted papers that in her limited imagination seemed capable of making the lives of those who surrounded themselves with them dreamy; painted papers that were like transplanting the Forest of Enchantments into a house, with its arbitrary blue flowers twisted against backgrounds striped with gold.

And this dream of her seventh year had been as intense in her as, later, when grown, the idea of the pleasure she would feel if she could have a Rolls-Royce, whose leather upholstery was as precious in her imagination as those impossible wallpapers that cost only sixty cents a roll.
She had declined in times gone by.

Now, with the man’s head on her knees, she remembered those Sunday evenings when the weather would suddenly cloud over and the cold breeze would drive her mistresses from the garden into the drawing room.
Rain pecked at the windowpanes; she would take refuge in the kitchen, gleaming with cleanliness, and through the rooms came the voices of the visitors.
The ladies talked while the girls leafed through magazines, pausing at photographs of wedding ceremonies, or played the piano.

And she, seated at the table, the tip of her apron twisting between her fingers, her bust slightly inclined, let herself be penetrated by the sounds, which were always sad to her, even when they spoke of cheerful things.
Like a leper she felt cut off from happiness.

The music brought her a vision of different places, hotels among mountains, and she would never be the newlywed who descends to the dining room in the company of her handsome husband while the china tinkles and birds flutter around the windows through which one can see the fall of a cascade.
She slowly twisted the tip of her apron between her fingers, her forehead bowed, her legs crossed.

She would never have a husband like Marcelo, nor would she spread her mantilla over the velvet railing of a box while diamonds sparkled in the ears of duchesses and violins before the proscenium squeaked softly.
Nor would she be a lady, one of those young ladies she had served whose husbands caressed them sweetly as pregnancy advanced their suffering bellies.
And her sorrow grew gently like the darkness at twilight.
–To serve... always to serve!
Then a rancor seeped into her anguish, her forehead grew heavy and her red eyelids fell, sanctioning a resignation.

And in the drawing room the piano made different countries pass before her dreamy attention and she imagined that the education of those young ladies must make their souls more beautiful and desirable to the longing of their fiancés, and her head weighed as if her skull had been transmuted into a helmet of lead bones.

Everything that surrounded her—saucepans and stoves and the clean wood of the kitchen shelves, and the mirrors in the bathroom and the red lampshades—seemed to her to represent a value that placed those objects forever beyond her reach, and the dishcloth as well as the carpet, and the children’s tricycle, seemed to have been created to provide happiness to beings made of a different stuff from that of which she was formed.
Even the girls’ dresses, the light fabrics with which they adorned their precious bodies, the lace and ribbons, seemed to her of a different nature from those she could buy with the same money.
This sensation of living provisionally among people situated in a world unlike the one she belonged to unsettled her to the point that despair appeared like a stigma upon her face.
What could she be but a servant, always a servant!
From her heart there rose sullenly a deaf negation, an answer to the invisible phantom that tormented her.
Her life was an upright resistance against domesticity.
She did not know how she would escape that chain of misfortunes, yet she kept repeating to herself that this state was temporary, ignorant, however, of what was to come.

And she continually observed the manners of the young ladies and studied how they inclined their heads, and how they said goodbye to their friends at the doors of their houses, later reproducing before a mirror the greetings and gestures she remembered.

And these acts that she performed in the solitude of her little room left on her lips and in her soul for several hours a sensation of ladylike refinement, and then she would reproach herself for earlier clumsy manners, as if those earlier manners detracted from her authentic and present personality as a young lady.

For several hours her life would be inflamed with a penetrating and soft delicacy like the fragrance of a perfumed cream with vanilla, and she seemed to feel in her throat the honeyed voices of “yes” and “no,” until she had the illusion that she was answering a delightful interlocutor who wore a blue fox fur around her neck.
Her servant’s room would repopulate itself with insinuating phantoms.
Seated in an armchair covered in crocodile-colored silk, she received her friends who had come to say goodbye before leaving for “Paris, France,” and she spoke of engagements.
“Her mother would not allow her to go to X... for the summer because they would run into S..., that indiscreet man who pestered her excessively.

” Or she crossed the sea, a sea as still as the lakes of Palermo, seated in a wicker basket as she had seen in photographs of the decks of luxury steamers when she passed through the streets on her way to do the marketing.
She would have a Kodak abandoned in her lap while a young man, cap in hand and leaning toward her, would speak to her with timidity.
Her servant’s soul drowned in happiness.
She understood that it was so beautiful that, had she been able to enjoy it, her charity would have been infinite.
And she saw herself on a winter evening walking down a darkened alleyway, wrapped in a petit-gris coat, in search of an orphan, daughter of a blind man.

She brought her aid, made her her adopted daughter, and one day the orphan would make her debut in society; she would then be a delightful young woman, her shoulders bare among plumes of gauze, and, above her clear forehead, a wave of blond hair would harmonize with the delicacy of her almond-shaped eyes. And suddenly a voice called her:
–Hipólita... serve the tea.
Erdosain lifted his head abruptly, and Hipólita, as if she had been thinking about him, said:
“You too... you too have been very unhappy. ”
Erdosain took the woman’s cold hand and pressed his lips to it. She continued slowly:
“Sometimes this life seems like a bad dream to me.
Now that I feel I belong to you, the old sorrow returns.
Always, everywhere, suffering. ” Then she said:
“What must one do not to suffer? ”
“It’s that we carry suffering inside us.
At one point I even thought it floated in the air... that was a ridiculous idea; but the truth is that discontent lives within us. ”
They fell silent.
Hipólita slowly stroked his hair; suddenly her hand left his head and
Erdosain felt the woman press his hand against her lips.
Erdosain, sitting down beside her, murmured:
“Tell me, what have I done to you that you make me so happy?
Don’t you understand that you bring heaven down to me?
I have never felt so enormously unhappy. ”
“Has no one ever loved you? ”
“I don’t know; but love was never shown to me in its terrible passion.
When I got married I was twenty and I believed in the spirituality of love. ”
He pondered for a moment, but soon stood up, turned off the light, and sat down on the divan beside Hipólita. Then he said:
“Perhaps I was a wretch.
When I married I had never kissed my wife.
It’s true I had never felt the need to, because I mistook for purity what was coldness in her senses and also... because I believed one must not kiss a young lady. ”
The other woman smiled in the darkness.
He was now seated on the edge of the sofa, elbows planted on his knees and cheeks resting in the palms of his hands.
A violet flash of lightning lit up the room. He went on slowly:
“In my mind the young lady represented the truest expression of purity.
Besides... don’t laugh...
I was modest... and on the night we were married, when she undressed quite naturally in front of the lighted lamp, I turned my head away in shame... and then I went to bed with my trousers on. ”
“You did that?
” – indignation trembled in the woman’s voice.
Erdosain burst out laughing, highly excited:
“Why not?
” – while he rubbed his hands and looked sideways at the Cripple.
“I did that and many far worse things.
And the ones I will do...
‘The times have come,’ your husband used to say.
I think he’s right.
Of course those episodes belong to a period of my life when I lived like an idiot.
I tell you this so you can be sure that if I had to go to bed with you I wouldn’t do it with my trousers on... ”
For a moment Hipólita felt afraid.
Erdosain did nothing but watch her out of the corner of his eye while he rubbed his hands. Cautiously she added:
“It must be that you were ill.
Like me when I was a servant.
One lives between heaven and earth... ”
“That’s it, between heaven and earth...
Exactly that.
Yes, I remember when they called me an imbecile. ”
“You too?... ”
“Yes, to my face...

I would stare at the person who had insulted me, and while all my muscles went slack in an immense weakness, I would ask myself what I had done, I don’t know in what lifetime, to endure so many humiliations and acts of cowardice.
I suffered a great deal... so much... that more than once I was tempted to go and offer myself as a servant in some rich house...
Could I swallow any more shame?
Then I felt terror, a dreadful fear of not having any noble purpose in my life, a great dream, and finally now I have found one...
I have condemned a man to death...
Stay there sitting down...
Tomorrow, since I do not oppose it, a man is going to be murdered. ”
“It’s not possible! ”
“Yes, it’s true.
The man of the lie, the man I spoke to you about before, needed money to carry out his project.
That is how it will be done, because I want it to happen.
Tomorrow he will give me a cheque to cash.
When I return he will be executed. ”
“No... it’s not possible. ”
“Yes, and if I don’t return they won’t murder him, because without the money the crime is useless... it’s fifteen thousand pesos...
I could run away with them... society can go to hell... the man is saved.
Do you realise?
Everything depends on my criminal honesty. ”
“My God! ”
“I want the experiment to be carried out...
You understand, certain decisions turn one into a god.
For a long time I have been resolved to kill myself.
If earlier, when I told you, you had agreed, I would have killed myself.
If you only knew how beautiful and great I feel!
Don’t speak to me any more about the other... it’s already decided; it even pleases me to think of the pit I am sinking into.
Do you realise!...
And any day... no, not during the day... any night, when I am sick of so much farce and incoherence, I shall go. ”
A wrinkle forked across Hipólita’s forehead.
There was no doubt about it.
That man was mad.
Her adventurous soul foresaw future events, and she told herself: “With this imbecile one must proceed prudently.
” And folding her arms over her coat, she asked, as if in doubt:
“Would you have the courage to kill yourself? ”
“It’s not what you say.
There is no longer courage or cowardice.
From deep inside I have the sensation that committing suicide is like going to have a tooth pulled.
When I think that way, everything rests within me.
It is true that I had thought of other journeys and other lands, of another life.
There is something in me that desires everything delicate and beautiful.
Many times I thought that yes... let’s say those fifteen thousand pesos I am going to collect tomorrow...

I could go to the Philippines... to Ecuador to begin my life again, marry some delicate millionaire maiden... we would lie during siestas in a hammock under the coconut palms while black servants offered us split oranges.

And I would gaze sadly at the sea... and do you know?... this certainty that tells me that wherever I go I shall gaze sadly at the sea... this assurance that I shall never again be happy... at first it drove me mad... and now I have resigned myself. ”
“Then why are you going to carry out the experiment? ”
“You know?...

I still have not reached the bottom of myself... but crime is my last hope... and the Astrologer knows it, because when I asked him today whether he wasn’t afraid I would run away, he answered: ‘No, not for the moment...
You more than anyone need this to succeed in order to relieve your anguish...’ You see how far I have come. ”
“I would never have imagined such a thing.
And are they going to kill him in Temperley? ”
“Yes.
Although...
Who knows!
The anguish.
Do you know what anguish is?
To have anguish rooted in your bones like syphilis?
Look, this happened four months ago: I was waiting for the train at a country station.
It would be three-quarters of an hour before it arrived... and so I crossed to a square opposite.
A few minutes after sitting down on a bench, a little girl... she must have been nine, came and sat beside me.
We began to talk... she was wearing a white pinafore... she lived in one of the houses opposite...
Slowly, unable to contain myself, I steered the conversation toward an obscene subject... but cautiously... testing the ground.
A dreadful curiosity had taken hold of my conscience.

The child, hypnotised by her half-awakened instinct, listened to me trembling... and I, slowly, at that moment must have had the face of a criminal... note that from the signalman’s cabin two switchmen were watching me attentively, I revealed the sexual mystery to her, urging her to devote herself to corrupting her little girlfriends... ”
Hipólita pressed her temples with her fingers.
“But you are a monster! ”
“Now I have reached the end.
My life is a horror...
I need to create terrible complications for myself... to commit the sin.
Don’t look at me.
Possibly... look... people have lost the sense of the word sin... sin is not a fault...
I have come to realise that sin is an act by which man breaks the frail thread that kept him joined to God.
God is denied him forever.
Even if that man’s life after the sin became purer than that of the purest saint, he could never reach God.
I am going to break the frail thread that joined me to divine charity.
I feel it.

From tomorrow I shall be a monster upon the earth... imagine a creature... a foetus... a foetus that had the power to live outside the maternal womb... it never grows... hairy... small... without nails it walks among men without being a man... its fragility horrifies the world around it... but there is no human force that can return it to the lost womb.
That is what will happen to me tomorrow.
I shall move away from God forever.
I shall be alone upon the earth.
My soul and I, the two of us alone.
The infinite before us.
Always alone.
And night and day... and always a yellow sun.
Do you realise?
The infinite grows... above a yellow sun and the soul that has separated from divine charity walks alone and blind beneath the yellow sun. ”
A dull thud shook the floor, and suddenly something extraordinary occurred.
Erdosain fell silent, horrified.
Hipólita was kneeling at his feet...
She took his hand and covered it with kisses. In the darkness the woman exclaimed:
“Let me... let me kiss those poor hands of yours.
You are the most wretched man on earth. ”
“Get up, Hipólita. ”
“No, I want to kiss your feet” – he felt her arms tighten around his legs.
“You are the most unhappy man on earth.
How you have suffered, my God!
How great you are... how great your soul is! ”
Erdosain lifted her with infinite tenderness.
He felt himself softened by an infinite pity; he drew her to his breast, smoothed the hair on her forehead, and said to her:
“If you only knew now how easy it will be to die.
Like a game. ”
“What a soul you have!... ”
“But are you feverish?... ”
“Poor boy! ”
“Why?
Now we are like gods...
Sit beside me.
Are you comfortable like that?
Look, little sister, everything I suffered has been paid for by your words.
We shall live a while longer... ”
“Yes, like sweethearts... ”
“Only on the great day will you be my wife. ”
“I love you so much!...
What a soul you have! ”
“And afterwards we shall go away. ”
And they spoke no more.
Hipólita’s head had fallen upon his breast.
Dawn was not far off.
Then Erdosain folded that weary body onto the sofa... she smiled, exhausted; then Remo sat down on the carpet, rested his head on the edge of the sofa, and thus curled up he fell asleep.
Semi-reclined on a sofa, arms crossed and his bowler hat pulled down over his forehead, the Astrologer meditated that night on his worries, in the darkness of his study.
