The rain beat against the windowpanes, but he did not hear it, lost in numerous projects.
Besides, something strange was happening to him.
The nearness of the crime to be committed accelerated, within normal time, another particular time.
Thus he received the sensation of existing sensitized in two times.
One natural to all states of ordinary life, the other extremely fleeting and heavy in the beats of his heart, slipping between his fingers locked by meditation like water from a basket.

And the Astrologer, held within clock time, felt sliding through his brain that other time, extremely rapid and interminable, which, like a cinematographic film sliding at vertiginous speed, wounded his sensibility with the images it carried, in an imprecise and fatiguing way, since before he could clearly perceive an idea it had already vanished to be replaced by another.

So that when he looked at the clock by striking a match, he verified that the time elapsed was only minutes, while in his understanding those mechanical minutes, accelerated by his anxiety, had another length that no clock could measure.
A sensation that kept him in the darkness, on the alert.
He understood that any error committed in that state could prove fatal to him later.
The murder of Barsut did not worry him greatly, but rather the precautions he had to take so that the deed would not acquire undue importance.
And although he tried to prepare an alibi, it was difficult.

He had the sensation that the one thus pondering in the shadows was not he, but that he was contemplating his double, a double forged of emotion and that had his exact appearance, with the rhomboid face, arms crossed and the bowler hat pulled down over his forehead.
Nevertheless, he could not discern what nature the thoughts of that double were, so intimately linked to him and yet so distant from his comprehension.
Because he judged that his feeling of existing was in those instants more effective than the existence of his body.

Later, explaining the phenomenon, he said it was the awareness of the different speed of the time that his emotions lasted, within the other mechanical time, like those who say “that minute seemed a century to me. ”

An impossibility of thinking that was not without importance, since it was a matter of taking a man’s life, paralyzing the circulation of his five liters of blood, cooling all his cells, erasing him from life like a stain from a white sheet of paper, eliminating every trace on the surface.

As so grave a problem did not leave the Astrologer, he felt himself within the mechanical time of the clock, the physical man, while in the slow velocity of the other time that no clock could control his double was located, pensive, enigmatic, authentically mysterious, perhaps preparing alibis that would later surprise the intelligent man.

The certainty of having been converted by the nearness of the crime into a double mechanism with two notions of time so different and two inertias so dissimilar left him sunk gloomily in the darkness.
A terrible fatigue annihilated his musculature, his sturdy limbs, the joints of his bones.

The rain set the brief mechanism of the frogs working in the gutters, but he, a man of action, softened by uneasiness as if his bones had been made flabby and he could not stand up, “I, a man of action,” he told himself, “remain here, inside my span of mechanical time, throbbing with another time that is not my time and that relaxes me for precaution.

Because it is undeniable that killing a man is the same as cutting a lamb’s throat, but it is not the same for the others, and although they are distant and my conduct is a mystery to them, this abnormal time brings them close to me, and I can scarcely move, as if they were there, in the shadow, spying on me.

It must be the time of nervousness that disables me, or the subconscious Astrologer who keeps his ideas to himself and leaves me squeezed like an orange so that I may conceive the thoughts I now need.
Yet once Barsut is dead, life will continue as if nothing had happened... and nothing has happened if this is not discovered. ”
He struck another match.
The room was pierced by moving vertices of shadow.
Not a minute had passed.
His thoughts were simultaneous and contained in the nothingness of time events that, to be present in the time that gathered them, would have needed months and years under other circumstances.

Thus he had been born forty-three years and seven days ago, and that past was continually annihilated in the present, a present so fleeting that he was always the Astrologer of the following minute, in the time of the minute or second to come.

Now his life, focused on a fact that did not yet exist but would be consummated within a few hours, stretched within mechanical time like a bow, whose contained violence gave clock time the extraordinary tension of that other time of uneasiness.
And although he had often told himself that if he had the opportunity to murder someone he would not waste the chance, he again halted his worries at those times of mystery.

Then he leapt from there to the imagination of a dictatorship that would sustain itself by means of terror imposed through numerous executions, and the way to annul that repugnant momentary impression was to picture the executed men as horizontal men.

Indeed, he imagined in the center of the plain the small body of a man lying down, and by comparing the length of the dead man with the thousands of kilometers that measured the earth tyrannized by him, he was seized by the certainty that a man’s life had no value.
The other would rot beneath the earth, while he, having eliminated the human obstacle whose length was the millionth part of his own earth, would advance toward all conquests.
Then he thought of Lenin, who, rubbing his hands, repeated to the Soviet commissars:
“It is madness.
How can we make the revolution without shooting anyone?
” And this gladdened the Astrologer’s heart.
He would establish that principle in society.
The future patriarchs of races would be educated with an inexorable homicidal criterion; and once again his hopes expanded.

Then he recognized that every innovator must struggle with ancient ideas, stamped by custom upon himself, and that all his present ponderings were the consequence of a contradiction between principles yet to be sanctioned and those already established.
Time ran between his fingers locked by pondering.
The murderer of today would be the conqueror of tomorrow, but in the meantime he endured the sullen malevolence of the present kneaded with yesterdays.
He rose angrily.
It was still raining.
He went out to the steps, where he stopped, scrutinizing the wild darkness, shaken by the water that fell thick and slow.
The shadows there seemed to form part of the existence of a monster that panted heavily in the darkness.
The wet earth had turned ochre...
And he was a steadfast man in the night, an animator of grandiose events, and yet no phantom rose from the thicket to sanction his attitude.

Now he asked himself whether men of other ages had suffered his indecisions, or whether they marched toward the achievement of their ends satisfied that Death gave their determinations the thickness of armor.
But did death matter?

He told himself that as a philosophical being the only thing that could interest him was the species, not the individual; yet those who assailed him with scruples were his feelings, which against his will split the necessary time into two strange times.
A lightning flash interposed blue distances between the blocks of the cloud mountains.
Wet and with his hair disheveled, the Man Who Had Seen the Midwife stopped at one side of the steps.
“Ah!
It’s you,” said the Astrologer.
“Yes; I wanted to ask you what you think of this interpretation of the verse that says: ‘The heaven of God.’ That clearly means there are other heavens that are not of God... ”
“Whose, then? ”
“I mean that there may be heavens in which God is not.
Because the verse adds: ‘And the new Jerusalem will descend.’ The new Jerusalem?
Could it be the new Church? ”
The Astrologer meditated a moment.
The matter did not interest him, but he knew that to maintain his prestige before the other he had to answer, and he replied:
“We, the enlightened, know in secret that the new Jerusalem is the new Church.

That is why Swedenborg says: ‘Since the Lord cannot manifest Himself in person, and having announced that He will come and establish a New Church, it follows that He will do so by means of a man who not only can receive the doctrine of this church but also publish it by means of the press...’ but why, independently of any other writing, do you come to admit the existence of several heavens? ”
Bromberg, sheltering in the portico, looked at the panting darkness shaken by the rain, then answered:
“Because the heavens are felt like love. ”
The Astrologer looked at the Jew in surprise, and the latter continued:
“It is like love.
How can you deny love if love is in you and you feel that the angels make your love stronger?
The same happens with the four heavens.
One must admit that all the words of the Bible are of mystery, because if that were not so the book would be absurd.
The other night I was reading the Apocalypse sadly.
I was thinking that I would have to murder Gregorio, and I asked myself whether it is permitted to shed human blood. ”
“When you strangle someone you don’t shed blood,” replied the Astrologer.
“And when I reached the part about ‘the heaven of God’ I understood the reason for men’s sadness.
The heaven of God had been denied them by the shadowy church... and that is why men sin so heavily. ”
In the darkness, Bromberg’s childlike voice sounded as sadly as if he were lamenting that he had been excluded from the true heaven. The Astrologer argued:
“The winged man who speaks to me in dreams has told me that the end of the shadowy church is near... ”
“So it must be... because hell grows day by day.
So few are saved that heaven beside hell is smaller than a grain of sand beside the ocean.
Year after year hell grows, and the shadowy church, which should have saved man, fattens hell day by day, and sad hell grows, grows, without there being any possibility of making it smaller.
And the angels look with fear upon the shadowy church and the red hell swollen like the belly of a dropsical man. ”
The Astrologer replied, adopting a high-sounding tone to speak:
“That is why the winged man has told me: ‘Go, holy man, to edify men and to announce the good news.

And exterminate the antichrists and reveal your secrets and the secrets of the new Jerusalem to Bromberg the Jew’”—and suddenly the Astrologer, taking his companion by the arm, said to him—“Don’t you remember when your spirit conversed with the angels and you served them white bread at the edge of the roads, and made them sit at the door of your cabin and washed their feet? ”
“I don’t remember. ”
“Well, you ought to remember.
What will the Lord say when He learns that?
How shall I answer for your soul before the Angel of the New Church?
He will say to me: What has become of that beloved son, my pious Alfon?
And what shall I tell him?
That you are a blockhead.
That you have forgotten the times when you led an angelic existence and that you spend the whole day in a corner farting like a mule. ” Gravely sulky, Bromberg objected:
“I do not fart. ”

“And you fart very noisily... but never mind... the Angel of the Churches knows that your spirit burns with sincere devotion, and that you are an enemy of the King of Babylon, of the shadowy Pope, and that is why you are chosen to be the friend of the man who, by command of the Lord, will establish the New Church upon the earth. ”
The rain sounded softly on the leaves of the fig trees and all the sharp and soft darkness shook its damp vegetal stench in the night. Bromberg predicted gravely:

“And the Pope, the very Pope terrified, will go out into the street barefoot, and everyone will draw away from him with terror and haste and on the roads the hedges will fill with flowers when the holy Lamb passes. ”
“That’s exactly how it is,” the Astrologer continued.
“And in the half-open sky it will be given to all to see the repentant sinners, the golden gates of the new Jerusalem.
For so immense is the charity of God, dear Alfon, that no man could enter directly into contact with it without falling to the ground with spongy bones. ”
“That is why I will give men my interpretation of the Apocalypse and then I will go to the mountain to do penance and pray for them. ”
“So it is, Alfon, but now go to sleep because I have to meditate and it is the hour when the winged man comes to speak in my ear.
You too must sleep because tomorrow, otherwise, you will have no strength to strangle the reprobate... ”
“And the King of Babylon. ”
“So it is. ”
Slowly the Man Who Had Seen the Midwife moved away from the steps.

The Astrologer entered the house and, climbing a staircase that stood at one side of the vestibule, went into an extremely long room crossed high up by the beams that supported the ceiling joists, which there spread its oblique wing.
On the peeling walls there was no engraving.
In one corner stood Gregorio Barsut’s trunks and beneath an ox-eye window a wooden bed painted red.
A black blanket formed a jumble with the white sheets.
The Astrologer sat down pensively on the edge of the bed.
His overcoat fell open, revealing his hairy naked chest.
He opened the tips of his fingers like a fork over his seal mustache, and, frowning, remained contemplating a trunk in the corner.

He wanted to make his thought leap to an external novelty that, breaking the monorhythm of his sensations, would restore the presence of mind that, before the decision to murder Barsut, had been in him.
“They are twenty thousand pesos,” he thought, “twenty thousand pesos that will serve to set up the brothels and the colony... the colony... ”
Yet he did not see clearly.
Ideas escaped him like shadows; his thoughts, diluted by permanent alarm, made all concentration sterile.
Suddenly he slapped his forehead and, jubilant, passed into the adjacent attic dragging a crate from whose lid, poorly held by the iron bands, thick dust came loose.
Paying no attention to the cuffs of his overcoat that filled with white earth, he opened the crate.
There lead soldiers mingled with wooden dolls, and it was a heap of clowns, little generals, clowns, princesses and strange fat monsters with damaged noses and toad mouths.
He took a piece of rope and, going to the corner, tied it to two nails, thus joining the angle formed by the two walls with an improvised bisector.
Having done this he took several puppets from the crate and threw them onto the bed.

With pieces of twine he tied the throat of each rag doll, and he was so absorbed in the work that he did not notice that the wind was pushing through the open little window the water of the rain, which had grown heavier.
He worked with enthusiasm.
When he had collared the throats of the dolls with strings that he cut from longer to shorter, he carried them to the corner and tied them to the rope.
When his work was finished he stood contemplating it.
The five hanged puppets moved their hooded shadows on the pink wall.

The first, a pierrot without trousers but with a blouse of white and black checks; the second, a chocolate idol with vermilion lips, whose watermelon skull was at the height of the pierrot’s feet; the third, still lower, was an automatic pierrot with a bronze plate nailed to its stomach and a monkey face; the fourth was a sailor of blue cardboard paste, and the fifth a noseless black man showing a plaster sore through the white stock of a patrician collar.
Satisfied, the Astrologer contemplated his work.
He stood with his back to the lamp, and his black silhouette reached to the ceiling. He spoke loudly:
“You, pierrot, are Erdosain; you, fat one, are the Gold Seeker; clown, you are the Pimp; and you, black man, are Alfon.
We are in agreement. ”
When his harangue was finished, he moved Barsut’s trunk away from the wall, placed it in front of the puppets and sat down before them.
And thus began a silent dialogue, whose questions came from him, receiving the answer inside himself when he fixed his gaze on the interrogated puppet.
His thought took on a surprising clarity.
He needed to express his ideas in a telegraphic, vibrant, interrupted system, as if all of him had to adjust the rhythm of thought to a mysterious vibration of enthusiasm. He thought:
“It is necessary to set up factories of asphyxiating gases.
Get a chemist.
Cells instead of automobiles, trucks.
Solid tires.
Colony in the cordillera, nonsense.
Or no.
Yes.
No. Also on the bank of the Paraná a factory.
Armored automobiles, chrome steel nickel.
Asphyxiating gases important.
In the cordillera and in the Chaco revolution will break out.
Wherever there are brothels, kill the owners.
Band of assassins in airplanes.
All feasible.
Each cell radiotelegraphs.
Code and wave changing synchronously.
Electric current with waterfall.
Swedish turbines.
Erdosain is right.
How great life is!
Who am I?
Factory of bubonic and exanthematic typhus bacilli.
Set up an academy of comparative studies of the French and Russian revolutions.
Also a school of revolutionary propaganda.
Cinematograph an important element.
Careful.
See cinematograph.
Erdosain should study the field.
Cinematograph applied to revolutionary propaganda.
That’s it. ”
Now the rhythm of thought moderated. He told himself:
“How to put into every conscience the revolutionary enthusiasm that is in mine?
That, that, that.
With what lie or truth?
How fast is the time that passes!
And how sad!
Because that is true.
There is so much sadness in me that if they knew it they would be astonished.
And I alone sustaining everything. ”
He curled up on the sofa.
He was cold.
The veins in his temples beat strongly.
“The time that escapes.
That.
That.
And all of them letting themselves lie fallen like sacks.
No one who wants to fly.
How to convince those donkeys that they have to fly?
And yet life is something else.
Something else they do not even conceive.
The soul like an ocean stirring inside seventy kilos of flesh.
And the very flesh that wants to fly.
Everything in us is desiring to rise to the clouds, to make the countries of the clouds real... but how?...
This ‘how’ always appears and I...
I here, suffering for them, loving them as if I had given birth to them, because I love these men...
I love them all.
They are on the earth just because, when they ought to be in another way.
And yet I love them.
I am feeling it now.
I love humanity.
I love them all as if all were tied to my heart with a fine thread.

And through that thread they carry away my blood, my life, and yet, in spite of everything, there is so much life in me that I would like there to be many millions more so I could love them even more and give them my life.
Yes, give it to them like a cigarette.
Now I understand Christ.
How he must have loved humanity!
And yet I am ugly.
My enormous broad face is ugly.
And yet I ought to be handsome, handsome as a god.
But my ear is like a cabbage and my nose like a tremendous bone fractured by a punch.
But what does that matter.
I am a man and that is enough.
And I need to conquer.
That is all.
And I would not give a single one of my thoughts in exchange for the love of the most beautiful woman. ”
Suddenly some earlier words cross his memory, and the Astrologer says to himself:
“Why not?...
We can manufacture cannons, as Erdosain says.
The procedure is easy.
Besides, it is not necessary that they withstand a thousand discharges.
A revolution that lasted that time would be a failure. ”
The words fall silent in him.

In the darkness a gloomy alley opens toward the interior of his skull, with beams crossing the space joining the sheds, while between a mist of coal dust the blast furnaces, with their cooling harnesses that feign monstrous armor, occupy the space.
Clouds of fire escape from the armored throats and the forest beyond stretches thick and impenetrable.
The Astrologer feels his personality recovered, which the sensation of the strange time had snatched from him.
He thinks, he thinks that it is possible to manufacture nickel steel and construct cannons of socketed tubes.
Why not?
His thought now slides over the obstacles with flexibility.
Then with the money supplied by the brothels plots of land would be bought at insignificant prices at various points of the Republic.
There the members of the lodge would lay the reinforced concrete bases to emplace the artillery pieces, simulating constructions of sheds for storing grain.
The possibility of creating a revolutionary army inside the country, which would rise at a radiotelephonic signal, exalted him.
Why not?
Steel, chrome, nickel.
Like a spell the word cleaves his imagination.
Steel, chrome, nickel.
Each cell leader would be in charge of a battery.
What is necessary, in short?
That the cannons fire five hundred, four hundred projectiles.
And the automobiles with machine guns.
Why not?
Every ten men a machine gun, an automobile, a cannon.
Why not try?
Slowly, in the depths of the black night, a gigantic egg of white-hot steel, between two columns, slowly bends its tip toward a dome.
It is the Bessemer converter operated by a hydraulic piston.
A torrent of sparks and burning flames escapes from the tip of the steel egg.
It is the iron that is converted into steel, agitated at the base by a jet of air of hundreds of atmospheres of pressure.
Steel, chrome, nickel.
Why not try?
His thought fixes on a hundred details.
Not long ago the inner voice had asked him:
“Why does human happiness occupy so little space? ”
This truth saddens his life.
The world ought to belong to a few.
And these few should walk with giant steps.
It is necessary to create complication for oneself.
And to see clearly.
First kill Barsut, then set up the brothel, the colony in the mountain... but how to make the corpse disappear?
Is it not stupid that he, the man who finds it easy to build a cannon and manufacture steel, chrome, nickel, should have so many doubts about making a corpse disappear?
It is true that he ought not to think... it will be burned... five hundred degrees are enough to destroy a corpse contained in a receptacle.
Five hundred degrees.
Time and fatigue run through his mind.
He would not like to think, and suddenly the voice, the voice independent of his mouth and his will, whispers from inside to distract him a little:
“The revolutionary movement will break out at the same hour in all the towns of the Republic.
We will assault the barracks.
We will begin by shooting all those who might cause a stir.
In the capital several kilograms of exanthematic typhus and bubonic plague will be released days before.
By means of airplanes and at night.
Each cell near the capital will cut the railway tracks.
We will let neither trains enter nor leave.
Once the head is dominated, the telegraph suppressed, the leaders shot, power is ours.
All this is a possible madness, and one always lives in an atmosphere of dream and as if in somnambulism when one is on the way to realizing things.
Yet one goes toward them with a slowness so rapid that everything is surprising when it has been achieved.
For that only will and money are necessary...
Apart from the cells we can organize a gang of assassins and raiders.
How many airplanes will the army have?
But with communications cut, barracks assaulted, leaders shot, who moves that mechanism?
This is a country of beasts.
One must shoot.
That is indispensable.
Only by sowing terror will they respect us.
Man is that cowardly.
A machine gun...
How will the forces that must fight us organize themselves?
Telegraph and telephone suppressed, rails cut...
Ten men can terrify a population of ten thousand people.
It is enough that they have a machine gun.
There are eleven million inhabitants.
The north, with the yerba mate plantations, would answer us.
Tucumán and Santiago del Estero, with the sugar mills...
San Juan, with the semi-communists...
We only have the army before us.
The barracks can be assaulted at night.
With the armory seized, the leaders shot and the sergeants hanged, with ten men we can take a barracks of a thousand soldiers provided we have a machine gun.
That is so easy.
And the hand grenades, where do I leave the hand grenades?
Only simultaneous surprise throughout the country, ten men per town and Argentina is ours.
The soldiers are young and will follow us.
We will promote the corporals to officers and we will have the most improbable red army that America has known.
Why not?
What is the assault on the San Martín bank, the assault on the Rawson hospital, the assault on the Martelli agency in Montevideo?
Three bold newsboys and a city is finished. ”
A dull rancor makes his veins beat hurriedly.
The blood runs in tumult through his sturdy body tense in an attitude of assault.
He feels stronger than ever, the strength of one who can have people shot.

The electric light oscillated beneath the sonorous discharges of the storm, but the Astrologer, seated with his back to the bed, on the trunk, legs crossed, chin driven into the palm of his hand and elbow resting on his knee, did not take his eyes from his five rag dolls whose ragged shadows trembled on the pinkish wall.

Behind him the rain that entered through the little window made a puddle on the floor; the questions and answers crossed in silence; at moments a wrinkle darkened the Astrologer’s forehead, then his motionless eyes, in his rhomboid face, assented with a slow blink to an answer in agreement with his desires, and thus he remained until dawn, the hour when, rising from the trunk, he ironically turned his back on the five dolls that remained in the solitude of the little room, swaying beneath the fanlight like five hanged men.
He pondered a moment, then hurriedly descended the stairs, left the doorway, and with long strides set off through the darkness toward the coach house where Barsut was.
It was no longer raining.
The clouds had cracked, revealing in a blue clearing a yellow piece of moon.
While these events were taking place in the Hospicio de las Mercedes, Ergueta was entering what he would later call “the knowledge of God.
” This is how it happened.
He awoke at dawn in the ward.
A parallelepiped of moonlight laid a blue rectangle on the whitewashed wall facing his bed.
Through the bars of the open window the sky appeared framed by the casement, a porous sky, dry blue like plaster dyed with methylene.
In the grid of the iron bars the watery threads of a star trembled.
Ergueta scratched his nose conscientiously, though he felt no great concern.
He understood that he was in the madhouse, but that “was a matter that did not concern him. ”

What worried him was whether they had imprisoned his spirit, yet the one who was truly locked up in the asylum was his body, his body that weighed ninety kilos and that now, with a certain inexplicable resentment, remembered how it had rolled through the brothels.
And without being able to stop himself he reviewed, like a shameful spectacle, the sensual life in which he had wallowed.
But what did his spirit have to do with such furious flesh?
This was a reality so evident to his understanding that he was astonished the doctors had not yet noticed the difference.
Ergueta felt amazed by his discovery.
He was no longer a man but a spirit, “pure sensation of soul,” with shores sharply outlined inside the butcher’s frame of his physique, like clouds in infinite space.
He felt slightly cheerful.
On previous nights he had already been certain he could detach himself from his body and leave it behind like a suit.
Upon discovering this, the sudden certainty gave him a light fear.

At certain moments he even had the sensation on his skin that he was touching himself only with the edges of his soul, so that the equilibrium of his body on the verge of falling, and of his own skin, made him nauseous.
It was as if he were descending at full speed in an elevator.
He was also afraid of having the will to abandon his body, because if they destroyed it, how could he re-enter it?
The orderly had the face of a scoundrel, and although he had spoken to him about some big bets for the next “meeting,” he did not feel entirely safe.

But once this first impression passed he took pleasure in believing he was a weak child, which did not prevent him from laughing in his bed at the comedy with which he tried to calm his ninety kilos, discounting the fact that he could go wherever he wished... but no... it was not a matter for joking.
His goodness could not allow that.
And how beautiful it was to feel oneself so filled with charity!
His mercy spread over the world like a cloud over the rooftops of the city.
His body remained farther and farther below.
Now he saw it as at the bottom of a drawer; the sanatorium among the white cubes of the houses was another cube; the streets turned bluish between sheets of shadow; the green lights of the F.C.
S. signals shone faintly, and space entered him like the ocean into a sponge, while time ceased to exist.
Heights fell through his delight.
Ergueta felt stillness, a stagnation of goodness toward himself, by the will of an external force.
Thus would a dry pond rejoice in the rain the sky sends it.
From the earth toward which his charity turned, he saw the rounded greenish edges licked by the blue ether.
And since it was not natural to remain silent, he could only manage to say:
“Thank you... thank you, my Lord. ”
He felt no curiosity whatsoever.
His humility grew stronger in obedience.
In the celestial smoothness he suddenly glimpsed the stepped formation of a rocky outcrop.
A golden light bathed the stones despite the night, and the blue in the distance fell into deep ravines of golden hills.
Ergueta, with his body restored, advanced with cautious steps, his fierce pupil rigid in his hawk-like profile.

Naturally he did not feel at ease, because his body had sinned countless times and because he understood that his face, despite its present grave expression, bore the energetic lines and the ferocity of the toughs he had imitated as a youth in the suburbs and with the gangs.
But his spirit was contrite and perhaps that would be enough, which did not prevent him from saying to himself:
“What will the Lord say about my ‘mug’?
How can I appear before him?
” And when he mechanically looked at his boots he saw they were dull, which increased his confusion.
“What will the Lord say about my ‘mug’ and this face of a racetrack tout and a pimp?

He will ask me about my sins... he will remember all the stupid things I did... and what am I going to answer him?... that I didn’t know, but how can I tell him that when he left testimony of his being in all his prophets? ”
Once more he examined his boots, dirty and battered.
“And he will say to me: ‘You’ve even turned into a lowlife... a shameful bum, and you who went to the university...

You gambled on the horses what could have been the consolation of the orphan and of life... and you dragged the immortal soul I gave you through orgies, and you dragged your guardian angel through the brothels and he wept behind you while your butcher’s mouth filled with abominations...’ And the worst is that I won’t be able to deny it...
How can I deny the sin?
What a mess, my God! ”
The sky above his head was a dome of blue plaster.
Remote planets spun in their ellipses like oranges, and Ergueta looked humbly at the golden scree.
Suddenly a great disturbance unsettled his modesty.
He raised his head and to his left, halted ten paces away, he saw the Son of Man.
The Nazarene, covered in a celestial tunic, turned toward him his emaciated profile where the serene almond-shaped eye shone.

Ergueta suffered a great desolation; he could not kneel, “because a gentleman always keeps his dignity” and does not kneel before a Jewish carpenter, yet he felt a sob twisting his soul and in silence he stretched out his arms, fingers joined, toward the silent god.
He felt his entire brazen face becoming impregnated with devotion toward him.
Thus, silent, he looked at Jesus halted on the rocky ground.
Ergueta’s eyes filled with tears.

He lamented that there was no one there with whom to strike himself in order to show the Lord how much he loved him, and already the silence seemed so unbearable that, overcoming the terrible annihilation, he humbly begged:
“I would like to be different, but I cannot. ”
Jesus looked at him.
“Believe me... it makes me feel strange to tell you that I love you very much. ”
Ergueta turned his back on him, walked three steps, then, turning again, stopped.
“I have committed all the sins and many stu... stupid things...
I would like to repent and I cannot...
I would like to kneel... it’s true, to kiss your feet, you who were crucified for us...
Ah! if only you knew all the things I wanted to say to you and that escape me... and yet I love you.
Could it be because we are man to man? ”
Jesus looked at him.
A new smile graced Jesus’s face.
Ergueta fell silent for a moment, then, blushing, murmured timidly:
“Oh! how good you are,” exclaimed Ergueta, enraptured.
“How good!
You have deigned to smile at me, a sinner...
Do you realize?
You have smiled.
Beside you, believe me, I feel like a boy, a ‘kid.’ I would like to adore you all my life, to be your bodyguard.
Now I will sin no more; all my life I will think of you, and woe to anyone who doubts you...
I’ll break his soul... ”
Jesus looked at him.
Then Ergueta, wishing to offer the best of himself, said:
“I kneel before you.

” He advanced a few steps and, reaching Jesus, bowed his head, placed one knee on the golden scree, and was about to prostrate himself when Jesus stretched out his pierced hand, laid it on his shoulder, and said:
“Come.
Follow me always and sin no more, for your soul is beautiful like those of the angels who praise the Lord. ”
He tried to speak, but already emptiness and silence whirled around him vertiginously.
Ergueta understood that he had entered the knowledge of God.
This was quite clear, because when he turned toward some voices sounding in the dark ward, a mute madman, mute from birth, exclaimed, looking at him with astonishment:
“It looks like you’re coming from heaven. ”
Ergueta looked at him, amazed.
“Yes, because, like the saints, you have a wheel of light around your head. ”
Ergueta, gently frightened, leaned against the wall.
A one-eyed madman, who until then had remained silent, exclaimed:
“Miracles... you work miracles.
You have given speech back to the world. ”
The conversation woke a third possessed man, who spent his days killing imaginary lice between his calloused, worn fingers, and the bearded one, turning his pale face, said:
“You have come to resurrect the dead... ”
“And to give sight to the blind,” interrupted the world.
“And also to the one-eyed,” assured the madman missing an eye, “because now I can see on this side.
” The mute, supporting his torso with both arms resting on the mattress, continued:
“But you are not you, but God who is in your body. ” Ergueta, annihilated, affirmed:
“It is true, brothers... it is not I... but God who is in me...
How could I, a miserable brothel-keeper, work miracles? ”
“Why don’t you work another miracle? ”
“I did not come for that, but to preach the word of the Living God.
” The louse-killer drew one foot up onto his knee and maliciously insisted:
“You ought to work a miracle.
” The mute placed his pillow on the floor of the ward and, sitting on top of it, said:
“I’m not speaking anymore. ”
Ergueta pressed his temples, stunned by what he saw. The one-eyed man meditated amiably:
“Yes, you ought to resurrect that dead man. ”
“But there is no dead man here! ”
The one-eyed man limped forward to Ergueta, took him by the arm and, almost dragging him, led him to a bed opposite where a little man with a round head and enormous nose lay motionless.
The world approached, lips compressed.
“Don’t you see he is dead? ”
“He died this afternoon,” grumbled the one-eyed man.

“I tell you that man is not dead,” exclaimed Ergueta, irritated, convinced the others were mocking him; but the louse-killer jumped from his bed, approached the other bed, bent over the little man with the round head and pushed the motionless body so hard that it fell with a dull thud on the floor of the ward, remaining between the two beds with its legs in the air, like the fork of a newly pruned tree.
“See?
He is dead. ”
The four madmen remained dismayed around the fork, framed by the blue rectangle of moonlight, their nightshirts swollen by the wind.
“See?
He is dead,” repeated the bearded one.
“Work a miracle,” begged the one-eyed man.
“How are we to believe in Him if you don’t work a miracle?
What does it cost you? ”
The world, suddenly bowing his head, made signs of acquiescence to Ergueta.

Gravely Ergueta bent over the corpse; he was about to pronounce the words of Life when suddenly the walls of the ward spun their cubic planes before his eyes, a dark wind howled in his ears and once more he had time to see the three madmen framed by the blue rectangle of moonlight, their nightshirts swollen by the wind, while he slid along a tangent that cut the whirling vortex of darkness, into unconsciousness.
Erdosain remained at the Hunchback’s feet for perhaps an hour.
The earlier emotions dissolved into his present drowsiness.
He felt alien to everything that had happened in the course of the day.
Anguish and malevolence hardened inside his chest like mud under the sun.
He remained motionless, however, subject to the power of the dark somnolence that emanated from his exhaustion.
Yet his forehead furrowed.
And through the mist and the darkness his other despair grew, the hopeless fear of seeing himself lost like a ghost on the edge of a granite pier.
The gray waters traced bands of different heights that ran in opposite directions.
Iron launches carried blurred figures toward remote emporiums.
There was also a woman there, primped like a cocotte, with a diamond chinstrap, leaning her elbows on the table of a tavern and pressing her cheeks between her jeweled fingers.
And while she spoke, Erdosain scratched the tip of his nose.

But since this attitude was not explainable, Erdosain remembered that four young girls had appeared, their dresses reaching to their knees and their yellow hair disheveled around their horselike faces.
And as the four girls passed beside him they held out a plate.
It was then that Erdosain asked himself: “Is it possible they can feed themselves by doing only that?

” Then the star, the cocotte, who had a dewlap of brilliants under her chin, answered that yes, the four girls lived by begging, and she began to speak of a Russian prince, in her most feminine voice, whose way of life, though she tried to match it, did not accord with that of the four girls.
And only then could Erdosain satisfactorily explain to himself why he had been scratching the tip of his nose while the precious woman spoke.
But his sadness deepened when he saw the silent people turn their heads and board the cars of a long train with all its blinds lowered.
No one asked about routes or stations.
Twenty paces away, a desert of dust stretched its dark boundary.
The locomotive could not be seen, but he did hear the painful grinding of the chains as the brakes were released.
He could run; the train was sliding slowly; he could catch it, climb the steps and remain a moment on the platform of the last car, watching the convoy gain speed.

Erdosain was still in time to leave that gray solitude without dark cities... but immobilized by his enormous anguish, he stayed there looking, with a sob caught in his throat, at the last car with its windows rigorously closed.

When he saw it enter the curve of the rails that the wall of fog covered, he understood that he had remained alone forever in the desert of ash, that the train would never return, that it would continue sliding forever in silence, with all the blinds of its cars strictly lowered.
Slowly he lifted his face from Hipólita’s knees.
It had stopped raining.
His legs were frozen; his joints ached.
He looked for an instant at the sleeping woman’s face, blurred in the bluish clarity that came through the windowpanes, and with extraordinary caution he stood up.
The four girls with horselike faces and frizzy yellow hair were still inside him. He thought:
“I ought to kill myself... –But upon observing the red hair of the sleeping woman, his ideas took a heavier turn–: She must be cruel.
And yet I could kill her –he gripped the butt of the revolver in his pocket–.
One shot in the skull would be enough.
The bullet is steel and would only make a tiny hole.
Of course, her eyes would pop out of their sockets and perhaps blood would run from her nose.
Poor soul!
And she must have suffered a great deal.
But she must be cruel. ”
A cautious malevolence bent him over her.
As he looked at the sleeping woman his eyes acquired the fixed stare of a madman, while with his hand in his pocket he cocked the hammer, squeezing the trigger.

A thunderclap rumbled in the distance, and that strange incoherence that enveloped his brain like a veil withdrew from him; then, with numerous precautions, he took his overcoat, closed the shutters without letting the hinges creak, and left.
As he went down the stairs he recognized with joy that he was hungry.
He headed toward one of the many grilled-meat restaurants near the Spineto market and hurriedly covered several blocks.

The moon rolled across the violet crest of a cloud; the sidewalks, here and there under the moonlight, seemed covered with sheets of zinc; the puddles sparkled with depths of dead silver, and with a swirling buzz the water ran, licking the granite curbs.
The roadway was so wet that the cobblestones looked soldered together by a recent casting of tin.
Erdosain entered and left the sky-blue shadows that cut the façades obliquely.
The smell of dampness gave the morning solitude a certain maritime desolation.
Undoubtedly he was not in his right mind.
The four girls with horselike faces and the sinister sea with its iron waves still preoccupied him.

The heavy stench of burnt oil vomited by the yellow door of a dairy made him nauseous, and then, changing his mind, he headed toward a brothel he remembered was on Paso Street; but when he arrived the door was already closed and, disconcerted, shivering with cold, his mouth tasting of copper sulfate, he entered a café where they had just raised the metal shutters.
After a long wait they served him the tea he had ordered.
He thought of the sleeping woman.
He half-closed his eyes, leaned his head against the wall, and surrendered to his sorrows with greater desolation.

He was not suffering for himself, the man registered with a name in the civil registry, but rather his conscience, detaching itself from his body, looked at him as if he were a stranger and said to itself:
“Who will have pity on this man? ”
And these words, which his thought managed to gather, disturbed him, filling him with painful tenderness for invisible fellow beings.
“To fall... to fall always lower.
And yet other men are happy, they find love, but all suffer.
What happens is that some realize it and others do not.
Some attribute it to what they lack.
But what a stupid dream that is.
Still, her face was pretty.
What was logical was what she said about the adventurer prince.
Ah! to be able to sleep at the bottom of the sea, in a lead room with thick glass.
To sleep years and years while the sand piles up, and to sleep.
That’s why the Astrologer is right.
The day will come when people will make the revolution because they lack a God.
Men will declare themselves on strike until God appears. ”

A bitter smell of cyanide reached him; and perceiving through his eyelids the milky clarity of morning, he felt himself diluted as if he were at the bottom of the sea and the sand were rising indefinitely over his little lead hut.
Someone touched his shoulder.
He opened his eyes at the same moment the café waiter told him:
“You can’t sleep here. ”
He was about to reply, but the servant moved away to wake another sleeper.
This one was a fat man who had let his bald head fall onto his arms crossed on the table.

But the sleeper did not respond to the waiter’s calls, and then, surprised, the owner approached, a man with mustaches as enormous as bicycle handlebars, and shook his customer so hard that the man remained doubled over the chair, not falling only because the edge of the table held him.
Erdosain stood up, astonished, while owner and waiter, looking at each other, observed the singular customer out of the corner of their eyes.
The sleeper remained in an absurd position.
His head fallen on one shoulder revealed his flat, pockmarked face with the black circles of smoked glasses.
A thread of reddish drool stained his green tie, escaping from between bluish lips.
The stranger’s elbow pressed a sheet of written paper on the table.
They understood that he was dead.
They called the police, but Erdosain did not move from there, intrigued by the spectacle of the sinister suicide with the black glasses, whose skin was slowly becoming covered with blue spots.
And the smell of bitter almonds that hung motionless in the air seemed to escape from between the open jaws.
A police assistant arrived, then a sergeant, later two constables and an inspector, and these people prowled around the dead man as if he were a steer.
Suddenly the assistant, addressing the inspector, said:
“Don’t you know who he is? ”
The sergeant took from the corpse’s pocket a hotel bill, several coins, a revolver, three sealed letters.
“So this is the one who killed the girl on Talcahuano Street? ”
They removed the dead man’s glasses, and now his eyes could be seen, the pupils squinting, the cornea turned upward, the eyelids tinged red as if he had wept tears of blood.
“Didn’t I tell you?
” the assistant continued.
“Here is his identity card. ”
“He was going to Ushuaia for life. ”
Then Erdosain, upon hearing these words, remembered as if he had read it a long time ago.
(And yet it was not so.
The previous morning he had learned of it in a newspaper.) The dead man was a swindler.

He had abandoned his wife and five children to live in concubinage with another woman by whom he had three children, but two nights earlier, perhaps tired of his concubine, he had appeared at a hotel on Talcahuano Street in the company of a seventeen-year-old girl, his new lover.
And at three in the morning he had gently covered her head with a pillow and fired a shot into her ear.
No one in the hotel heard anything.
At eight in the morning the murderer dressed, left the door ajar, and calling the chambermaid told her not to wake the lady until ten because she was very tired.
Then he left, and only at noon was the dead girl discovered.

But what impressed Erdosain extraordinarily was to think that the murderer had spent five hours with the dead girl, five hours beside the corpse of the young woman in the solitude of the night... and that he must have loved her very much.
Yet had he not thought the same thing hours earlier in front of the red-haired woman?
Was that an unconscious reminiscence or the suicide doubled over there?...
The Public Assistance wagon arrived and the dead man was loaded.
Then they questioned him.
Erdosain stated the little he knew as a witness and went out into the street, intrigued.
A vague and painful question lay at the bottom of his consciousness.
He remembered now that the corpse had mud on the cuffs of his trousers, a dirty and damp shirt and, in spite of that, how had he managed to make the young girl he killed love him?
Did love exist then?
In spite of his two women and his eight scattered children and his dissolute life as a thief and swindler, the murderer loved.

And he imagined him in the sullen night, there, in that hotel frequented by prostitutes and individuals of undefined profession, in a room with torn wallpaper, looking at the waxen little face of the cooled girl on the blood-soaked pillow.
Five somber hours contemplating the dead woman who before had pressed him between her naked arms.
Thinking thus he reached Plaza Once, painfully stupefied.
It was five in the morning.
He entered the railway station, looked around, and since he was sleepy he took refuge in a corner of the waiting room.
At eight the noise a passenger made with his suitcases woke him from his deep sleep.
He rubbed his sore eyelids with his fists.
In a cloudless sky the sun was shining.
He went out and boarded a bus heading for Constitución.
The Astrologer was waiting for him at the Temperley station.
His robust figure in a gabardine coat, with the top hat pulled down over his eyes and his enormous mustaches drooping in Gallic fashion, was immediately spotted by Erdosain.
“You look very pale,” said the Astrologer.
“Am I pale? ”
“Yellow. ”
“I slept badly... and to make it worse I saw a suicide this morning... ”
“Well, here is the check. ”
Erdosain examined it.
It was for fifteen thousand three hundred and seventy-three pesos, to bearer, but dated two days earlier.
“Why did you backdate it? ”
“It will inspire more confidence.
The bank clerk knows that if that check had been lost, by the time you presented it for payment there would already be a stop-payment order. ”
“Did he protest?... ”
“No... he was smiling.
That man thinks he’s going to put us all in jail...
Ah!... before going to the bank, go to a barbershop and get a shave... ”
“And has the other one been warned? ”
“No, when the moment comes we’ll wake him. ”
There were only a few minutes left before the train arrived.
Erdosain looked at the Astrologer, smiling, and said:
“What would you do if I ran away with it?
” The other, with his fingers forked, stroked his mustaches, and then:
“That is as impossible as that the train coming here will not stop here. ”
“But let’s suppose it for a moment. ”
“I cannot.
If for a moment I admitted that, you would not be the one going to cash the check...
Who was the one who committed suicide this morning? ”
“A murderer.
Curious.
He killed a little girl who didn’t want to live with him. ”
Wasted strength.
“And would you be capable of killing yourself? ”
You understand that I am destined for a higher end. ” Erdosain asked a strange question:
“Tell me, do you believe redheads are cruel? ”
“Not so much... but rather asexual; hence that coldness with which they examine things produces a sour impression.
The Melancholy Pimp used to tell me that in his long career as a pimp he had known very few redheaded prostitutes...
You know.
Don’t forget to shave.
Go to the bank at eleven, not before.
You’re having lunch with me today, aren’t you? ”
Yes, see you later.
Behind Erdosain the Major boarded, who made a friendly sign to the Astrologer.
Erdosain did not see him.
And already sunk in his seat, Erdosain thought:
“He is an extraordinary man.
How the devil did he know I won’t deceive him?
If he is right about the other things as he is about this, he will triumph –and overcome by the swaying of the train he dozed off again.
Behind him was the Major.
And already at the bank, with his heart pounding violently, he approached the window when the paying teller called him:
“Do you want it in large or small bills? ”
“Large. ”
“Sign. ”
Erdosain signed the back of the check.

He thought they would ask for identification, but the clerk, impassive, with his arms protected by black-lustring sleeve protectors, counted ten thousand-peso bills, five five-hundreds and the rest in smaller currency.

And although Erdosain wanted to flee out of fear, he scrupulously recounted the money, put it in his wallet, placed the wallet in his trouser pocket, gripping it tightly, and went out into the street.
Among forests of white clouds appeared, like freshly washed metal, a snail shell of sky.
Erdosain felt happy.

He thought that in other climates and under a space always blue like the one he was looking at there must exist singular women, with luxurious manes and smooth faces, with large almond eyes, shadowy in the darkness of their long lashes.

And that the always perfumed air would issue from the grottoes of morning toward the street corners of cities stepped upon lawns of gardens, surpassing with their spherical towers the plumed crests of parks and terraces.

And the rhomboidal face of the Astrologer, with the points of his mustaches drooping along the corners of his lips, and his cab-driver top hat, enthused him; then he thought that united with the society he could continue his electrotechnical experiments, and now he crossed the streets like an emperor fallen on hard times, without noticing that his bearing seduced the ironing women who passed with baskets under their arms, and moved the trouser-makers who returned from the shops with heavy bundles.

He would invent the Death Ray, a sinister violet lightning whose millions of amperes would melt the steel of dreadnoughts as a furnace melts a drop of wax, and would blow the Portland cities into fragments as if volcanoes of trinitrotoluene were heaving them up.
He saw himself transformed into Master of the Universe.
With a peremptory note he summoned the Ambassadors of the Powers.
He found himself in an enormous hall with glass walls, whose center was occupied by a round table.
Seated in armchairs around it were the old diplomats, bald heads, leaden countenances, hard and furtive glances.

Some tapped the glass tabletop with the back of a pencil, others smoked in silence, and a gigantic Negro in green livery stood motionless beside the red velvet of the curtains that covered the entrance.
And he!
Erdosain, Augusto Remo Erdosain, the former thief, the former collector, rose.
His bust modeled by a black double-breasted jacket was reflected in the glass of the table with the four fingers of his right hand tucked in his pocket, and in his left a few papers.
Already on his feet, he examined with glacial eyes the impassive faces of the Ambassadors.
A terrible pallor immobilized him with its delicious cold.
Heroes of all epochs survived in him.

Ulysses, Demetrius, Hannibal, Loyola, Napoleon, Lenin, Mussolini, passed before his eyes like great burning wheels and were lost on a slope of the solitary earth beneath a twilight that was no longer terrestrial.
His words fell in short sounds, with solid clashes of steel.
And seduced by the theatricality of the spectacle, he contemplated himself in an imaginary mirror, trembling and angry.
He imposed conditions.
The States must hand over their war fleets, thousands of cannons and bundles of rifles.
Then from each race a few hundred men would be selected, isolated on an island, and the rest of humanity destroyed.
The Ray would blow up cities, sterilize fields, turn races and forests into ashes.
The memory of all science, all art and beauty would be lost forever.
An aristocracy of cynics, bandits oversaturated with civilization and skepticism, would seize power, with him at its head.

And since man, in order to be happy, needs to rest his hopes on a metaphysical lie, they would strengthen the clergy, establish an inquisition to cut off every heresy that undermined the foundations of dogma or the unity of belief that would be the absolute unity of human happiness, and man, restored to the primitive state of society, would devote himself as in the times of the pharaohs to agricultural tasks.
The metaphysical lie would restore to man the happiness that knowledge had dried in the bud within his heart.
His words fell with short, dry sounds, like the clashes of steel cubes. And he said to the Ambassadors:
“Our city, the city of us Kings, will be of white marble and will stand on the shore of the sea.
It will have a diameter of seven leagues and domes of rose copper, lakes and forests.
There the professional saints will live, the rascally patriarchs, the fraudulent magicians, the apocryphal goddesses.
All science will be magic.
The doctors will go along the roads disguised as angels, and when men multiply too much, in punishment for their crimes, luminous flying dragons will scatter cholera vibrios through the air.
“Man will live in a full stage of miracle, and will be a millionaire of faith.
During the nights we will project on the clouds, with powerful searchlights, the ‘Entrance of the Just into Heaven.’ Can you imagine it?
Suddenly, above the mountains surges a green and lilac ray, and the clouds become covered with a garden where white air floats like snowflakes.
An angel with rose-colored wings crosses the flowerbeds, stops before the gate of Paradise, and with open arms receives the ‘Just,’ a man of the people, with a dented hat, long beard and club.
Do you understand, you scoundrels, professionals, cynics and eminent ones?
Do you understand?
The angel with rose-colored wings receives the man who on earth sweats and suffers.
Do you realize how genial my idea is, how marvelous the easy miracle?
And the multitudes will adore God on their knees, and only the sky will not exist for us, sad bandits who possess power, science and useless truth. ”
He trembled as he spoke.
“We shall be like gods.

We shall bestow upon men stupendous miracles, delicious beauties, divine lies; we shall give them the conviction of a future so extraordinary that all the promises of the priests will be pale before the reality of the apocryphal prodigy.
And then they will be happy...
Do you understand, imbeciles? ”
A porter bumped into him and threw him against a wall.

Erdosain stopped, horrified, clutched the money convulsively in his pocket, and excited, ferociously joyful like a little tiger released in a forest of brick, spat at the façade of a fashion house, saying:
“You shall be ours, city. ”
Behind him walked the Major.
The Astrologer was waiting for him in Temperley.
A smile full of kindness lit up his face.
Erdosain almost ran to meet him, but the other man, taking him by the arms, held him for a moment while looking into his eyes.
Then, addressing him with the familiar *tú*—something he had never done before—he said:
“Are you happy? ”
Erdosain blushed.
In that instant a double mystery was revealed in his consciousness.

This man was not lying, and he felt such friendship toward him that he would have liked to talk with him indefinitely, to tell him the most intimate details of his wretched life; yet all he managed to say was:
“Yes, I’m very happy. ”
The Astrologer paused for a moment on the station platform.
Now he addressed him with the formal *usted* as usual.
“You know, many of us carry a superman inside.
The superman is the will at its maximum power, rising above all moral norms and carrying out the most terrible acts as a kind of naïve joy... something like the innocent game of cruelty. ”
“Yes, and then one no longer feels fear or anguish; it’s as if one were walking on the clouds. ”
“Of course.
The ideal would be to awaken this jovial, naïve ferocity in many men.
It falls to us to inaugurate the era of the Innocent Monster.
Everything will be done, without a doubt.
It’s a matter of time and daring.
But when people realize that their spirit is sinking into the latrine of this civilization, before they drown they will twist away from the path.
The trouble is that man has not noticed he is sick with cowardice and Christianity. ”
“But didn’t you want to Christianize humanity? ”
“Not the herd... but if that project fails we’ll take the opposite road.
We haven’t yet adopted any principle, and the practical thing will be to monopolize the most opposing principles.
Like in a pharmacy, we’ll have perfect and varied lies, labeled for the most fantastic diseases of the mind and the soul. ”
“You know, you strike me as the madman from the factory, just as Barsut told me yesterday. ”
“What we call madness is simply thinking differently from other people.
Look, if that porter were to confess the ideas that occur to him, you’d lock him up in an asylum.
Naturally there can’t be many like us... the essential thing is that our actions give us vitality and energy.
There lies salvation. ”
“And Barsut? ”
“He doesn’t even suspect what’s waiting for him. ”
“And how will you get rid of him? ”
“Bromberg will strangle him...
I don’t know, it’s a matter that doesn’t concern me. ”
Under the sun, avoiding the puddles, they set off toward the house. And Erdosain said to himself:
“And our city, the city of the Kings, will be of white marble and will stand on the shore of the sea... and we shall be like gods.
” And looking at his companion with shining eyes, he said:
“You know that one day we shall be like gods? ”
“That’s what the brutish people don’t understand.
They have murdered the gods.
But the day will come when, under the sun, they will run along the roads shouting: ‘We want God, we need God.’ What savages!
I can’t understand how they could have murdered God.
But we shall resurrect Him... we shall invent beautiful gods... supercivilized ones... and then what will life be! ”
“And if everything fails? ”
“It doesn’t matter... another will come... another who will replace me.
That’s how it must be.
The only thing we should wish for is that the idea germinate in imaginations... the day it lives in many souls, beautiful things will happen. ”
Erdosain was astonished at his own serenity.

He no longer feared anything, and once again he remembered the Hall of Ambassadors, and his malevolent gaze settled on the unease of the old diplomats—bald heads, leaden faces, hard and furtive glances—and then, unable to contain himself, he exclaimed:
“What a lot of ‘fucking around’ just to wring that beast’s neck! ”
The other man looked at him in surprise.
“Are you nervous, or do you get angry all by yourself, like elephants? ”
“No, this old burden of scruples disgusts me. ”
“That’s how young men are,” replied the Astrologer.
“Their lives are like a cat caught between a half-open door. ”
“Will I attend the execution? ”
“Does it interest you? ”
“Very much. ”
But as they crossed the gate of the quinta, a nausea churned his stomach and he felt in his throat the gastric reflex of vomiting.
He could barely stand.
In his eyes, shapes were veiled by a milky mist.
His arms hung from their joints with the heaviness of bronze limbs.
He walked without any sense of distance; the air seemed to vitrify, the ground undulated beneath his feet; at times the vertical of the trees turned into a zigzag inside his eyes.
He breathed with difficulty, his tongue was dry, and he tried in vain to moisten his parched lips and burning throat; only a sense of shame kept him on his feet.
When he half-opened his eyes he was descending the little staircase of the coach house in the company of Bromberg.
The Man Who Had Seen the Midwife walked as if stunned, his shaggy hair disheveled.
His trousers were held up superfluously by the waistband, and a piece of white shirt, like the corner of a handkerchief, escaped from his fly.
He covered his mouth with his fist, letting out enormous yawns.
Yet his sleepy, wandering gaze seemed alien to his loutish attitude.
His eyes were beautiful, serious and incoherent like those of great beasts, between heavy-lidded lashes that shaded the circles under his eyes in a round, delicate maiden’s face.
Erdosain looked at him, but the other seemed not to see him, submerged in his magnificent incoherence.
Then he stared vacantly at the Astrologer; the latter gave him a nod, and after opening the padlock the three of them entered the stable.
Barsut leaped up: he was about to speak.
Bromberg described a curve in the air and the crash of a skull against the boards echoed through the coach house.
In the dust the sun stretched out a yellow lozenge.
From the shapeless heap came muffled snores.

Erdosain followed the struggle with cruel curiosity, and suddenly Bromberg’s trousers, which had been bunched up over Barsut with the two enormous arms tense in the grip of a neck pressed to the floor, slipped down, leaving his white buttocks exposed and his shirt up around his kidneys.
And the muffled snoring ceased.
There was a moment of silence while the half-naked killer, motionless, pressed the dead man’s throat even harder.
Erdosain simply watched.
The Astrologer waited with his watch in his hand.
Thus they remained for two minutes that had no length for Erdosain.
“Enough.
It’s done. ”
Clumsy, with hair stuck to his forehead, Bromberg turned, and without fixing his incoherent gaze on anyone, blushing, he seized the waistband of his trousers and buttoned them hastily.
The killer had left the coach house.
Erdosain followed him, and the Astrologer, who was last, turned to look at the strangled man.
The latter lay on the floor, head turned toward the ceiling, jaws slack and tongue pressed against the apex of lips twisted in a corner that revealed his teeth.
At that moment a strange thing happened, of which Erdosain took no notice.

The Astrologer, pausing beneath the lintel of the coach house, turned his face toward the dead man; then Barsut, shrugging his shoulders up to his ears, stretched his neck and, looking at the Astrologer, winked one eyelid.
The Astrologer touched the brim of his hat with his index finger and went out to join Erdosain, who, unable to contain himself, exclaimed:
“And that’s all? ”
The Astrologer raised a mocking glance toward him.
“Did you think ‘that’ was like in the theater? ”
“And how are you going to make him disappear? ”
“By dissolving him in nitric acid.
I have three demijohns.
But, while we’re on the subject, do you have news of the copper rose? ”
“Yes, it turned out perfectly.
The Espilas are delighted.
Last night I saw a very good sample. ”
“Good.
We’ll have lunch... we’ve certainly earned it. ”
But as they were about to enter the dining room, the Astrologer said:
“What... aren’t we going to wash our hands? ”
Erdosain looked at him in surprise and instinctively raised his hands to where the lapels of his jacket crossed in order to look at them.
Then, hurriedly and in silence, they headed for the bathroom, took off their jackets, and turned on the taps.
Erdosain picked up a bar of soap and, sleeves rolled up to the elbows, rubbed himself conscientiously.
Then he put his arms under the stream of water and dried them vigorously on the towel.
But before leaving, the Astrologer performed a strange act.

Taking the towel, he threw it into the bottom of the bathtub, picked up a bottle of alcohol, poured its contents over it, then struck a match, and for a minute the two faces in the darkened room were illuminated by the bluish flames of the flammable liquid consuming the fabric.
Afterward all that remained was a blackish deposit of ashes.
The Astrologer opened a tap; once more the water ran, carrying away the light carbonization, and then both men left for the dining room.
An ironic smile played across Erdosain’s face.
“So you’ve done like Pilate, eh? ”
“You’re right.
Unconsciously. ”
In the shady dining room the half-open blinds revealed the garden.
Tender honeysuckle stems climbed up to the wooden frame.
Transparent insects glided through the air beside the lemon tree, and the white walls were reflected in the golden opacity of the waxed floor.
The fringes of the tablecloth fell around the square legs of the table.

In an Etruscan vase a bunch of carnations scattered its peppery fragrance, and the silver cutlery shone on the linen and on the porcelain; shadows curled like ringlets on the glassy convexity of the goblets or spread in triangular bands across the plates.
On an oval platter lay a mayonnaise of prawns.
The Astrologer poured wine.
They ate in silence.
Then the Astrologer brought a yellow broth of egg yolks, a dish of asparagus swimming in oil, artichoke salad, and later fish.
For dessert there was ricotta sprinkled with cinnamon and fruit.
Afterward he served coffee, and Erdosain handed him the money. The Astrologer counted it:
“Here are three thousand five hundred.
Have several suits made.
You’re a good-looking fellow and it’s advisable that you dress elegantly. ”
“Thank you very much... but listen...
I’m dead tired.
I’m going to sleep for a while.
Will you wake me at five? ”
“Of course.
Come.
” And the Astrologer accompanied him to his bedroom.
Erdosain took off his boots, already exhausted, and threw his jacket over the headboard of the bed.
An enormous burning stung his eyelids, thick sweat covered his chest, and he thought no more.
He awoke when it was already dark, to the sound of the Astrologer opening a blind.
He sat up with a start while the other man told him:
“Finally!
You’ve been sleeping for twenty-eight hours.
” And as he expressed doubt, the Astrologer handed him the day’s newspapers, and indeed two days had passed.
Erdosain jumped out of bed thinking of Hipólita.
“I must go. ”
“You were sleeping like a dead man.
I’ve never seen anyone sleep like that, with such exhaustion, even forgetting natural needs... but, by the way, where did you get that story about the suicide in the café?
I’ve seen yesterday evening’s and this morning’s papers.
None of them carries that news.
You must have dreamed it. ”
“Still, I can show you the café. ”
“Then you dreamed it in the café. ”
“Maybe... it doesn’t matter... and that other matter? ”
“It’s done. ”
“Everything? ”
“Everything. ”
“And the acid? ”
“We’ll pour it down the drain. ”
“So then it’s as if...? ”
“As if he had never existed. ”
When he took leave of the Astrologer, the latter said to him:
“Come on Wednesday at five.
We’ll have a meeting at night.
Don’t forget to buy yourself a ready-made suit while the others are being made.
